en: Even for the cakravāka birds, whose minds are purified by the desire to serve Your lotus feet, intuitive wisdom (*prātibha*) immediately shines forth as they discern the separation of milk and water;
[a wisdom] which is like the moon to the mass of the most intense darkness consisting of unrestrained ignorance.
I bow to that Goddess Śāradā, the root of bliss, who is as radiant as the moonstone.
May this side-glance of Kālikā, possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal, produce an abundance of contentment for those who offer their salutations—
she who reveals upon the body of Purāri, which has the brilliance of the inner leaf of a ketaka flower, the inscription of the praise of the five-arrowed god of love.
Triumphant are the eloquent verses of the great poets— verses as tender as the sprouts of fresh lotus stalks, as pure as the shimmering rays of the moon, and the sole abode of the essence of nectar.
[3] From the waters of the shimmering rays of the clusters of jewels upon the crowns of gods and demons...
He who, with the tender sprouts of his radiance— like a constant sprinkling upon the roots of his feet—
ever provided consolation through compassion to the herd of bewildered deer, became the Sage Vatsa, purifying the earth by the placement of his holy footsteps.
In his lineage was born Dādā, lord of a multitude of elephants, who was ever the primary source of gifts;
by whose prowess in battle the army of King Vijjaṇa fell into a state of wretchedness upon being beheld. To him were born four sons, distinguished by their statesmanship.
Constantly adorned with the glory of their prowess, they shone like the arms of Hari;
they appeared like the Vedas issuing from the mouths of the four-faced Brahmā.
They were known as Mahīdhara, Jalha, Sāmba, and Gaṅgādhara.
Through those four well-employed means, as it were, at the proper time,
the kingdom of King Maulugī became perpetually exalted.
He, having churned the ocean of the Vijjaṇabala army with his mountain-like arm as the Mandara churning-stick, [attained sovereignty].
To whom was that mountain not praiseworthy, with the glory of a hero seated upon his lap?
What wonder is it if Ananta, the lord of serpents, became his son?
Having brought the nāgas dwelling in the abode of Bali, he restored them to their own master.
When the mountain-king had conquered Bijjana and departed for the world of the gods,
Jajha led the Bhillas to a sovereignty free from decay.
By him, on the mountain peak of Dhūrjara— which was rugged with thorns and exceedingly difficult to traverse— [the kingdom was established].
The wicked elephant was led away at will by Bhagadatta, who possessed the fame of [Indra];

Mailugi, the wrestler, caused great terror with his swelling thighs; Muñja made the enemy forces tremble on all sides; and the Brahmin was indeed the Brahmā of the three worlds, whose prowess limped [with grace].
Indeed, even now he performs the task of seizing the hopes of the elephants of the quarters;
for I suspect that the Lord of the Gods, terrified by his valor, restrains his own elephant in the hollows of the forest at the appointed place of rendezvous, as he repeatedly remembers him. 13.

Even today, when they see the headless trunks of enemy kings dancing, the intoxicated female Vetālas— adorned with pearls smeared with the blood from the tusks of slaughtered elephants and holding skull-bowls in their hands— strike the rhythm of the *tāla*.
He had a brother named Gaṅgādhara, who was like the god Gaṅgādhara (Śiva) himself.
He bound some serpents and released others at his own will;
he formed no attachment with wicked double-tongued ones and never bore a fool upon his head.
He burned away desire when provoked by people, yet he remained the very bearer of the Gaṅgā.
He had a son named Janārdana, possessed of undiminished courage and the lord of a multitude of elephants;
like the ocean, he bore this entire world together with its wondrous prosperity. Though born into a family of the wise, he was abandoned for even a moment by all the learned.
That which has never once been forgotten by the virtuous, nor is it ever practiced by the wicked;
even for such great poverty, no one has ever extended a helping hand as it fell into the flowing stream of the river of charity. 18.
By him, even Siṃha was taught that wonderful elephant-training,
by which he uprooted Arjuna— along with his shining leaves and his very roots.
He was devoted to the protection of the world, and the multitude of supplicants before him was honored with shimmering, great golden gifts.
From him was born the wise Śrī Lakṣmadeva of wondrous valor, who,

having conquered through mantras the ministers of the gods whose intellects were headed by Bṛhaspati, established the kingdom of King Kṛṣṇa as firm and unimpaired by means of ever-vigilant political strategies. 20.
Like Agastya, whose sword shone as it bent down the kings,
he too made the ocean of battle strange by causing headless trunks to dance.
Through the guise of pomegranates bursting from ripeness, the beauty of a garden was fashioned there.
With its manifold activities, it seems to laugh at the Nandana grove, as if revealing its teeth;
with its formidable matted locks of tangled trees, its shimmering streams, and its adornment by the blue-throated peacock, that garden shines like the head of Lord Śiva. (22-23)
"Ah, its saltiness has been entirely cast off; that nectarine sweetness, so naturally beautiful, has been swiftly assumed as its primary quality.
Thus the Lord of Rivers, his former appearance vanished, has gone to another land."

Because of fear of Agastya, it is conjectured by the people that this is a tank; yet, O Ocean of Policy, you have a son named Śrī Jalhaṇa on this earth—he who is a friend to the wise, highly intelligent, and skilled in discerning between the essential and the non-essential. || 24 ||
From the ocean of his fame— which flows like rivers of water from the clouds of his generosity— there has arisen another moon, ever-risen and intense, that brilliantly whitens the worlds;
it was bestowed upon him by my father, its afflictions from the host of powerful enemies having been repelled.
To King Kṛṣṇa, whose virtues were celebrated through his vast power, [the king] offered the kingdom with devotion; and he,

the devoted younger brother, whose intellect, strength, and devotion were doubled by the thought "I must carry this out," performed every task for his master with a heart captivated by right policy and a spirit of service.
It is certain that he possesses in his lotus-hand a troop of elephants blinded by rut;
otherwise, how could the stream of ichor-beings' gift-water be seen here?
For the entire sphere of Brahman is strung together by his infinite, pure virtues.
It provides the playful charm of a sport ball for the maiden Fame.
Shall we speak of the unfathomable depth of this ocean of the sword, wherein hundreds of enemy armies, once submerged, are no longer seen? (28-29)
With crushed black gram, pieces of fresh ginger, and powdered rock salt,
that which serves as food for Death in battle is rendered by the edge of his sword in the kitchen.
It causes the circle of the earth to sink, the mountains to tremble, and all the oceans to be agitated.

How could that day of the victorious expedition not be known— the day when the onset of rain was initiated by the tears from the eyes of the trembling wives of the enemies, and the path of the sun was shrouded by the mass of dust shaken up by the hooves of the surging lines of horses?
That day when the celestial beauties, filled with longing, [gazed upon] the enemy heroes whose limbs were mangled by sword-blades...
In the battle, the mass of dust appears like a scattered powder for subjugation.
For a moment, his mind is filled with agitation manifested by the passion for the forest;
for a moment, his heart is drawn away by the cries of flocks of birds upon the laps of the *śāla* trees.
For a moment, his hair stood on end at the sound of the leaf-fall; then, out of sheer terror,
the enemy entered the forest as if he were the king himself, while those who were once supported by him—
now rendered as insignificant as straw by the wretchedness of their begging— were left without refuge.
Those multitudes of suppliants who were carried away from every house by the wind of poverty—
by him their excessive weight was so counteracted through the offering of high heaps of gold that even now they bear the likeness of mountains with their variegated ridges.
This is surely some other Kalpa-tree shining upon the surface of the earth,
since even a single sprout-like hand of his renders the celestial tree inferior;
for by his fame, the Sahya mountain and Mount Mandara have been made white throughout the three worlds.
On Mount Vindhya and on the golden mountain Harakṣitidhara, no other form shines; for if he,
while bestowing gold upon those who seek it, had not freely distributed it throughout the world, how indeed would the Golden Mountain have become so renowned and exalted?
Therefore, having observed various collections of sublime sayings,
this *Sūktimuktāvalī* (String of Pearls of Elegant Sayings) is composed as an ornament for the neck-lotuses of the virtuous.
It consists of many verses compiled by wise men who understand how to arrange them.
Although there are well-spoken verses that resemble the essence of nectar,
nevertheless, having reduced the mountain of pride to a mere hillock,
why do the wise still constantly look upon this envy even toward virtues?
If you wish to easily understand the heart of the science of literature,
then behold this *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Jalhaṇa.
It is not by finger-rings, nor by armlets, nor by necklaces, nor by bracelets [that one attains it].
It shines forth just as it does when held by the learned man at his throat.
These [verses] belong to Śrī Vaidyabhānu Paṇḍita;
first comes the salutation, followed by words of benediction.

Then follows the praise of well-spoken words and the eulogy of poets and their poetry (42). Next is the censure of bad poets, followed by [the praise of] those with noble minds and the description of the wicked. Then comes the path of the miserly, and finally the two-fold path of *anyokti* (indirect or allegorical expressions) (43).
The divisions of sky-dwellers (*khecara*) and land-dwellers (*bhūcārin*) were established; among them, first was the Sun.
Among the sky-dwellers followed the Moon, the wind, and the clouds, and then the birds.
Among those [birds], first was the cuckoo, then the swan, the peacock, the crow, the crane, and so forth.
Then the firefly and the cātaka bird were mentioned as the sky-dwellers;
among those who move on the earth, the lion was first, followed by the track of the elephant,
and then separately the tracks of the donkey, the bull, and the deer.

The description of miscellaneous objects— such as the ocean, gems, conch shells, rivers, lakes, lotuses, trees, and mountain peaks— is called *anyokti* (indirect expression), which is of two kinds. Furthermore, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) consists first of the erotic of separation (*vipralambha*) and subsequently the erotic of union (*sambhoga*).
In that regard, separation begins first with the longing for union with the beloved; this is the state of passion arising among women.

(48) Then there are the questions of female friends, the various lamentations of those separated from their lovers, the dispatching of a messenger, the state of muttering prayers born of love, and the lamentations of the separated man as well. (49)
The beloved messenger’s words; the message of the separated lover to his dearest;
the description of her state of separation; the messenger’s inquiry after the beloved;
the messenger’s jesting; and thereafter, the words spoken upon seeing the lover. 50.
Childhood, the transition of age, and youth—the description of all the limbs in sequence;

[then] the state of the proud woman regarding honor, followed by the heroine's reception of the guest, the conciliation by the female friend, and subsequently the utterances and counter-utterances. 51–52.
Then there is clarity, enjoyment, the seasons, and the gathering of flowers;
thereafter, play with balls and water, and the setting of the sun;
and finally, the amorous chatter of lovers at the beginning of their secret trysts.
The rising of the moon; drinking parties; beyond that, the lover’s endearments;
praise of sexual union during lovemaking; the company of a young bride; the words of a female friend;
amorous play with a new bride; and the reversal of roles in love-making. 54–55.

The cessation of lovemaking at its outset, a quarrel, and the heroine’s subsequent conciliation; then the dawn and the breeze that accompanies it. (56) Following this is the lamentation of the woman separated by a quarrel, and the instruction of the hero.
The manifestation of enjoyment, the unchaste woman, and the "mixed" (*saṃkīrṇa*)—these constitute the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

(57) The sentiments (*rasa*) such as the comic (*hāsya*) and so forth, genus (*jāti*), the description of kings, the varieties beginning with the concealment of action (*kriyāgupti*), and likewise the path of "crooked speech" (*vakrokti*). (58)
A sequential description of chariots, artisans, mountains, oceans, rivers, lakes, and excellent cities;
then the praise of the Tortoise and others, followed by various hymns to all categories of entities.
[59] [Also the praise of Bhairava, the Tortoise, and others, as well as a description of hunting and so forth.]
Policy, learning, destiny along with human effort, daring, fortune,
charity, a woman of noble birth, her conduct, offspring, the qualities of a friend,
the arts, service, virtue, wealth, greed, and the path of poverty.
Contentment, forbearance, compassion, and dispassion, followed by praise—
this hundred [verses] on the thirty-three paths of Hari and Īśa was composed by the illustrious Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa. 61–62.
Thus ends the section on the table of contents in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva.
Salutations to Śambhu, who is beautiful with the moon as a chowrie kissing his lofty head, and who is the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds. || 1 ||

Salutations to the enemy of Yama (Kārttikeya), who acts as a watchman during the nights of the dissolution of the world for Bhaṭṭabāṇa, while Brahmā, Govinda, Candra, Indra, Dhanada, and the others sleep.
Salutations to that one of uneven gaze (Śiva), who, taking up the mountain as his bow and making the serpent his string,
shattered the wondrous target with an infallible arrow. 3.

When the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), exhausted by the sparks of the fire from his eyes as he fled while pursuing [the serpent] with the hope of assuming the form of the Ancient Puruṣa embodied in the speech of Śrī Bhojadeva, [took refuge...]
Victorious is the hermitage of the limit of aiming by the Destroyer of Cities, whose arrow was launched from a bow drawn by the virtues of the preeminent serpent-king, who bowed low in salutation.
Salutations to you, O Conqueror of Smara, whose feet are bathed by the streams of light from the rubies in the crowns of gods and asuras; who,
even while the wheel of the world was being offered into the fire of the Great Kalpa,
seemed to offer that very fire itself as a sacrifice to desire, so as to restrain its further arising.
These two belong to the illustrious Murāri:
[He] who is radiant with a crest-tuft shimmering with the beautiful crescent moon perched upon his topknot;
who has playfully consumed the flickering moth of Kāma; and who flashes at the very peak of the state of supreme bliss.
Victorious is Hara, the lamp of awakening in the inner chamber of the hearts of yogis, who utterly destroys the mass of the blinding darkness of deep-seated and most malignant delusion.

Victory to the full añjali of the one whose crest is the young moon, which was formed by the offering of the hoods of the lordly serpent upon his rising bracelets when his lotus-hand was angrily withdrawn by Girijā as he bowed at twilight before the body of the prostrating lady.

I bow to that singular body of Śiva and Śivā, from the left side of which the self-born Hero, the Mind-born (Kāma), having attained his death under the guise of her jar-like breasts, indeed became manifest in the form of a *liṅga*. 8.
As the touch of his hand began upon her broad jar-like breasts, which were covered in horripilation, the left half of her body emitted sweat born of the passion of love;
for the Lord had repeatedly performed the rite of smearing sacred ash over her.
The ash-bath upon his body has somehow been completed; he reigns supreme. || 9 ||
Because of his silence, flattering speech has set; because one hand has fallen limp, the joining of palms has gone far away; and since his head is half-stiff, how can there be prostration?
Thus, by being embodied in a single form, the God who is the teacher of the three worlds, though distracted, conquers the enraged Lord of Mountains through his act of conciliation.
O Pārvatī, become half of someone’s body so that my footing may be firm; take a bow in your hand,
and if it is moist with sweat, let the palm be wiped with the ashes from my body-unguent.
Even as he was speaking thus, the arrow took flight like a fire-breathing serpent; when the cities were set ablaze by its hissing fumes, the smiling face of the Enemy of Tripura triumphs.
Victorious is the dawn,
which, like a spark from the fire of the cities [of Tripura], is joined with the scattering of ashes;
it dispels the onset of night with its abundant and expansive light.
The crest-jewel of the serpent upon the matted locks of Śiva, the destroyer of Smara,
shines like a star brought down by the flood of the celestial river.

May those Tandava dances of Śambhu be victorious—dances in which the confluence of the celestial river with his crown is revealed by the ocean as it surges with a roar from the falling masses of mountains tossed by the wind of his high-arching, wildly leaping forest-like arms;

and in which the descent of a rain of flowers is intercepted by the multitude of stars falling away in great numbers due to their collision with the tips of his clearly visible, formidable matted locks. 13.
Victorious is that certain fire in the eyes of Bherībhāṅkāra, which are marked upon his forehead by the blue-and-red [Siva];
for whose kindling the Self-born [Brahmā] became the cause for the destruction of the world that was being protected.
Victorious is the mass of matted hair of Śiva, belonging to Murāri, within which the celestial river flows entirely undisturbed,
with her shimmering moon as a royal swan and her spreading foam as a garland of Brahmā’s skulls. 15.
Bow down to the eyes of Hara, which have been made into a cluster of worship-lotuses at the feet by those who have achieved their purpose;
for upon seeing them, the wondrous simultaneous opening and closing of the lotuses occurs at once.
From among the thousand fine sayings, he is victorious;
for this crescent moon of his shines forth, turned toward Umā, like a silver oyster shell seeking to grasp the collyrium from the lamp of her eye. 17.
The moon of the playful grace of Subandhu— who has conquered Smara and whose crown rests at the feet [of the Lord]—
has filled the quarters with its full orb by means of the jewel-like nails that radiate beautiful moonlight.
Triumphant is the mark gradually inscribed by the falling tears of Pārvatī, which, though consisting of very small particles due to her offense, are enriched with collyrium. 18.
I bow to that digit of the Moon belonging to Śrīkaṇṭha, which is bitten by the leader of the serpent-chiefs exhausted from being bound in his matted locks;
it is as if it were being turned on a pair of tongs by the flames of the fire from his forehead-eye in order to fill out its orb. 19.
I bow to Umā, whose eyes are closed in the bliss of embracing the throat of Murāri’s consort,
appearing as if she has fallen into a swoon from contact with the Kālakūṭa poison.
I bow to the lotus-feet of Girijā, which were playfully struck by Bāṇa’s foot;
upon them the crescent moon fell, appearing like a broken bangle caused by the impact when the glory of Śiva’s fortitude was cast aside by Kāma.
Seeing his son-in-law’s lips stained with morning collyrium and the finger-ash marks upon the bud-like breasts of his daughter, Gotrānanda—
Victorious is that indescribable, sweet whispering into the ear of Gaurī’s mother by her smiling friends, arising from the overflow of love.
There was someone bearing a pair of jars that rivaled the two halves of the lofty cosmic egg, and who was beautiful with large ears like the flapping wings of a swaying peacock.
Victorious is that Lord of the worlds, the elephant-faced son of Śambhu, whose trunk grows in size rivaling the body of the king of serpents, and whose form is a marvel to the three worlds. 23.
O Mother Bhāgīrathī, salutations be to you, who are doubly profound upon the head of Hara, where you mingle with Gaurī’s half as she is being divided by the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara). 24.
The family preceptor of young women, the supreme friend of the lover of Rohiṇī in bestowing the initiation of amorous play,
and even the conqueror of the God of gods with his flower-arrows— [such is Ananga].
Victorious is the director of the drama that is the play of amorous dalliance! 25.
This very Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is celebrated throughout the three worlds, now bears a woman in his own body, distressed by the pangs of separation— so says Rājaśekhara.
"By him, indeed, have we been conquered!"—thus laughing, Smara (the God of Love) triumphs, striking his beloved’s hand with his own hand. (Verse 26.
By someone.)
The goddess Rati is triumphant, upon the surface of whose broad breasts there shines a decorative pattern of musk;
it appears like the dark luster of the whetstone used by the God of Love to sharpen his arrows when he approached his beloved after conquering the three worlds.
We bow to Hari, the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, who is embraced by the creeper of Lakṣmī, radiant with the cluster of the Kaustubha gem,
and who bestows the fruits of both heaven and liberation. 28.

Victorious is that Śauri, whose form is darkened by the swarms of bees that are the lotus-buds of his navel; for upon the moon of his glorious face, his splendor appears like the shadow of a spot. 29.
Victorious is Hari, who, as if searching for it, has seized Lakṣmī’s own heart after she had, in private, caressed with her hands his exceedingly vast pair of breasts. 30.
In the orb of Rādhā’s breasts, as clear as golden jars belonging to King Arasiṭhakkura, her own luster— dark as a fresh rain-cloud— is reflected.
Victorious is Hari, who, repeatedly lifting up His garment out of the mistaken impression that it was a black snake, provoked a bashful laugh from His beloved.
"May there be a glance from the one seated upon Kamalā; may there be some slight knowledge of the Wind-god.
Thus informed by Tārkṣya regarding the gods who were bowing down, Śrīkaṇṭha exclaimed:
"Where is that seat of my beloved, where is her voice, and where is her throat?"
Victorious is Hari, whose mind is inhabited by Lakṣmī, who is both asleep and yet awakened.
The Self-born Architect of the city of the three worlds, whose sole dwelling is the path of the navel, does not cease even for a great kalpa; rather, he creates it anew at every moment.
"Having what as its locus, of what nature is it, and how is it established?"—desiring to see this, he entered the belly; salutations to that treasure-house of the universe.
May those drops of sea-salt prevail, which, rising from the lashing of the tail of the Lord Murāri as he took the form of a fish, made the vault of the sky appear as if filled with a hundred moons.

By those [flames], as they rose up and fell back, the body of Aurva’s fire— tawny with its mass of flames— was made for a long time the abode of diseases of indigestion caused by the swelling from drinking [the water].
It does not take on a coating of mud due to the dissolution of the earth; it does not seek out musta grass, terrified by the collapse of the city of serpents;
nor does it utter a gurgling roar for fear of the bursting of the cosmic egg.
The Boar, though his body was contracted, triumphs by virtue of his majesty. || 35 ||
Victorious are these two [arms] of Hanūmat, the lion among men, with their quivering sprouts of fingernails,
as if marked by fragments of the crescent moon drawn forth by the wrath of Hari.
Of a certain lord of the Daityas, whose form was terrible with a mass of thick, tawny manes, and who was established within the corner of a hut made of sprouting claws...
Victorious is that glance of Hari, the lion of sport, at that moment— filled with anger, wonder, and heavy shame, yet accompanied by a gentle smile.
When his enemy had entered his own claws during the frantic struggle of crushing Indra’s body,
Indrakaṇi cast his eyes everywhere in amazement, wondering, "Where has he gone?"
Seeing the Dānava fallen upon the earth like dust, struck down by the blows of his hands as Hari cried "In vain!", the Lord laughed with joy.
I clearly salute the pair of lotus feet of the Primordial Being, whose root is familiar to the two hands of Lakṣmī and who is the source of the upward-streaming Vedas.
Where the lotus-born Brahmā, trembling with prostration, performed the washing of one who was already drenched by the powerful [Śiva] pouring forth water for his feet. 39.
From this *Sūktisahasra*,
the earth— with its four boundaries demarcated by the temples of the world-elephants— is being established;
and as we speak of it as already established, behold, our hair stands on end!
What more need be said? Homage to that Rāma, to whom this was offered by the sage, from whom this wonderful tale emerged, and into whom it has finally dissolved.

Victorious is Hari, who, laughing, stood with slackened arms as the cowherds—whose own arms were bent and rendered useless by the weight—said to him, "You are weary; lay down the burden, for we shall carry it. 41.
"O thief, where indeed are you going? It is clearly seen that my second ball has been stolen; you are carrying it here within your bodice!"
Victory to Keśava in Gokula, who, while forcibly churning the pair of breasts of the young cowherd girl, stands as a cage of shimmering horripilation, crying out, "Leave them! || 42 ||

Seeing that the arm of Hari, which had tossed up Mount Govardhana like a mere firebrand, had become slender, he supported it with his own hand at the slope of its shoulder, while the foot of the mountain rose up from its base.
Victorious for a long time are the futile searches for camels by Rādhā in the sky, while she remained untouched by Govardhana as she desired to go to the aid of Śailoddhāra. 43.
I bow to that Lord whose abode is the lotus, who is perpetually consecrated by the three streams of the Gaṅgā under the guise of the fringe of his sacred thread. 44.
The form of Rājaśekhara dispels the delusion of those who remember him; his speech is the supreme deity,
his utterances are the Vedas, and this entire universe, both moving and stationary, is his family.

We praise the Blessed One, the Brahma, who is the ultimate source of this work whose method has been demonstrated as being rooted in the Vedas, and who is himself free from all internal limitations. 45.
Salutation to that subtle and pure one, whose essence is speech and whose threads are the principles (tattvas);
it is his variegated arrangement that weaves the cloth of the universe. 46.
From the rising mountain of Jayatuṅga,

I take refuge in that certain, wish-fulfilling stream of Sarasvatī— a stream of nectar which is light that removes darkness, visible to the eye, possessing a flavor difficult for the tongue to reach, and far beyond the skin’s range of horripilation. 47.
From the *Sūktisahasra*. Thus ends the section on Homage in the *Sūktimuktāvalī*.
May the water-formed body of Śambhu, the life of the world, protect you.
Within which even the cosmic egg acts like a floating bottle-gourd. || 1 ||
May that mass of matted hair of Lord Dhūrjaṭi bring you victory—
within which the Gaṅgā even today creates the illusion of a single grey hair.
May Śiva,
whose half-body consists of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain, whose crown is bound by the river flowing from the moonstone,
and who wears as an ear-ornament the digit of the cool-rayed moon, remove your inner torment. 3.

Umāpatidhara was unable to endure the asceticism of the Daughter of the Mountain, which at that time manifested its innate intensity, yet he was a connoisseur of the confidential conversations she held.
May the Destroyer of Smara grant you joy— he who was simultaneously assailed by both haste and slackness in casting off his disguise as a deceptive young brahmin.
On the hand of one [Lord Śiva], there is a bracelet that is the lord of serpents with its hoods raised; his eye is a blazing fire;
his throat is curved by the suppressed Kālakūṭa poison; and his garment is the skin of a lordly elephant.
"His attire is so charming as to captivate Gaurī’s eyes"—may that emergence of laughter from Pashupati, manifested by the glow upon his cheeks, protect you! 5.

Agitated by the interruption of his entire ritual procedure— which had become disordered due to the bristling of his hair and other physical reactions as he grasped the hand of Pārvatī, who was being presented to him by the Lord of Mountains—
Rudra cried out everywhere, "Alas! How cool are the hands of the Snowy Mountain!"
May Śiva protect you, seen by the hosts of the circle of the wives of the mountain's inner apartments.
As if touching with the edge of his matted locks those [rays] marked by particles of the crest-ash of someone else,
and as if sprinkling with his hands those [rays] scorched by the brilliance of the fire of his eye, he drenched them with the nectar-rays of the moon.

May the Lord of the Mountains be for your prosperity— he who repeatedly washes the feet of the proud Daughter of the Mountain King with the waters of the Gaṅgā, as if they were stained by the breath of his serpent-king.
O Umāpati-dhara,
you who frequent the Dāruvana forest, cease now these useless flatteries;
if I should ever do so again, then the moon shall fall to the earth!

Thus addressed by the Daughter of the Mountain, may the Moon-crested Lord—who was pleased by her prostration at his lotus feet, which were signaled under the pretext of the moon hanging down from his crest—protect you. 8.
When Harṣapaṇḍita prostrated himself with his thousand limbs before his lord, the husband of the celestial dwellers, he offered himself as if he were a garland made of blue lotuses.
And may the husband of Mṛḍānī, laughing as he desires to seize the prince who is eager for play along with his attendants, establish auspiciousness for you. 9.

When the performance of Murāri was interrupted, he displayed anger; when it was completed, he expressed praise; and he experienced horripilation born from the touch of the *sthāna* and *kriyā* movements fashioned by his own hand.
May the tutelage of Paśupati protect you— his teaching consisting of various emotional states, as he comforted the weary daughter of the mountain with firm embraces.

May that Śaṅkara protect you— he whose face was graced with a smile at their words as they asked, "What else could he do when a verbal quarrel arose between the gods and demons— those who were mutually hostile, whose heads were revived by the nectar of the half-moon rising from the eye-rays of those wearing crests and crowns, and who had become utterly exhausted by their laughter?"
May these two garlands of skulls on the head of the Lord of the worlds be for your prosperity— those whose letters are not very well-known, which his attendants read word by word here and there.

"He shall create the universe; he shall support the earth; he shall rule over the waters; he shall be instructed in the portions of the sacrificial oblations; he shall delight in the multitudes; he shall eat the world; and he shall enjoy the heavens."
May the eye-fire of the wielder of the khaṭvāṅga—who brought about the burning of the bodiless Cupid like a moth—protect you;
in the presence of which, the crescent moons upon his crown take refuge in the splendor of its white flame. 13.
Maṅkhaṇa’s one eye is closed like a bud in meditative absorption, while his second is languid with the weight of passion upon the lotus-face and the slopes of the breasts of Pārvatī.

May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you— eyes which, at the time of his meditative absorption, possessed distinct natures, yet were ignited by the fire of the wrath of Madana as he drew his bow far back.
May the throat of the Blue-throated One protect you—his throat resembling a dark rain-cloud, wherein the creeper-like arms of Gaurī shine like streaks of lightning. 15.

These two belong to two of the stars of great luster, which have been resorted to by their lord— the one whose fish-bannered emblem has his bow forcibly restrained by the fire of his eye, blazing with terrible brilliance.

May the body of the Enemy of Tripura—dependent on Rāma, pure as a white water-lily, and adorned with a shining blue neck—along with the other monkey army, which caused the severing of the heads and faces of the [demon] Plavaṅga, be for your prosperity. 16.
May that body of Śiva and Śivā, which is half-male and half-female, purify you— (a pun on *dhanapāla* and the army of monkeys)—
by virtue of which today it might be Śiva alone, and tomorrow Śivā alone. 17.

May the form of Purārī, whose body consists of half-woman and half-man, grant you prosperity—He who, out of the excessive weight of His love, submerged His other half in the ocean of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa). 18.
May the body of Śiva and Śivā, which belongs to Vairañdhra, bring you prosperity— that body whose dark-hued root of the throat,
even on its side other than the left, being white in luster, creates the suspicion that it has begun to transform into the daughter of the mountain. 19.

May the fourth *prakṛti* of Śambhu grant you happiness—his body which transcends the categories of female, male, and neuter; the dust from the ashes on whose fingers dries the decorative leaf-patterns moistened by perspiration upon the left breast of his beloved, who delights in such poetic fancy. 20.

May the Blessed Lord Ardhanārīśvara grant you happiness— he whose single breast possesses the splendor of Svacchandā, whose moon-crest on the head of both sides glimmers, who wears the lord of serpents as a sacred thread,

and whose third eye creates a *simisima* sound from the mutual impact of its own force, one half of which is a light spreading with the calamity of burning the universe, while the other half sheds tears arising from compassion.

Let alone the embraces, the kissing of the bimba-like lower lips, the pleasant conversation, and the smiles of Murāri; for the time being, even this mutual gazing at each other’s faces has become difficult to obtain.
"Thus, what kind of mockery of love is this between us two, who have rendered the composition of our single body so futile? May the smiling Ardhanārīśvara protect you! 22.
May Giriśa, whose hand rests upon the single breast of the Mountain’s Daughter, protect you for a long time—
he who touches the golden linga as if to reassure the Mind-born God (Kāma). 23.

May that Great Bhairava, who has become a fisherman, cast away the delusion of the virtuous; he who, at the end of the aeon, has bound the great skeleton of Trivikrama once it was stilled, and whose hand holds the flesh of the Primeval Boar impaled on the claws of the Narasimha he has stitched together with the quivering Shesha; and he who, while the entire universe is a single ocean, joyfully drags along both the Fish and the Tortoise, who are delighted by their state of being submerged in that universal flood.

May the playful sports of the Lord of Caṇḍī at the end of the aeon protect you—those sports which resound with the deep, thundering roar of swallowing fragments of the cosmic egg placed between his formidable fangs protruding from a mouth made terrifying by clearly drawn-back tusks; and those sports which effortlessly drink up the oceans of universal dissolution with the flames from the victorious eye on his forehead, which flickers incessantly. (25)

May the roars of the conqueror of Tripura—He who is wrathful at the end of an aeon and wanders about in sport—protect you; those roars uttered when He, having failed to find satisfaction despite making all living beings guests within the cavity of His own mouth, beheld the walls of the quarters empty and felt His anger aroused by the fruitless labor of His attempt to swallow His own form as it was cast into the ocean of dissolution.

"These are the bones, the very bones of Bherībhāṅkāra; this is his skin, his skin; this is his ash, his ash; this is the moon, the moon; this is the Gaṅgā, the Gaṅgā; this is the serpent, the serpent"—thus [they spoke] with overflowing agitation.
May the words of the Gaṇas protect you— words uttered by those busy with the preparation and provision of ornaments, dress, and requisites, while Śiva is intent on the commencement of the dance.
"O Lord of Beings,
from among the collections of bone ornaments of Dhanapāla, of Indra, of Brahmā, of the Lord of the Gods, or of Kṛtānta, what should be extracted by me and given?"
May that Śaṅkara protect you—he from whom the gods were terrified by the terrifying speech issuing from the interior of his dressing-room as he engaged in the rite of adornment. || 28 ||
Ambikā places a garland of fresh lotuses hanging from her knees around her lotus-like neck;
Nandin fixes his matted locks with the lord of serpents, treating him as a crescent moon;
Kāla fastens his skin, while Kālarātri brings a skull to his hand.
May that assembly, which was separately engaged during Śambhu’s descent into the dance, purify you. || 29 ||
These two belong to both [the worlds].
O guardians of the quarters, move away; O clouds, leave the sky;
O earth, go to the netherworld; O mountains, enter the surface of the ground!
"O Brahmin, move far away from our lord Śambhu’s abode as he dances; this is a narrow space!"—may this exclamation of Nandin protect you all.
From the Mahānāṭaka:

May the gale-winds of Bharga protect you—winds that delight in the grand display of the *tāṇḍava* dance at twilight, and which, as they whirl with fierce rotation, sweep across the circle of his outstretched, staff-like arms;
winds by whose sudden force the mountain ranges are instantly uprooted from their ranks.
As they flew upward, Indra beheld that thunderbolt once more.

Having fashioned a cage for it— encircled by the staff-like waters of the celestial Gaṅgā falling through the channels of his matted locks, which were spread wide by the force of his violent whirling— [he imprisoned it] at the command of Somanātha.
May the Lord, the master of the new dancer in the drama of the dissolution of the three worlds, protect the universe— he who acts as a swan with his pair of wings formed by his two whirling arms.
When the wheel of the earth is violently mounted upon by him as it reels from the whirling of that dance...
While the circle of day and night revolves at his side, hundreds of fiery lightnings arise; for how could even those born in the darkness be seen?
May that omnipresent Lord, who performs the final sacrifice for the worlds, purify you.
These two [arms] belong to Murāri,
the enemy of Kāma, whose exertion in his fury was not even perceived by the three worlds,
and who, with his limbs expanded at the onset of his dance, seemed to burst open the cosmic egg.

May the body of the Great Tortoise protect you— its head emerging from the water's edge, its forefeet extended forward, its sprout-like arms uplifted, appearing like a tortoise moving upon the surface of the waters.
(34) [From the Kūrma-avatāra]
"Blessings to you, O digit of the moon! Prosperity, O celestial river! Welfare, O row of skulls! Good fortune, O serpent-king's vine!
Well-being, O mass of matted locks!"—thus these [deities] say to one another when he has attained tranquility.

May the Tandava dance of the Lord, who acts as a dancer in the dramatic performance at the end of the aeon, lead to your prosperity—He who applied medicinal powder to a certain snake and bound herbs to another that was a mere earthworm. 35.
