May the Daughter of the Mountain protect you—she who, at the time of her marriage, held in her hand potent gems against the poison residing in the throat; she who, instructed by the elderly women of her clan, uttered the syllables of the mantra for her husband’s host of spirits; and who was both joyful and afraid.

While Rājaśekhara was occupied with the worship of the gods during the preparations for her wedding adornment, she saw before her the very form of Gaṅgādhara, her future husband, as if he were painted there.

May Gaurī protect you— she whose mind was filled with madness, laughter, anger, and shame, yet who, after a long time and with great difficulty, at the word of an old woman, finally offered a handful of flowers to her beloved.
(37) She stood on the tips of her toes, repeatedly bending low under the weight of her breasts.

May that handful of flowers protect you, which was cast by Girijā between Śambhu’s eyes as she, bashful during his worship, approached the path of his three longing glances; her head bowed down with horripilation, perspiration, and trembling, the handful of flowers fell apart in mid-air.

In her new union, Gaurī was hurried on by an eager longing born of youth, yet turned back by bashfulness; led once more toward him by various words from her female kinsfolk, she stood before her husband at their first meeting, filled with the essence of trepidation upon seeing him.
May she, embraced by the laughing Hara, her hair bristling with joy, bring you happiness— she who,
in the tiger-skin garment, has her face bowed down and her eyes closed like buds. (These two verses are by Śrīharṣa.)

May Pārvatī’s gaze—trembling at the sight of the serpent, unblinking at the moon dripping with nectar, closing its brows at the sight of the celestial river, and languishing within the hollow of the skull—be for your welfare; a gaze full of affection for her first union with Śiva. 40.

May that Pārvatī protect you— she whose eyebrows and face are exuberant with laughter, whose gait is full of graceful charm, whose hips are swelling, and who possesses a half-smile and playful speech in the transitional age between childhood and youth.
The two eyes of Madana quickly reached the edge of her ear, as if having traveled along the path within it out of longing to behold the Lord who had taken up residence in her heart. (41)

Tearing open the cavernous mouths of the radiant Vāsuki as he spat forth blood, and touching the sprout-like fangs variegated with poison with his forefinger, [the serpents] disregarded the sequence of numbers, crying out:
"One! Three! Nine! Eight! Seven! Six!"—thus utterly destroying the order of numeration.
May the words of the enemy of Krauñca, though lacking the power of sharpening, nourish your welfare.
Having rolled at will upon his father’s chest, his body white with the dust of funeral ashes,
he suddenly leaps from his mass of thick matted locks into the unfathomable waters of the Gaṅgā.
May Guha protect you from calamity— he who immediately utters a hiss of pain as his row of teeth chatters from the numbness caused by the cold water,
trembling as he places his hand over his eye which blazes with the flame of fire.
(43) These two [verses] are by Bāṇa.

May that Kumāra grant you the glory of celibacy—he who always dwells upon the clusters of blue lotuses that are the eyes of the blossoming celestial nymphs, having surpassed them through his self-restraint; he who resides upon a peacock with a fresh and beautiful plumage. May that elephant-faced Lord protect this world, whose great trunk has risen up into the sky.
The lotus of the sun’s orb has become its stalk by means of the white-tusk-sprout of Gaṇapati, which is rooted in the base;
its golden mountain is the pericarp, and its shimmering pupils are the filaments.

May that first leader bestow prosperity upon you— he whose hand performs the graceful sport of a swaying stalk upon the lotus of the world, which has moving clouds for its bees and the eight quarters of space for its blossoming petals. 46.
By Kṣemendra’s thousands of streams of generosity, with the mass of his tooth-like rays appearing like floods of vermilion from jars,
the playful beauty of the evening twilight of the night was manifested all at once.

May the dance-playful gestures of Heramba protect you— gestures that cause the serpent-king’s wives to be overwhelmed by the tumultuous clamor of many large bells swinging to and fro, and that make the earth tremble with the rhythmic movements of his limbs.
May he protect you, whose excessive sprinkling is received from the streams of ichor falling from the vicinity of his temples.

May the broad vine-like trunk of Gaṇapati grant you the desired fruit— this trunk which bears a sprout in the guise of teeth shaped like the rising young moon, which has hovering bees swarming around its trembling ear-flaps, and which is covered in flowers in the form of a shower of spray. 48.

May the playful antics of the Child of the Destroyer of Cities protect you—those antics by which the lords of the elephants of the quarters were made to flee, driven away by the fresh spray from the joyful sprinkling at will obtained after they had been swallowed and then spat out from the hollows of his long trunks; and by which the lofty peaks of the mountains were shattered through the collision with the swelling temples of his trunk when he suddenly scratched them out of an itch.
These belong to the Lord of the Universe.
May that Lord of Obstacles protect you during his playful pastimes, he who, having drunk the oceans with the tip of his trunk,
is seen by the gods in the sky as he vomits forth the water—
here a little water, there Viṣṇu, elsewhere the lotus-born Brahmā, somewhere Ananta, and in another place Śrī.
In one place are the Aurva-fire, in another the mountains; here are clusters of jewels, and there are creatures such as crocodiles.
May the digit of the moon, shining with fragments of moonlight upon the river that flows from the tip of Śiva’s matted locks, grant you prosperity.
May the digit of the moon grant you joy— that digit which, being drawn in and lost through the illusion of the water’s ripples,
causes the serpent of the thousand eyes to repeatedly contract and expand his hood in the mistaken belief that it is a darting saphari fish, as he strives intensely to seize it in his delusion.

May that crescent moon on the matted locks of Śambhu protect you— he who, having entered the body of the Daughter of the Mountain as a second half of his own lunar orb, has come here desiring to attain the state of fullness.
(52) By Bilhaṇa.

The Gaṅgā appears like pearls within the shells of human skulls, like jasmine flowers upon the creepers of his matted locks, like parched grain in the fire, like gems amidst the coils of the serpents' hoods.
May the droplets of the Gaṅgā’s water protect you— those droplets tossed up by the surging, swirling, and eddying waters as they play upon the head of Hara. (53)
— By Kṛṣṇamiśra.

May the waters of the celestial river, filling the belly of the sky with clusters of blossoming spray-drops tossed by playful waves in the intense collision of powerful elephants and sea-monsters galloping along their thighs— waters that travel the path of the road through Śiva’s matted locks— may they thoroughly dry up the ink of the stains of sin arising from the fierce, wakeful Kali age. (54) By Vedavyāsa.
When Caṇḍikā gave birth to her son Bhṛṅgiriṭi, the goddess said, "O Gaṇas, dance! Why do you stand still?
and as she spoke these words with uplifted arms, she embraced Bhṛṅgiriṭi with joy while his voice was bent down.
May the sound born from the skeletons of those two, whose bone-cages were shaken against one another and which surpassed the deep resonance of the beaten celestial drums, protect you. (55) Sūrya.

Out of a longing for vermilion, elephant-drivers touch the temples of the elephants; out of a suspicion that they are tender sprouts, a Bhilla woman searches for it thickly upon the hollows of the trees;
and out of a desire for saffron, beloved women rub it with their palms where it has adhered.
May that solar heat, which first arose and causes delusion, protect you for a long time!
(56) Trivikramabhaṭṭa’s:
That process of burning which intensely heats one eye at a time during the course of time.
May that glorious Sun, the Great God, protect you—he by whom [the world] was stretched out; at whose time of shining, the state of night becomes difficult to find;
and whose presence as light is known throughout the world even in the parts of the sky—though he is served for but a moment. 57.
There is a pun on the words *hara* and *sūrya*.
Those who illuminate the sky of someone, having severed the darkness; those who shine even upon their own nails;
those who nourish the beauty of the lotus; and those who have surpassed the splendor of the water-born [lotuses].
May those rays of the Lord of Day— those which shine upon the crests of mountains and those which tread upon the heads of gods— both of these bring us prosperity. (58)
— Ānandavardhana.
May the row of Savitṛ’s horses protect you— shining with Aruṇa at its center,
it appears like a single emerald vine of the Goddess of the Sky, having attained lofty breasts.
(59) By someone.
May that Earth protect us—
she who has the Bhagirathi as her necklace, the Yamuna as the mass of her braided hair,
Mount Sumeru as her crest-jewel, and the ocean as her garment. 60
May the heart of Viṣṇu, which belongs to Rājaśekhara and shines with the Kaustubha gem, nourish your prosperity.
For a moment, the light of the jewel-lamps was turned away from Kumuda, its opening faltering due to his fresh awakening, as if it had been sealed by Śrī to prevent Rādhā’s entrance.

May that squinting glance of Hari protect you for a long time— a glance heavy with his own efforts, causing drops of sweat through his yawning and the stretching of his limbs, deep red from the breaking of his sleep, as he desires to leave his serpent-couch whose pillow is the great circle of hoods.
His face was drunk in by the crooked glance of Śrī, whose eyebrows quivered with joy, as she emerged half-way from the waters of the ocean while it was being churned for Viśākhadeva.
May Nārāyaṇa protect you— he who, in the void, performs many comings and goings, while his great serpent-king Manthara has slipped away from his two hands as they remain unnoticed.
[63] His glance, beloved by those bowed in devotion, rivals the blue lotus.

May the eyes or the body of Hari bring about the pacification of the suffering of worldly existence for you— He who, when led by those devoted to meditative concentration as an object of meditation for the sake of attaining welfare, acts as a great treasure-house of beauty, imparting aesthetic relish to the eyes of Lakṣmī.
A play on words (vacanaśleṣa): "O child of him who bestows the nectar of the Bhāgavata, do not fall into despair! Abandon this upward-moving breath of great speed;
let whatever heavy trembling may come upon you be [endured]; go there with the one who has expanded [the Veda] like Indra."

May that ocean, who under the pretext of pacifying the fear of the gods caused them to renounce [the churning], and who bestowed the Goddess Lakṣmī upon him [Viṣṇu], burn away your misfortune— he who was himself bewildered by the churning. (65) By someone.
May the Fish [incarnation], who at the beginning of time created an ocean in the sky with waters tossed up by his breath, and the sky within the great ocean— may he be victorious today. 66.
Kṣemendra’s tortoise,
which was tossed far away by the swelling force of his breath.

May that Lord Hari protect us from misfortune—He who, in the form of the playful tortoise, supports the worlds; whose earth, embraced by the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, bears the splendor of a royal parasol; and for whom the four-faced mouth of the Vedic poet falters when attempting to compose his praise.
May he who, acting as the pivot during the churning of the great ocean,
withdrew his breaths along with his limbs so that Mount Mandara would not fall upon his own back and the ocean would not overflow— may he indeed protect you.
Hari, whose body was made to serve as a tortoise at will, is to be protected by the three worlds;
[these two verses] belong to some [unknown poets],
describing [the churning of the ocean] from the friction against the jagged peaks of the massive Mount Mandara as it revolved upon his back.
May the breath-winds of the Lord, who reclines in the form of a tortoise, protect you—
those winds by whose power of residual momentum the ocean’s waters, under the guise of tides, continue their ceaseless coming and going even today and have not yet come to rest.
May that tusk-staff of Hari as the Līlā-varāha, which served as Hanumān’s boar-form, protect you all.
Where the earth, with Mount Hemādri as its water-jar, has assumed the beauty of a parasol; there,
the sprout of the tusk of Vādīśvarakāñcana, remaining firm, shall cause the world to go elsewhere.
"Truly, the three worlds will fall into agitation when obstructed by these [demons] within his belly"—
may the waves of breath of the conqueror of Kaiṭabha, who bears the form of a blazing boar and whose throat was throbbing with such words as these, protect you;
he who sportively bore a sprout of tusks curved like the tip of the new moon.
May Hari, who assumed the form of a boar, grant you prosperity—
he by whom the lord of serpents, as he supported the lotus-pond of the earth for a moment when it was being lifted up, was reduced to the likeness of a trembling, young lotus fiber.
May that Blessed One, who assumes the form of a boar to eternally lift up the earth from the ocean, protect the three worlds— he upon whose single tusk-sprout the tortoise acts as the bulbous root,
the serpent Śeṣa the stalk, and the elephants of the quarters the leaves.
Mount Meru roars, the earth quivers, and even the sky trembles;
when Hanumān’s ear is withdrawn into a single part of his body, his gaze vanishes somewhere into the firmament.

May the complete majesty of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who assumed the form of a boar, purify you— his majesty while he was searching for the earth that had entered into a single pore among the hairs at the tip of his snout, as the wind was consumed by his breath and the ocean was drunk up through half of his foot’s hollow.
Nṛsiṃha,
the moon-crested one among the followers of Varāhamihira, whose teeth are the horses of the sun and whose inner face has become like the sky.

May Nṛsiṃha protect the world— he whose eyes are like the rising sun, whose playful creeper-like eyebrows are like a rainbow, and who fills the sky with his broad mane of manes flashing like lightning as they emerge from his throat, which is swollen by the suppression of the internal roar. (75)
— [From] Hanūmat.
What, what is this? A lion? Then why does it have a body like a man’s, O Lord? This is a marvel! It has been captured.
Even now it is not fierce; bring it here quickly—surely it has already arrived!
Draw the bow! Draw the bow! Its claws’ tips are swift—alas, alas! how rough the surface of its claws is!
May he who thus struck the king of the Daityas with his own nails as if they were thunderbolts protect you—
[he] for whom there arose the sound *caṭit-caṭit* upon the skin, *cham-it* upon the gushing blood, *dhagit-dhagit* upon the fat, and *ṣṭhād-it* upon the bone with its cracking noise.
May the sound born of the wrath of Hari— the clashing of the saw-like claws of his talons as they strike the chest of the lord of the enemies of the immortals— purify you.
(77) These two [verses] belong to Vākpatinātha.

"Where is this thundering? Why does this pillar burst asunder? Then that Man-lion rushed there; "Who is here, O sir? A bow! Hūṃ!"—as the lord of the Daityas was thus prattling, [Nṛsiṃha] emerged powerfully from the pillar with his own roar and slew him.
Alas! May that very Narahari be your protector in this single moment—
He whose nails possess the beauty of a digit of the cool-rayed moon colored by the twilight, surpassing a thousand well-spoken verses.
May the glances of the Lord who, as the sporting Man-lion, slew Kaiṭabha, increase your joy—
those glances which were looked upon with envy, curiosity, humility, and wonder by the wretched thunderbolt, blunted against the broad surface of the Daitya’s chest. 79.
The masses of water of the Bālasarasvatī overflow; the earth sinks down;
the netherworld is submerged; the cosmic egg shatters into a hundred pieces and falls from the heavens.
Thinking, "The enemy of the gods has been cast down by this body," the lion Hari bears the slain Hiraṇyakaśipu upon his lap; may he protect you.
(80) By someone.

May that quarrel of the worlds protect you—the quarrel between Vāmana and Aparaśarava when they cried, "O Earth, withdraw your waters! and "O Mountains, bow down!"—while Hari’s small belly was being filled. 81.
Drawn by the tuft of hair of someone, scratched with fingernails, touched on the surface of the cheek,
and struck on the head with garlands, he wandered playfully along the road in every direction.
May the waves of laughter of Viṣṇu, who assumed the graceful disguise of a dwarf at the sacrifice of the Daityas while being thus mocked by the courtesans, protect you!
"Who are you, O Brahmin? You are an unprecedented person; there is no one among my followers who is without a protector, for I alone am without a master."
"What desired thing shall I give you? Is this space for walking three steps sufficient for you?

The three worlds belong to me, a twice-born who is devoted to tranquility"—may these words of Viṣṇu, which were uttered with feigned footsteps to deceive the enemy of the gods, purify those whose minds were deluded. 83.
These two belong to Hanumān.
May that Trivikrama, whose foot was seized by Hari and who was lifted up by the Self-born One, protect you.
From whom the Ganges issued like a line of perspiration upon the forehead of the Sun—
was he Rājaśekhara’s parasol, or his crest-jewel, or his tilaka-mark, or his earring, or the Kaustubha gem? || 84 ||
May that solar disc and the enemy of the Danujas protect you— He who, upon the body of Bali, was seen by the celestial maidens as either a wheel or a lotus,
appearing respectively on the crown, the forehead, the ear, the heart, the hand, and the navel region,
increasing in size in each successive place.
Hanumān is the staff for the parasol of the universe, the stalk for the lotus that is the abode of Śatadhṛti (Brahmā),
the keel for the ship of the earth, and the flagstaff for the flowing river of the gods (the Gaṅgā).

May that staff of Viṣṇu’s third stride—which is the axle-pole for the wheel of the stars, the pillar for the mansion of the three worlds, and a staff for the feet—bestow welfare; it is a staff of death for those who hate the gods. (86) —Daṇḍin.

As long as the sun and moon exist, may the enemies of the Dānavas grant you auspiciousness— those who, acting as seeds for the rising of divine fortune in this field of the three worlds that is parched by the waters of the celestial river flowing from their feet, emerge on all sides, eager for the joy of traversing the trembling realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. (87)
— Devabodhiḥ.
Paraśurāma,
having effortlessly uprooted the crown of Sahasrārjuna’s head and brought his feet down upon the heads of the kings, stripped him of all branches of arms from the shoulders on every side.
That Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who— armed with an axe and delighting solely in combat— is the destroyer of kings, has erected that very pillar of victory upon the earth for you;
may he grant you auspiciousness.
"O Lord, having heard from the son of the Wind (Hanumān) that the tortoise is like the root, the lord of waters like the basin, the quarters like the creepers,
and the clouds, stars, sun, and others like the sprouts and fruits of this tree of the sky which I am about to ascend—
May Rāma, though modest, grant you prosperity by commanding the search for Sītā. May Kṛṣṇa,
honoring the songs of the flute with their sweet and deep resonance, wash away the profuse sweat drenching his face as he gazes upon the lotus-face of Rādhā before him.

May Hari, dressed as a cowherd—whose fingers tremble and falter, whose flute slips away, whose sound falters, and whose hands are perspiring—dispel all evil. "Mādhava had a son named Rāma; indeed, his wife was Sītā; yes, she was [the daughter] of her father... 90. Mādhavaśīla’s [work]. Rāma by name was born; yes, his woman was Sītā; yes, her [father was... the father.

May those agitated cries—"O Saumitri! Where is the bow? The bow! The bow!"—uttered by Rāvaṇa as he heard from his mother the ancient story of how he was carried away by Kṛṣṇa while dwelling in the forest of Pañcavaṭī, protect us. 91.
While the night of Vasundhara was turning in its course, and as the sound of the horns and flutes of the cowherds and their herds of cattle rose up tumultuously for the sake of the watch;

May the oscillation of the mind of the Enemy of Kaṃsa protect you—the mind which, bound by the creeper-like arms of Rādhikā in a firm embrace, is unable either to depart or to remain still. 92. Of Madana.
O Keśava, because my vision was obscured by the dust raised by the cows, I saw nothing at all;
for that very reason, O Lord, I stumbled. Why indeed do you not support me as I fall?
You alone are the refuge for all women whose minds are distressed by the uneven paths of life.
May Hari, who was thus addressed with a hint of reproach by the cowherd girl in the cow-pen, protect you for a long time.
"We hear no offense from you, nor has anything untrue been spoken by you,"—
may Kṛṣṇa, thus addressed by the cowherd girl and remaining silent, purify you all.
O Buddha, having resorted to the pretext of meditation, you contemplate these two; open your eyes for a moment!
"Behold this people afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god; though you are our protector, you do not guard us!
You are a hypocrite in compassion—what man could be more merciless than you?
Thus addressed by the wives of Māra, may the Buddha, the lion, protect you. 95
Śrī Harṣa, Nemi, and the Jinas—
these are the sources of abundant majesty for the Dharma, which dispels both passion and ignorance.
"May the Jinas, whose souls are liberated, grant auspiciousness; may others as well grant it.
(96) This is a pun on words (*vacanaśleṣa*) by Dhanapāla.
May Lakṣmī protect you—
she whose stainless moon-like cheek was turned into a deer by Hari, who,
through his reflection cast upon it, acted like a deer. 97.
O giver of honor, is it right for you now to cast aside even me— your devoted one who dwells upon your chest with undivided mind— and take a thousand other beloveds?

Having spoken thus, and perceiving her own body reflected in the jewels upon the hoods of the serpent-king as being Lakṣmī herself, may the embarrassed smile of Lakṣmī— which interrupted the sleep of Hari— protect you.
[98] Her broad hips, her deep navel, and her breasts, firm and high as mountains, were concealed by her garment.
May the beloved body of the Daughter of the Ocean, embraced by her lover, protect you—

she whose form at that moment was one whose eyes closed in bliss, as the Creator Brahmā, his mind at ease because his own abode was not destroyed, meditated upon her for the sake of that lotus-dwelling of Viṣṇu’s navel.
To some,

Hari is the one who possesses the praiseworthy entire body of Rukmiṇī, whose hand is the Sudarśana disc, who has conquered the three worlds with the playfulness of all his limbs, and who has pervaded the world with his moving lotus-feet.

May that Rukmiṇī protect you—she whose face bears a luster as beautiful as the moon, and whom her husband, whose forehead is like the crescent moon, beheld as surpassing his own body in beauty, quite appropriately.
(100) —by Ānandavardhana.
Regarding Rādhā:
May Rādhā purify the world—she who, while churning curd in an empty vessel with a glance bestowed by Acyuta, has her gaze fixed upon the tips of her bud-like breasts;
and may the Lord also purify it, as he restrains the bull with the intent of milking her, his eyes flickering toward the tips of her breasts which are like clusters of blossoms.
(101) —By Līlāśuka.

May Devakī protect you— she whose feet were reddened by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of the gods, when the Friend of the World took up residence in her womb to remove the burden of the earth.
At the forefront of battle against kings of formidable arms, the clanging sounds of weapons—
terrible with the snapping of shattered bones and heavy from being struck back— were the very object of the longing of her ears. (101) These two [verses] belong to certain [unknown] poets.

May that Pāñcajanya of the Lord of Śrī protect you—He who, having been seized in fragments by the moon-crested Lord, was obtained like the moon for the filling of his belly; and whose shell is now held by an arm resplendent with the light of the moon-like face of Lakṣmī. 102
May that single body of Hari and Hara, which captivates the splendor of crystal and emerald through their union in love, protect you— [the body] of those two who are the enemies of Kāma and Kaṃsa.
There exists a dispute over the boundary between the daughter of the Mountain and the daughter of the Ocean when they meet at the neck, which possesses a luster equal to their own. (103)
— By Kaviratna.
By him, who destroyed the Mind-born (Kāma), the body of the Conqueror of Bala was formerly turned into a woman;
he who wears a serpent as his necklace and bracelet and who bore the Gaṅgā;
and of whom the immortals say "Hara" because his head possesses the moon—a name worthy of praise.
May that Mādhava, the destroyer of Andhaka and the bestower of all things, himself protect you.
(104) [This is the blessing of Brahmā for Candraka.]

When the child, out of childishness, was prattling the words, "O Mother Kāpālika, since you have suffered humiliation from the biting of your lower lip, let that be told to Brahmā and the others," Gaurī, seeing herself unable to restrain the speech of the Six-faced One with her two hands, [was overcome].
May the long-lasting turning away of the four-faced Brahmā’s faces from shame protect you!

May the movements of the ancient sage’s speech protect you—movements which, at that very moment, were intent on the defense of Brahman against the self whose soul was bewildered by the fear produced by the churning of its own abode. 106.
Sarasvatī.

May that Sarasvatī be gracious to you— she whose speech, like the circle of planets seeking to obtain essential truths through envy for Vācaspati, attains the state of a rosary of pearls. (107) — By Bilhaṇa.
May the two frontal globes of the elephant of the gods protect you— those globes which, at the conclusion of the churning of the ocean,
were gazed upon with envy by the beautiful women of the gods and demons, who suspected them to be the breasts of the newly risen second Lakṣmī.

[The work] of Bhaṭṭendurāja. Thus ends the section on Benedictions (*āśīḥ-paddhati*) in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva; those whose horripilation serves as a cloak born from tasting the flavor of these elegant sayings (*subhāṣita*).
Even without the company of a beloved woman, poets dwell in happiness.
The weariness of someone is dispelled, perspiration cools, the heated is cooled, and the bewildered awakens.
And a mind that has consumed well-spoken words attains stability even when it is agitated.
How could a human being here enter the assembly of the hosts of the wise,
unless he has drunk the refreshing nectar of well-spoken words until his full satisfaction?
A king finds no satisfaction in the accumulation of wealth, nor does a fish find satiety in vast waters;
a wise man finds no contentment with eloquent speech, nor do the eyes find enough of a pleasing sight.
For men, that alone is an ornament and a primary source of benefit at the proper time which is wealth.
The fortunate ones here cherish well-spoken words—golden, auspicious, priceless, and blessed.

(5) Even when filled on all sides by the dull-witted, the lake of the king’s assembly does not possess beauty if its lotus-faces do not bear the sweet resonance of the swarms of well-spoken verses. (6)
For these [verses] of Vallabhadeva, what need is there for necklaces, or bracelets, or incomparable ear-ornaments?
Enough with armlets and jeweled earrings; enough, enough with ostentatious garments!
We consider this alone to be the one unbroken ornament of men:
eloquent sayings that resemble the flow of nectar from the full moon when it is squeezed.
(7) By someone.
Thus ends the section on the Praise of Elegant Sayings in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
Whom shall we ask? We gods dwell in heaven, while you live on earth.
Is the essence of poetry sweet, or is nectar sweeter still? 1. Of someone.
Homage to those poets whose stainless verses ascend to the ears and yet find a place upon the throats of the virtuous through their merits. —
Vallabhadeva.
I bow to the mind of poets, wherein the fourteen worlds float like swans upon the waters of their creative intuition. —
Rājaśekhara.

If the fame of the Lord of Laṅkā has been eclipsed and the son of King Raghu has become the vessel of glory, all this is solely due to the power of the First Poet; poets must not be provoked by rulers of the earth.
For a lord of the world who does not have masters of poetry at his side, from where could he obtain fame?
How many kings have not existed on this earth whose very names no one knows?
These poets merely bear the labor of Bilhaṇa’s fierce practice [of composition].
The utility of words lies in their application to the pure conduct of kings;
this throat of the long-lashed-eyed women is authorized solely to bear [the weight of] them.
A necklace is an ornament only for the jars of their breasts. (6)
The wealth of learning of the illustrious Murāri becomes manifest only through the utterances of poets;
the surging waves alone proclaim the boundless mass of waters of the ocean. 7.
Poets alone are the speakers who bring well-spoken verses to great value;
the ocean is the source of jewels, yet their accumulation occurs in the palaces of the lords.
Is he incapable because he is inattentive, or is he a man of supreme taste because he is entreated by the wise?
Even though time erodes everything, it does not obscure the well-spoken words of poets.
Victorious are those excellent poets, who rival Vallabhadeva and possess full breasts [of poetic merit], and whose compositions are well-rounded.
Those [poems] which shine forth through inwardness captivate the hearts of all people.

(10) This composition, though brilliant with the qualities of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and propriety (*aucitya*), is not worthy of the designation "poetry" (*kāvyavyapadeśa*), for it does not possess the power of a mantra to expel even a wicked man’s unbearable obsession with hatred. (11)
Even in a poem whose essence is meaning, Bilhaṇa maintains verbal variety;
for an elephant does not look graceful as it walks without the tinkling sound of its bells. 12
Even if its merits are unknown, the speech of a skilled poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the eye, even before its fragrance has been perceived. (13)
The faltering of Subandhu’s words in certain places is desirable both to the lords of poets and to amorous women languid from the weight of their thick hips and rounded breasts. 14.
The great take delight in the poems of Madana when they are delicate, sweet, and well-composed;
others, however, prefer those as fierce as deceitful cranes, jackals, formidable warriors, or actors. 15
Even beautiful poetry does not bring delight to one who lacks appreciation for aesthetic flavor (rasika),
just as sexual union with a deer-eyed woman fails to please if it is devoid of passion.
Words reach futility when addressed to a listener who is ignorant of the efforts of a skilled poet.
To a charming wife, they are like the amorous dalliances of mature women.
(17) By him, the entire earth was filled with gold and bestowed upon poets—upon those who understand the labor involved in composing faultless verses. (18)
In this poem, which requires the application of a vast heart, the dull-witted man suffers not from his own ignorance;
rather, like a woman with withered breasts, he generally blames only his bodice. 19
Even though the multitude of words has been mastered through the grammar of Pāṇini, it appears quite different when it comes from the mouth of a poet;
just as a dance gesture, though learned from a teacher, seems entirely different when performed by a young woman.
In the *Mālatīmādhava*, the Creator has indeed fashioned this pair of loathsome things:
the affliction of villains for poems and the arrival of winter for lotuses. (21)
In a poem produced from a thousand well-spoken verses, there are qualities that the wicked seek to disparage; yet,
bandits never install a bolt upon the door of a house belonging to the destitute.
What wretches are those wicked men who, having developed a pride in their own poetic genius among the dull-witted, can hope to rival the utterances of the Lord of Poets?
What can water do, even when it contains the power to extinguish fire, against the radiance of a sprouting jewel? 23

Bilhaṇa’s beloved’s face, though flushed with anger, and the jeweled lamp, though wiped with water; even when assailed by the wicked, the speech of the lord of poets carries an ever-increasing beauty. 24.
There are indeed many humans who are connoisseurs of the aesthetic essence of Śrīharṣa’s poetry, as well as the inhabitants of heaven who are gratified by the taste of fresh nectar.
These two are rare: one who can endure the lapses of a poet's speech among mortals, and he who can endure the poison of the ocean among the gods—
[these are the qualities] of the lover of *utprekṣā*.
In the midst of the nectar-ocean of true poetry, there is neither the submarine fire nor the Kālakūṭa poison;
yet, paradoxically, by plunging into it, the wicked man experiences the most intense torment.
(26) — By Vatsarāja.
Abandoning the nectar for the ears—the essence of eloquent speech—a wicked man exerts himself excessively toward faults;
like a camel that has entered a pleasure grove, it gazes only upon the thorny brambles.
(27) The virtues of poets become blunted in those who lack exertion in the science of literature.
What could the fragrance of black aloe-wood incense do for the hair of women that is not yet moist?
If these two faultless verses belong to Bilhaṇa, what loss is there to the ignoble?
Would sugarcane placed in a beggar’s armpit ever become sapless?
In some places, the subject matter of the *Mālatīmādhava* is vast, yet its qualities are conveyed by only a few words.

In some cases, even when the meaning is concise, the composition is made with abundant words; in other cases, words are placed like weights on a scale according to the expression. Thus, indeed, among poets, the regulation of word and meaning occurs through three alternatives. (30)
What is lost for those whose speech is like the playful Līlāvatī through its artistry in tender poetry, by the emission of harsh logical arguments and clever words?
Should those who joyfully planted their fingernails upon the orb of a beloved’s breast not also plant their arrows upon the frontal globes of rutting lordly elephants?
Even while they derive delight from their own verbal playfulness... [31]
How few among the virtuous find satisfaction in the compositions of others?
Does the mango tree, whose basin is already filled by the flowing nectar of its own sap, ever desire a watering from the water of a jar? 32.

These two verses of Jayadeva possess a brilliance as if engraved by a whetstone; their composition is swift enough to surpass even the praise of Ardhanārīśvara; their emergence of meaning is like a creeper bursting forth in the sky;
their aesthetic flavor is as delightful as nectar dripping from a slightly fragmented orb of the moon. Such is the very marrow of a poet’s work, and not merely the hollow clamor of a drum.
This certain nectar of Madana’s, consisting of the interplay between word and meaning, bathes the minds of the sensitive with streams of delight.
This poem shines forth as something worthy of being heard; yet that which is its subtlest essence is clearly manifest within the intellects of the wise, while remaining beyond the reach of words.
It lies upon the path of the joy of connoisseurs, made manifest through the clarity of its phrasing and expression.

The poetic genius of poets does not manifest in the work of those who are merely learned; for that path which betrays the onset of fresh bashfulness and the passion of love is indeed beyond the reach of courtesans, being the province of the side-long glances of noble wives.
(35) — Hariharācārya.
The essence of the meaning of words, when not proclaimed by sounds but made clearer through their structural composition, brings delight; however, a sentiment that is too overtly displayed does not.
This is just as the beauty of a slightly shimmering silk garment is enhanced when it moves gently in the breeze.
The fullness of the breasts of women brings pleasure, but not the chest when it is uncovered.
That which is merely the "sapidity" of Dharmāśoka is his lack of learning; if sapidity were simply erudition, then he would be devoid of flavor.
The union of these two, however, produces an indescribable fragrance, like the blending of camphor and musk.
[This is] the work of Vidhyapati,
preceded by [the titles] Vanajaladhi, Mahībhṛt, Siṃha, and Mātaṅga.
The entire range of emotional states appears terrifying when observed directly;
yet, when brought somehow within the path of hearing through the eloquent verses of great poets, that very same range becomes a cause of delight.
(38) From a Thousand Elegant Verses.
Thus ends the praise of poetry by ordinary poets:

"Since this [work], which from the very beginning resounds with a flood of supreme nectar and possesses the undulating movement of waves of sweet eloquent verses, has issued forth like the Ganges from the edge of Śiva’s matted locks, I take refuge in the First Poet (Brahmā) through my speech and conduct. (39)
Although the verbal proliferation of Vāmana Nāga was brought to utter exhaustion by eminent poets such as Vyāsa and others, it did not suffer even a fraction of emptiness;
for the lunar light, though drunk by a thousand cakora birds filled with bliss, does not diminish even in the slightest degree.

O King, do not disregard the playful charms of the poetic eloquence of the multitude of poets, which, through the discourses of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara, have attained the height of joyful sport for the minstrels.

Until this day, no song of the Lord of the Raghus has become renowned by name through anything other than the grace of Vālmīki alone; for it is Rāmabhadra who whitens the very earth with the seal of his fame.
[I bow] to that sage, the resting tree for the speech of words upon its entry into the world of men.
I pay homage to that which dispels the sweat of the threshold of descent from the celestial realm.

Victorious is the poet born of Valmīka, who was the first sound of the musical instrument resounding upon the stage of the lovely Kīrti— the ornament of the illustrious solar dynasty— belonging to the venerable Murāri.
Having drunk from the ocean of poetic nectar flowing from the moon-like orb of his face, the poet now rains down something extraordinary for all time— a cloud-mass composed of fresh clouds.
This is the moonlight of the fifth Veda that has issued forth from Jayadeva’s moon of bliss, streaming with the flow of nectar.
He indeed dispels the darkness and the fever of embodied beings through his various Vedic recitations;
may there be well-being from those thousands of eloquent verses belonging to that Pāṇini, by whose grace [this work was composed] through the favor of Rudra.
First was grammar, followed by poetry, and then the conquest of Jāmbavatī;
how indeed could Vararuci not be true to his name here?
For he, who delighted in constant ascents, composed the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa*. (45–46)

Through these multi-storied dramas of his, which begin with the stage-manager's prologue and are adorned with banners, Rājaśekhara has acquired fame, just as Bhāsa did through his temples of the gods. (47)
Even when Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s circle of plays was cast into the fire by clever critics for the sake of testing them,
the fire did not become the consumer of the *Svapnavāsavadatta*. 48
Those two delightful authors of the *Śūdrikakathā*, Rāmila and Somila,
whose joint poetic work was like the god Ardhanārīśvara;
[they were accompanied] by Bāṇa as his second, who assumed a submissive posture.
By means of his bow rich in virtues, he has delighted all people without exception.
I believe that [this work] was fashioned by Trivikramabhaṭṭa, having taken a single drop from the ocean of the Bṛhatkathā.
Therefore, other rambling tales do not shine in its presence.
Even that story of Dhanapāla, though rich in metaphors, was offered into the fire until only a small remnant remained.
Like the crescent moon licked by the sun, she became most worthy of worship in the world.
Having learned the verses composed for the earth by King Śātavāhana, they caused them to spread;
oh, what a succession of wonders!
By this *Vāsavadattā* of Rājaśekhara, the pride of poets has surely been made to vanish,
just as the pride of the sons of Pāṇḍu vanished when their spear came within the range of Karṇa’s vision. (54)

In this world, the organs other than the ears of Bāṇa obtain satisfaction from their objects through countless means; yet, for those of great magnanimity, even these four [senses] find fulfillment only through the objects of his poetry.
Only the meritorious and glorious verses of Kālidāsa grant satisfaction to the ears of those people who have ripened through good deeds.
How small a difference do the virtuous perceive between the *Raghuvamśa* and the *Kirātārjunīya*?
The wise indeed declare this to be the difference between the *Raghuvamśa* and the *Kirātārjunīya*:
that king, a hero who knew the rules of the scriptures yet was marked by daring,
made Mount Gandhamādana a place to be resorted to by the whole world.
Whose speech does not cause universal awakening like that of Bhāravi, who is like the sun?
And by whom is trembling not produced by Māgha, who is like the month of Māgha? (58)
Their enthusiasm thwarted by Māgha, poets no longer endure the study of the *padakrama* method;
they remember only Bhāravi, just as monkeys recall only [the name] Kapi.
Alas, even though he is but one, Kālidāsa is not surpassed by anyone.
Is it perhaps the triad of Kālidāsas manifesting in the graceful outpourings of the erotic?
These [verses] of Rājaśekhara,
flowing with the crooked speech (vakrokti) of Bhartṛmeṇṭha, take on the form of a goad.
Like those who have been struck, the elephant-like poets shake their heads;
the fame of Pravarasena, the protector of wealth, has spread forth, radiant with joy.
Having witnessed the formidable power of Bāṇa, the lord of speech, which was as fierce as that of the monkey army crossing to the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge.
His intellect, as if obstructed by a suppressed breath, could not find its way into speech.
Avanti, the crest-jewel of the Maukharis, honored the poetic composition of his lord Dhanapāla.
The disciple Bāṇa is a poet whose speech has transferred its lovely essence [to his compositions].
The speech of Bāṇa, like a noble woman, moves freely upon the earth, always possessing the *Harṣacarita* as her vehicle and constantly carrying the *Kādambarī*. 64–65.
Even a single arrow flashing from Rājaśekhara humbles the pride of poets;
how much more so when it is fitted to the string and placed in the hand of Pulinda? (66)
That even the slowest pace of the deer-like poets has become sluggish because of Dhanapāla’s arrow lodged in their hearts— therein, for the most part, lies the cause of their fickleness. 67
Having reached the range of hearing of the connoisseurs of poetry,
the speech of Mayuri cuts away their pride, just as the peacock’s spell against poison destroys it.
For embodied beings, noble birth is not the primary factor among those purified by Sarasvati.
In the *Bhārata*, the poet Droṇa was a potter who rivaled Vyāsa;
oh, what power belongs to the Goddess of Speech, that even Caṇḍāladivākara became a courtier of Śrīharṣa,
equal to Bāṇa and Mayūra!
No one other than the Three-eyed Lord is capable of achieving victory for Pārtha;
how, then, can that purpose be perceived by those possessing only two eyes?
Therefore, I bow to Gaṇapati, the bestower of great joy.
The thundering roar of whose throat is worshipped by hosts of Vidyādharas—
other than Pradyumna, no one else here possesses eloquent speech in drama;
other than Pradyumna, no one else here has arrows that are harsh, even though they be made of flowers.
The three fires, the three gods, the three Vedas, the three qualities,
and the three lineages of staff-bearers are renowned throughout the three worlds. (74) These two [verses] are by Rājaśekhara.
When Vālmīki was born, the word "kavi" became established [as a title];
when Vyāsa was born, it became "kavī"; and when Daṇḍin was born, it became "kavayaḥ. [This is] Kālidāsa’s [view]. (75)
While the *Raghuvaṃśa* stands as the standard for composing the *Jānakīharaṇa*,
if the poet Kumāradāsa and Rāvaṇa were indeed capable [of it],
then let these four oceans of jewels not exist at all. (76)
Thus, as if created by the Creator as another ocean of jewels for poets,
who would not have had their joy increased by Ānandavardhana, through his profoundly deep resonance that penetrates the essence of poetry? (77–78)

Let these other works of Rājaśekhara, beginning with the *Ratnāvalī*, remain as they are; for Bhavabhūti alone is the supreme ornament of his speech, which consists of aesthetic enjoyment, just as [the moon] is the supreme ornament of the breast of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain. (79)
He composed two hundred and two verses, seven great epics (mahākāvya) in succession,
eleven lakhs of hymns praising the Destroyer of the Three-eyed God (Śiva),
and many dramatic works consisting primarily of plays (nāṭaka), short plays (nāṭikā), and dramatic compositions (prakaraṇa).

No other Kalacuri poet was born equal to Māyūrāja;
how many moons have ever risen from the ocean?
That lovely moonlight of her face belongs to the moon that is an unseasonable cloud;
it is perpetually drunk by the cakora-birds of poets, yet it never wanes.
It is as if she were adorned by verses composed by herself, which are like unseasonable clouds.
Born as Kādambarīrāma, he is a preeminent poet in drama;
how could there be anyone equal to Gonandana in composition characterized by alliteration? His very name is significant, for it speaks of his own beauty. (84–85)
Having inscribed a bouquet of wonders in the hearts of the virtuous even from afar,
Kulaśekharavarman composed the *Aścaryamañjarī*, enriched with the crest-jewels of noble lineages.
That Dhanañjaya rendered it skillful in its double entendre.

she was the daughter of Mekhala among rivers, the battle-scarred body of kings, the delight of the gods among poets, and the ornament of the Chedi region. (87-88)
She was the ornament of the lineage of Yāyāvara sages and of the pearl-necklace, like a shimmering drop of mercury beautiful with its golden binding;
If the speech of Śaṅkara is pleasing to some,
[it is because] the Pāñcālī style is said to be a composition in which word and meaning are balanced;
that style is found in the speech of the venerable Śīlābhaṭṭārikā and in the compositions of Bāṇa.
Who, once delighted by the composition of words from the jeweled slopes of [her] hips,
would disparage the speech of their own beloveds, so sweet with its artless charm?
This Karnāṭī woman, marked by victory, triumphs like Sarasvatī herself.
She who is the abode of Vaidarbha speech after Kālidāsa, the ground of the grace of elegant sayings, amorous sports, and the arts— Queen Lāṭī,
though she has gone to Lāṭa, remains as my sovereign in my heart. (93–94)
By means of Subhadrā’s skill in the diction and expression of poets, she quickly gained a place in the heart of Pārtha. (95) These [verses] are by Rājaśekhara.
By Daṇḍin, who did not know that Vijjākā was as dark-hued as the petal of a blue lotus,
it was said in vain that "Sarasvatī is entirely white.
The poet Amara, the poet Acala, the poet Abhinanda, and Kālidāsa.
Other poets and monkeys set foot only in mere restlessness; whereas his union with the Supreme Body has no limit other than his own will,

To drink the elixir for the ears and to compose words esteemed by the virtuous—[such are his qualities]. 98.
If you have the curiosity to attain supreme proficiency, to find the limit in the stream of aesthetic flavor (rasa), and to enjoy the sweet fruit of the tree of life,
then listen, O brother, to the nectar-dripping eloquent verses of the poet Rājaśekhara. 99
Disregarding Bhavabhūti, I, Śrī Śaṅkaravarman, whose mind is set on liberation,
now direct my thoughts toward the contemplation of the feet of Murāri. 100

Arjunadeva’s body is the dwelling for the night; the King of Cedi is encompassed by his breasts;
and this earth, girt by the ocean as its moat, has wandered about.
Except for the feet of beautiful women, no other head has ever been bowed here by the lords of poets or the great kings; such is this charming tale of Bilhaṇa. 102.
The garment is white, the season is spring, and the flower is the autumn mallikā jasmine.
The archer is the flower-armed god of love; the fragrance is musk; the weapon is the bow;
the speech is radiant with the essence of logic; the beloved is a dark-complexioned woman; the body is fresh;
the path is exclusively that of the Buddha; the song is in the Pañcama rāga; and the poet is Bilhaṇa. 103.
Whether it be in literature, which deals with delicate subjects, or in logic, which is knotted by the grasp of firm principles—
while I am present, the Goddess of Speech plays equally in both. Let my bed be either one with soft coverlets or one strewn with sprouts of darbha grass.
If the earth is heart-pleasing, then for the fair-browed woman, her husband is equal to it;
what need is there for the lute-playing of Somaka, or even for the humming of the female bees?

What need is there for the tinkling of the weapons of Kandarpa or even the *huṃkāra* of a young woman, if the speech of a glorious, wise, and excellent poet—beautiful as the water from the frontal globes of Ganesha and a companion to nectar—penetrates the hollow of the ear?

He who makes the path ahead ripple with two drops (or: he who makes the head of his work marked by two dots) shall be the creator of the dot upon the head (or: he shall be a poet whose verses are graced by the *śirobindu*).
Salutations to those who have merely acquired knowledge through gradual instruction and can recount their ancestral lineage;
however, against those poets like Ralhaṇa—who compose with strokes of speech whose flaws are worn away by the whetstone of thousands of texts—I now prepare my armor. (106)

By me, who am naturally exceedingly crooked and extend the length of my virtues, [the enemy] is driven far away, just as an arrow is cast by a bow. Some [are subdued] by the seizing of their throats through pride, while others by the fever of uneven hatred.
Some here, their higher peace extinguished, are perpetually closed by the impurity of ignorance.
Therefore, O walls of our temple, become our refined audience for these sublime hymns; for in their recitation, there is for you a most excellent and profound response beyond all reproach. 108
These two [qualities] do not belong to the "all-knowing" Loṣṭa; his method of grammar possesses neither the burden of sweetness nor the beauty of the flow of ever-new aesthetic sentiments.
"O Lord, with such affection as this goddess speaks in her words,
so does that very physician named Bhānu compose poetry worthy of being heard.

Even for him whose speech was unfailing, Sarasvatī remained ever submissive.
Bhāsa, Rāmila, Somila, Vararuci, the illustrious King Sāhasāṅka, the poet Meṇṭha, Bhāravi, Kālidāsa, Tarala, Skanda, and Subandhu—[all these were under his influence]. || 110 ||
If Sarasvatī herself were accomplished in his praise— who possesses Daṇḍin, Bāṇa, Divākara, Gaṇapati, Kānta, and Ratnākara as his [poetic] treasures— then who could rival him?
For her, the mass of hair is a thief, and the peacock is an ear-ornament.
Hāsa, Bhāsa, the preceptor of the assembly of poets Kālidāsa, Vilāsa,

Thus ends the section on the praise of particular poets in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva.
[Some] are endowed with an extraordinary quality of audacity through certain unprecedented fragments of others' poetry.
Victorious are those certain "ragged poets" (kanthā-kavayaḥ) who carry only the bombast of words!
1. Kṣemendra says: Fie on you, O Kali age! Go to destruction! What is this perversion?
Alas, what misery! The conduct of those who possess learning is seen to be fit for barbarians:
by some the divine Goddess of Speech is brought out for sale, while by others she is shamelessly dismembered limb by limb during the process of examination.
For Ralhaṇa,
one person cools his dwelling with garments by means of the flowing nectar of their tender words;
yet another constantly seems to carve him with the harsh salt of their sharp speech.
Are you composing poetry for Vallabhadeva? Do you have no friends who will restrain you when you are driven by a violent wind?
Drink cow’s ghee and enter a windless chamber;
for men with an excess of wind become wise. (4) — Of someone.
Some wise men enter the rank of a sovereign poet with only five or six verses, even though they have been fashioned with great effort;
yet others meditate upon the Lord with such a power that restrains the mind, which is the most subtle of states.
Why then do the eight great supernatural powers not sport in their very hands?
Laughing with ease at Hari, Hara, Vyāsa, and other preeminent poets for their unworthy imputations—
Speak loudly, close both eyes, and recite verses with pride;
appropriate poetry composed by others and vie with the wise, if you, devoid of learning, desire to forcibly attain scholarship. (6)
Of another person who suffers from a stiff neck, whose head aches at the mere mention of another's rise,
and whose appearance is overwhelmed by agitation, dizziness, delirium, and great distress;
Exhaling hot breaths of uneven anger as the poison of internal hatred enters them,
the painful transformation of the unwise is surely the breeding ground for the onset of a terrifying fever.
Those who argue in assemblies are pierced by the thorn of another's fame and are distressed by that pain.
Those who strive to conceal the virtues of the virtuous by praising their own qualities—
their inner vision clouded by the dregs of anger, sighing hot with rage— their learning is as terrifying to people as the flaming crest-jewel of black serpents. (8)

For Kṣemendra, the tip of the tongue is his own to command; how many words have been mastered by him? Nowhere is a lord of the earth his restrainer; the assemblies are peaceful, and the world is independent.
"Therefore, you poets, shouting at will in every house, 'We are poets, we are poets!'—we, meanwhile, have taken up the vow of silence.

Sandalwood, the orb of moonlight, the lute, garlands of campaka flowers,
and the fifth note— thus from these five was that virtuous man born.
Surely these two, the good man and the wicked man, have arisen from the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
However, the elder brother of Indu [is Rājaśekhara], while the other is the younger brother of Kālakūṭa;

Being both full of water and possessed of great being through this [virtue],
they perfume both hands with the flowers held in their palms;
for generally, the conduct of those who are well-minded is the same toward both the left and the right.
These two—
the waters of the oceans and the minds of the wise— are both clear yet agitated, fearing both their own persistence and their own transcendence.
Even one of dull nature becomes exalted by taking refuge at the feet of the great;
the torrent of the Gaṅgā reached the head of Śambhu by resorting to the foot of Viṣṇu.
A virtuous person does not vomit a fault from his heart through his mouth, nor does he cast it down; rather,
like a lord, he digests the poison within himself.
Great-souled beings bestow their grace upon those who seek them, even if they are enemies;
rivers carry even rival mountain streams to the ocean. 8.
Even one who does harm during the month of Māgha generally obtains a great reward;
the ocean, even while being scorched by the Aurva fire, only serves to satiate it. 9.
An angry virtuous person is like the needle and its handle: sharp at the tip, yet primarily intent on closing up a hole;
upright, he becomes most effective in his subsequent actions. Thus do the wicked and the virtuous imitate the front and back portions of a needle respectively.
One person creates a flaw, while another virtuous person covers it over. O Gobhaṭa,
such a good man, devoted to the welfare of others, does not undergo a change of character even at the time of his own destruction.
Even when being cut down, the sandalwood tree perfumes the blade of the axe.
(12) For the great, even a trifle leads to merit; for the wicked, even a great deed leads to fault.

Though living among others of equal birth, a noble person does not learn foul speech;

even though he dwells in the house of crows, the cuckoo does not become a screecher like them. The virtuous find delight in acts that benefit the world, while other people are satisfied with mere wealth.
The radiant sun wanders through the worlds, while the Lord of Wealth dwells upon Kailāsa.
Water placed at the roots of trees appears upon the tips of the sprouts;
even that which is offered in secret, the great carry aloft.

— Kṣemendra.
Those virtuous ones are the crowns of the world's circle who display goodness even toward those who have done them no favor;

The virtuous rejoice in the noble conduct of a good person and quickly abandon even meanness toward a slanderer.

Fortitude in adversity, forbearance in prosperity, eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle,

— Bhartṛmeṇṭha.
In this world, there is never a separation among virtuous people, who are treasuries of excellence, that could cause the severance of their affection.
Does the moon, even when obstructed by thick clouds or situated at a great distance, ever cause the breaking of love for the beds of night-lotuses?
(24) For indeed, through the union of a fertile field and excellent seed, things bear fruit for the sake of benefiting the world, but not for the sake of one's own subsistence.

Even when the heart of a virtuous person has been soured by internal anger due to the wicked deeds of others, auspicious words alone emerge from his external actions and speech in their true meaning;

Waves constantly manifest, emitting pearls;

who worship [the moon] as non-different from the interior of a night-lotus.

Whether it be a bee that has come from a lotus—the very opposite of its natural state—or [a person] who has approached [the virtuous], there is no limit to the continuous stream of service rendered by the good to themselves and others; such is this [conduct] of the virtuous, which delights in being free from self-interest.
(28) —Śrī Murāri.
Even while sinking into the depths of the ocean of calamity, the virtuous, firm in their vow of disinterested heroism, continue to perform acts of service for others according to their ability;
for even Rāhu, though overwhelmed by the swallowing of his fierce and gaping maw, is fully capable of it.
Does not the moon make people happy even with its rays remaining after being eclipsed?

Those who are compassionate toward the wretched, whom even a slight display of wealth does not affect, who are intent on performing service for others, and who rejoice when asked for help—[they alone truly possess light]. (29)

Those who remain healthy even during the violent onset of the great disease that is the arrival of youth— with them, as with firm pillars, this earth, oppressed by the weight of the Kali age, is supported.
Thus ends the section on "The Path of the Good" in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva.

Wise men do not subsist by showing their fingers and such [signs of distress].

He whose name,
when uttered with respect in an assembly, seems to swallow up the very vital energies of others—
even his enemies rejoice; he alone is truly a man.
For any proud and spirited man who desires to ascend to a high and beloved station,
his own manly effort is considered the support capable of averting a downfall. (8)
For one whose wealth is pride and who desires enduring fame through fleeting lives,
prosperity— which is as flickering as the play of lightning— is surely but a secondary consequence.
(9) These two [verses] are by Bhāravi.
In one place he wears a mere rag, and in another he wears celestial garments;

(By someone)
The conduct of one who is fearless of censure, indifferent to virtues and faults,
and of wicked behavior— ah, it is as difficult to discern as the way of Fate! — Bhāravi.
The boat and the tongue of the wicked person, both creeping in a contrary direction—
by whom was this cruel thing fashioned solely for the purpose of deceiving others? (Riṣuka)
Even in the heart of a wicked person, which is empty within and covered by a multitude of flaws, it is a marvel that not even a single atom of the quality of generosity exists— let alone envy. (4)
— Bhaṭṭa Govindarāja.
People fear a wicked person even when he abides for a moment in goodness;
who would trust a butcher who buys even a goat for the sake of milking it?
A base person who has risen up inevitably fails to attain support from others.
One finds no pleasure in a flaw; the illustration for this is that which arises from the hip [the anus].
For one who is hard by nature, even when assuming artificial humility, both the quality and the vice serve only to harm others—just as the string of a bow and the character of a wicked man.
A virtuous person may find satisfaction even with the wicked, provided they do not inflict harm upon him;
this is a gain for the snake that it is not bitten while being coiled around.
The sky of the venerable sage Vyāsa contains both rain and thunderbolts; the earth holds both the virtuous and the wicked; and alas, my friends, even the great possess both virtues and faults. 9.
Even if praised with a thousand eloquent verses, this wicked man leads only to harm; therefore, it is better that he be reviled.
Even when praised, a snake will surely bite; its mouth does not remain closed even when firmly pressed.
The fire of anger in both the virtuous man and the wicked man is something unprecedented:
in one it is extinguished by affection, while in the other it increases even when restrained. (11) — Gobhaṭa’s.
Even water becomes undrinkable from the salt ocean and from a wicked person— both of whom are a sole repository of enmity, cruel by nature, and dull-witted. (12) By someone.

As if fearing tautology, the unscrupulous wicked, well-versed in slandering others, speak one thing behind one's back and another in one's presence. (13) [Regarding the word *punarukta*: "Tautological word."
It is fitting that the wicked, who have found birth for the purpose of oppressing those with abundant grain,
should be settled only outside the village;
they are those who increase the ruler's delight in sinful pursuits.
What distinction is there between those slanderers and dogs? These two wicked ones, though being treated with hospitality by Rāma, the upholder of sacred learning, provoke strife among the virtuous.
Does even a horse, though washed with milk, ever attain the state of a swan?
Though made clear by affection and the gift of prosperity, a wicked person remains as such;
like a mirror standing nearby, he divides even a single thing into two.
O virtuous ones, tell me, what indeed is the difference between a mirror and a wicked person?
For as long as a person remains before them, they remain within their heart. (18) — By some.

One who has acquired heat from another is base and generally difficult to endure; even the sun does not scorch as much as a mass of heated sand. Those of low birth cast away their own kin upon encountering them, even after having approached them, with harsh words.
Mares come from afar and urinate in the waters of the sacred ford.
These two verses belong to Vallabhadeva.
Furthermore, a wicked person who rejoices in the misfortunes of others does not even consider his own destruction.
Generally, when a thousand have perished at the front of battle, the headless trunk dances.

but the wicked, however, proclaim the faults of others, even if they do not exist, just as they boast of their own virtues. (22)
These two [verses] belong to Ravigupta:
A base person can by no means endure to behold even the rising splendor of one possessed of brilliant virtues;
like a moth, it abandons its own body and strikes at the bright flame of a lamp. 23.
O Vallabhadeva, do not feel affection for this arrow, which is straight and winged;
it generally lacks virtue and tears the heart with its fruit. 24.
"Thinking 'these are affectionate,' do not place your trust in these base men;
for even the affection of those who have achieved their goals causes tears to fall.
(25) These two belong to Cigobhaṭa.
The wickedness of the base becomes exceedingly foul when they destroy the virtues of others;
even the clouds, though they obscure the light of the moon, possess a greater darkness within.
"The wicked man is more treacherous than even a venomous serpent"—the wise do not speak this falsely.
For this one who hates the Nakula family is again a slanderer of that family. Just as a wicked man, like a hand soiled with dust, strikes against a virtuous person,
he makes him appear with a stainless luster, just as a mirror reflects its own clarity.
Though placed upon the head of Subandhu and constantly attended with great effort and much affection,
this [poison] does not abandon its crookedness, just like the hair of a young woman that remains lowly and curled.
When the slanderer wanders about with a blossoming face and wide-open eyes,
I believe that his labor in performing constant harm has finally borne fruit.
O Hālāhala poison, do not be so arrogant, thinking, "I alone am the teacher of the most cruel things."

Surely there are many such words of wicked men in this world as those of yours! To whom have these [words] not been directed by him? For what fault has not been forcibly attributed, or what virtue has not been seized by that villain?
Nevertheless, it is remarkable that even such a virtuous person is not free from faults, nor is he endowed with every single excellence.
As for those fortunate ones who, while increasing in merit, accomplish the welfare of others by renouncing their own self-interest—[how much more so is this true of you! 32.
