those who destroy the welfare of others for their own benefit are human demons (rākṣasas),
while as for those who destroy the welfare of others without any purpose, we do not know what they are.

In one who possesses modesty, dullness is imputed; in one who has a steady resolve, hypocrisy; in one who is pure, deceit; in a hero, cruelty; in a sage, perversity; and in one who speaks kindly, wretchedness.
In the spirited there is arrogance; in the talkative, an inability to speak when it is necessary; and in the steadfast, what virtue indeed could there be that has not been branded by the wicked?
Thus ends the section on the Wicked in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
The wealth of a miser is common to others because he does not enjoy it;
the connection that "this belongs to him" is realized only through the suffering felt when it is lost.
— Vyāsa.
Like a lute to one who lacks ears, like a tremulous-eyed woman to one who is blind,
or like a garland of flowers to one who is dead, the prosperity of a miser is fruitless.
For it produces aversion, distress, craving, delusion, and sleeplessness.
That wealth of the miserly is not true wealth; it is merely a disease of the heart.
It has been said: the wealth of the rich, when spoken of to others, becomes like meat; when unspoken, it passes into invisibility;
and at the time of death, it takes on the nature of a thorn within the heart.
The learning of one who lacks virtue is useless, as is the strength of a coward;

the exertion of one with little fortune is in vain, as is the wealth of one who lives like a miser. That which is acquired through the suffering of others, and that which, once acquired, is not enjoyed—[is of no avail].
Whatever is divided by others at the end, let that wealth not belong to anyone.
If these [pleasures] of Kṣemendra delight him with wealth buried in the middle of his house, would he not rather delight in that [wealth] according to its true measure, rather than in Mount Meru? 7.
Like a wretched corpse, even though dead, he does not give;
by merely increasing his own flesh, he has done a service for the crow.
Generally, among the wealthy, the thirst for wealth is most intense.
Behold this bow, endowed with two ends and inclined toward the target of a hundred thousand;
for some,
death is the protector of the body, and the earth is the guardian of wealth.

Like an unchaste woman, she laughs at her own husband who is devoted to his sons. If, when asked, one does not give to that virtuous man who entreats with a distressed mind despite possessing wealth— what answer can be given for such a person?
O Vyāsa, why have these riches sought refuge with me? Why do they kill me like poison?
For they are neither given away nor enjoyed by this wretch.

Between a miser and a sword— both of which have their fists tightly clenched, are seated within a sheath, are naturally dark, and are devoid of compassion— the only difference lies in their origin. 13.
The wealth of the miser Sūcigobhaṭa is unenjoyable by supplicants, corrupted by long-term accumulation;
whereas the wealth of the great is as beautiful as water from a stream, with its constant inflow and outflow. 14.
Neither wealth, nor wives, nor even one's own body serves as an instrument for another;
in this matter, the King of Nandana is a clear illustration for the miserly. By means of the riches of King Nandana, some most terrible evil deed was surely committed.
The baking heat from the depths of the earth has not even now ceased for you.
(16) Exhausted by the toil and hardship of being passed along through a succession of hands, the riches residing in the houses of the miserly sleep as if they were dead. (17)
Objects of desire, though daily enjoyed by the virtuous through coming and going and causing them weariness,
seem as if they fall asleep upon encountering the presence of the wretched. (18) —
Vallabhadeva.
Even when they have obtained them, the wretched do not get to enjoy their wealth due to their own past actions;
when the grapes reach full ripeness, it is the mouths of the crows that become parched.
(19) — Ravigupta.

His kinsmen were distressed by his loss of sleep; he was abandoned by the anxious physician; he was tormented by the attendants with decoctions of boiled herbs out of fear that he might fall into a stupor;
his hopes for health were shattered; and both his feet were firmly gripped by his beloved wife.
In the end, what can a helpless miser do with wealth that is like a thorn?
(20) Kṣemendra. Thus ends the section on the Miser in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
Since even the shadow of the sun— though he himself possesses powerful radiance and pursues it as it moves—
extends very far along with him, I believe that by this [shadow] a likeness to noble birth has been fashioned.
(1) By Śrī Bhojadeva.
May the Lord Hari bear that Kaustubha gem upon his chest; yet there is another, indeed, which is the very foundation of the sun:
for it is that [gem] alone which bears upon its head the lotuses whose fragrance is rippled by contact with its rays.
—By Śrī Rājapitāmaha Mahādeva.
Even though this darkness approaches as something hollow, you abandon your own orb— alas, even he who is the lord of lights,
yet is celebrated in the worlds by the independent words "hero, hero" because of his fame!
In that regard, reputation is more important than a powerful, substantial form.
By whom among the lords of the earth have the feet of the illustrious Bhojadeva not been borne upon their heads?
When that radiant eye of the three worlds was swallowed by Rāhu, the glow-worms flashed, the darkness arose, the stars expanded, and the owls woke up;
alas, what can I do here? What has not been set in motion by something?
The fall of the illustrious Muñja will not result in harm even for the great Pūṣan; for when the time has arrived, who here has not set, does not set, or will not set?
But this alone causes me even greater pain: that he has found a place within that very sky, which is vast by nature, yet filled with darkness alien to the world.
When that sun has set, the moon will not cause the pain of separation from the awakening of the three worlds; therefore, nothing remains improper.
This causes even greater distress to the mind here: that these lamps have arisen with their flames raised high in the destruction of darkness.
These two [verses] are by Bhaṭṭa Bhallaṭa.
Having come from somewhere or other and having made the expanse of the sky their own—
Having made even the moon and other luminaries the objects of his gaze upon existence and non-existence,
and having brought the world to a state of intense brilliance, the beloved lord of days has reached his end;
let him now either set, enter the ocean, or wander around Mount Meru.
It is only right that the illustrious Kalyāṇa spreads the destruction of darkness along with its very roots by means of his radiance;
yet this is not all, for he utterly robs all the luminaries of his own kind of their light.
Or rather, it is fitting that he desires to seize the position at the head of the entire world;
for while another equal lives, what is his splendor, what is his fullness, and what is his rise?
(8) [Of Vidyeśāna]
A radiant being cannot endure the radiance spread by others;
that is his own nature, uncreated because it is determined by his very constitution.
For if the divine Sun-god were not to scorch with his rays without ceasing, [who could bear it?]
Why does this stone of Agni, as if cut down, scatter its brilliance?
Bhavabhūti’s likeness to the unevennesses of the world has been destroyed, for he has attained the perfection of the bliss of the eye.
When the light of the path appears, the world no longer prevails; it spreads darkness as its sole umbrella.
Because of the favor of the Lord of Day, who makes all that is not its own nature vanish by time, that very same brilliance manifests with forceful impetuosity even in another continent. 10
Thus ends the section on the Sun from the *Sūktimuktāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
[Colophon: Although there are many luminaries such as the sun and others, they possess light; yet...
Only one possessed of true artistry is truly skilled in the work of carving stone;
for although Prahlādana’s acceptance by the Lord of Beings was equal to that of Daiva, [it was the former who achieved the result].
Nevertheless, how could the shards of a skull ever compare to the moon, the treasury of digits?
Let that one alone— the Moon— rightfully enjoy the title of "King" (Rāja) in the *Mālatīmādhava*.
He who does not abandon even this deer-like [moon] though it is as if stained—
its very rising is the cause of nectar for someone's body and a festival for the eyes of the world.
This moon sprinkles the three worlds with waters of moonlight upon them having been scorched by the rays of the sun;
he exerts himself to destroy the blinding darkness that obstructs all directions—fie on the Creator, whose mind has set about carving a mark even upon him! 4.
Even if the fierce son of Siṃhikā should mount upon someone's head out of anger,
even then he does not abandon a deer that has sought refuge with the Son of the Ocean.
O Darkness, desist from this rashness toward Madana! If the sun has set of its own accord, what of it?
Do you not see before you this moon, a treasury of great waves of light, rising up?
Ballālasena possesses this one certain digit of the moon, which is composed of nectar, exceedingly priceless, and by means of which alone—
Placed as a crest-jewel by the Supreme Lord who knows its virtues, the fault of its dark spot was not even taken into account. (7) By someone.

What need is there to speak of the ocean Ratnākara, his progenitor, or the group of innate [treasures]? What is the use of the nectar, the Kaustubha gem, and the Pārijāta tree? For here, that which is inconceivable is something else entirely.
This moon is a distinct entity from the lotus,
even though it is the creator of the world who fashions it in various ways. (Śrī Murāri)
Long ago there occurred a certain noble deed:
that the stain was placed upon the moon—the enemy of the rising sun—when it bloomed at his friend's rise, yet became the very cause of its ruin. 9
Is he not the son of someone? Is he not the crest-jewel of Śiva?
Does he not destroy the darkness? Or does he not dwell above the world?
That this tiny speck of beauty shines within it is the fault of the Creator, and not at all the fault of that treasure-house of virtues, the beloved. 10.
Vallabha.
It fulfills all hopes, bestows prosperity, removes the heat of the three worlds,
provides a guileless sprinkling of nectar, and extends supreme joy; yet,
by this cloud-like Time, it has been forcibly and for long removed.
When King Pūrṇa had passed away, the world was left as a remnant of a mass of most intense darkness.
Those who cause distress to Hari and Hara, and who quickly render the world joyless— [they are like this].
Even those rays of the sun, which are harsh and destroy the stability of flowers,
have been made by you— O moon of nectar— to pour forth abundant ambrosia; thus, O moon, as you dispel the heat of this entire world, you have placed yourself at the forefront of the great.
The quarters of the sky bear the pallor of King Bhoja through the humming of bees attracted by his fragrance;
the night-lotuses cry out with the sound of their bees, and the moonstones, agitated, shed their sweat.
O Moon, this single deer does not feel fear in its heart at the time of being swallowed by you, even though it arises from the crushing bite of Rāhu’s formidable fangs.
(13) By someone.
Of what use are these various luminaries such as Venus and others, rising with intense splendor and attaining great loftiness in their positions,
so long as you— who dispel the darkness of the world— do not spread your own glory?
O Moon, how does that ocean, the mine of jewels, attain such supreme prosperity?
[For] the moon and the sun belong to the Three-eyed One.
Who can gaze even face-to-face at the thousandfold brilliance of the sun,
who endures the shattering of the orb of the moon’s splendor?
(15) — Śrī Vallabhadeva.
What need is there for deliberation here regarding the Sun, who is the worthy recipient of unblemished praise,
since his rays sustain the existence of the entire world?
Otherwise, by whom could that wretched heat be dispelled?
If even this moon, the possessor of nectar-like rays, does not exert itself toward him, [then what can be done]? Thus ends the section on the Moon.

Many winds blow, pungent and capable of shattering the excellent trees; yet, in the arrangement of the abundant fragrance of their flowers, there is but one who is truly skillful. (1) By Vaidya Bhānupāṇḍita.
The supreme friend of the Maruts increases the brilliance of the blazing fire;
yet he extinguishes its lamp—this is known as the "fulfillment of what has been undertaken.
(2) By someone.
O wind, why do you scatter upon the vulgar this wave of fragrance from the deer’s footprint— fragrance followed by swarms of bees and dispelling the fever of the hearts of the sensitive?
(Mālatīmādhava)
These clouds are ever-risen for the sake of pacifying the people, regardless of their own interest;
those who restrain them while they are raining are indeed certain great-souled beings.
(4) — By Kasyapa.
O friend, look at those who are light by nature and have never been counted anywhere; who were daily crushed by feet and long remained dissolved in the earth—
now they have been tossed up into the sky by the fickle-minded wind.
These particles of dust take their stand upon the summits of lofty mountains.

O Wind, what kind of delusion is this of yours, Bhallaṭa? That you lead the mass of dust from the trampling of people’s feet to find its resting place in the sky, which is frequented by hosts of radiant beings!
While he is being raised up, let there first be obstacles for the path of people's eyes;
by what means can the impurity upon his body be endured? This fault is yours alone. (6) —Amṛtadatta’s.
May this tree, filling all directions with its branches, celebrate the festival of sharing its splendor; may it extend hospitality to the swarm of bees and to travelers alike.
Thus, as joy increases along with the expansion of the travelers' desires, [the tree flourishes].
"Alas, wicked wind! What is this that you have done to this young mango tree? [7] Thus ends the section on the Wind (Vāyupaddhati) from the *Prahlādana*.
The cātaka bird begs the cloud for water with its mouth open;
yet, out of generosity, the cloud constantly floods the earth with water.
For a long time, while languishing in the supportless sky, he has kept his upturned beak directed toward you.
O cloud, let alone your showers of water from afar; even your sweet sound has not been heard by the cātaka bird.
I consider the exaltation of that one cloud alone to be blessed.
The entire universe, including its mountains and forests, beholds his face;
and the ocean performs service for Prahlādana, who wields the plow, in order to support the weight of the whole world.
Even that [world] the fool, intent only on his own belly, treats as if it were the submarine fire (aurvāgni).
Now, for Vallabhadeva, there are no Kalpa-trees, no supernatural powers (siddhis), nor even deities who grant boons.
O Cloud, upon you this creation of the universe's interior rests.
O Cloud, dispel with your masses of water-laden showers the intense heat of the world for Vastupāla;
if not, then move far away and grant the sight of the moon's rays.
From Candraka:
O cloud, if you do not give even a few drops of water to the cātaka bird, then before long he will become worthy of receiving a handful of water from you. 7.
That even the heads of certain mountains, though firmly rooted, were suddenly struck down by mere blades of grass—
this is the behavior of a cloud unrestrained by abundant rain, for the course of water is difficult to fathom. 8.

Behold here this great lake, the sole life-sustainer for travelers, which is drying up excessively due to Bhāgavata-jayavardhana; O vain cloud, why have you increased the river flowing through the irrigation trench, thereby obstructing its proper course? 9

That salt ocean belongs to Prakāśavarṣa; it bestows lakes upon those who arrive as guests, while rivers are taken from it in measured amounts after being forcibly confined by embankments on all sides with great effort.
O Blessed One, Parjanya, we consider you alone to be the true renouncer; for even after reaching a well, one might somehow place a foot upon its rim, yet you have cast everything away.
(Prahlādana)
The heart-pleasing rivers, the lotus-lakes adorned with royal swans,
and the sacred streams born of the Snowy Mountains have been abandoned by you for my sake;
O cloud, now that this summer season has arrived, fierce with its burning heat like a fire.
O Parjanya, now accept this cātaka bird, whether it be a blessing or a transgression.
O Lamp of the World, before the ocean, whose shores are agitated by the playful surges that shake the great mountains—
O cloud, from where indeed do you vainly bestow your waters?
Attend with your rain to these trees that are exhausted by being consumed by the flickering flames of a blazing fire on all sides.
(12) By someone.
O cloud, abandon this delay; what is the use of these deep and sweet rumblings? Release your water instantly with a roar!
O pitiless one, look at the condition of this tree, its body entangled in the mass of flames from the forest fire ignited by the encounter with the wind.
Where the water instantly cast by Acala attains the state of pearls,
that ocean is renowned in the world as the beloved of the Tāmraparṇī.
O cloud of Svāti, though its mouth is opened under the pretext of a conch-shell, you have lost all interest in it; alas, you are now preoccupied with watering the groves of Khadira trees!
(14) — By Bhallaṭa.
Thus ends the *Meghapaddhati*.
Regarding this, I consider that sweetness of speech found in the cuckoo to be artificial, since once its wings have grown, it abandons those very people by whom it was reared. (1)
O cuckoo, as you have perched upon the branch of the mango tree belonging to the illustrious King Bhoja— where the clusters of blossoms are gathered by swarms of bees— the world considers you a fool.
Having heard the harsh cry of Karataka and Damanaka, which caused a fever in his ears,
the young cuckoo forgot even its own exquisite mastery of melody.
The loathsome cuckoo has indeed manifested his own base nature toward the illustrious Paṇḍita Bhīmasiṃha;
for at the very time of the latter’s exaltation, which bestows life upon others, the bird became silent.
In one place the sound of crickets, in another the quarreling of black crows; here the cry of ravens, there the clamor of monkeys;
and in yet another place this terrible roar of peacocks—alas, by the workings of fate!
"How does the young cuckoo warble so piercingly in its agitation?
"Is this the cry of a peacock? "Is the osprey not clever in speech?"—these two verses belong to some [unknown poets].
Is the parrot mute, or is that sweet-voiced one merely wounded in its cry?
O cuckoo, it is through your countless merits that you have obtained this sweetness and profound dignity;
why then are you so stubborn, not displaying your beauty here for a long time?
Whether by all one's possessions, or by any wealth that can be given away again,
or by means of protection, or even by one's life— whatever may be done for the benefit of others,
O cuckoo, that very thing shall now be accomplished by you through this sound.
Then, having somehow dispelled my laziness regarding his voice for even a moment,
[I partook] of food and drink through these playful, nectar-like words of the blind Vaidyanātha.
O clever parrot, compose [this] for those whose minds are deluded;
let this cuckoo, whose throat is nectar and who is free from the sin of the heat of serving others, frequent the groves of the forest. 8.
O young cuckoo, maintain your silence for now until these two wings become capable of taking flight into the expanse of the sky; otherwise,
you will surely be seen shattered by the blows from the beaks of crows enraged by a sound so alien to their own species.
O wretched crow! How is it that the chest of you, who have entered into a contest of sound with this male cuckoo, does not split asunder?
For hearing his speech, which is armored in nectar, even the minds of those observing a vow of silence become agitated and weave tales of love during the festival of spring.
In Bhallaṭa’s garden, the cuckoo desires to stay in hope of the nectar of mango buds, for he is the friend and minister of the King born of the Mind (Kāmadeva).

But when the ravens are stretching their throats, the cuckoos have begun their song, and there are the cries of "kreṃ" and the sounds of the fifth note, the listener does not perceive the difference between them.
Let the wretched crows and even the miserable ravens shriek in every banyan tree!

"O Pippala tree, O Pippala tree! May those who are skilled in song always utter their cries upon you—that other, indescribable one, whose manner of playful dalliance consists in the sweet, melodious warbling from the throats of cuckoos sporting with the skill that delights in devouring morsels of mango sprouts.
(12) These two verses are by some [unknown] authors.

Ah! That same young cuckoo, by whom days were formerly spent on the crest of the mango tree—resounding with swarms of bees drawn by the playful fragrance during the springtime of bliss—now, under the power of Time, runs about in every direction with its head repeatedly shattered by the pecking blows of wandering crows.
(The sound of the kettledrum: *Bhāṃkāra!* 13.
Let the gallinules cry out melodiously, let the peacocks sing with passion,
let the geese chatter sweetly, and let the lapwings warble;
for as long as fate does not allow him to reach the shade of the mango tree’s branches.
The young cuckoo, weary of the *kuṭaja* trees, has taken a vow of silence;
O *cakora*, remain silent for someone's sake, and you too, O parrot and pigeon, restrain your speech.
Let your cries cease, O peacock; let even your throat rest.

This sweet-voiced cuckoo, with its charming warbling made lovely by the consumption of fragments of fresh mango sprouts, scatters showers of nectar into our ears. 15 Thus ends the section on the cuckoo.

The water of the Gaṅgā is white, and the water of the Yamunā has the luster of collyrium; yet for you, O royal swan, as you bathe in both, that same whiteness of yours neither increases nor decreases.
May the Creator, though exceedingly enraged, destroy only the pleasure of the swan’s dwelling in the lotus-thickets.
Yet he is not capable of taking away his renowned fame for cleverness in the art of distinguishing milk from water. On some tree growing on the bank, with your body concealed by leaves,
pass this difficult rainy season with its falling torrents of rain.
But when she has turned away, in this lake where the lotuses have blossomed,
you are once again that very same swan, and those same graceful charms of yours are here. (By whomsoever [these were composed]).
Since you do not tolerate the rising of even that cloud— which dispels the heat of the worlds, which is capable of benefiting all, and which gratifies the eyes with its nectar-like form—
then by this much alone [your conduct is clear].
O swan, you are supremely white in color, yet you are black in your deeds;
O swan of the illustrious King Bhoja, you are as white as the luster of the autumnal moon and are elevated by the two wings of your [royal] lineage.
O ornament of the circle of the earth, is your firm footing not praiseworthy?
Yet, O dear one, that you create a division between milk and water once they have attained union—that is surely not at all fitting for one so exalted in every virtue. 5.
That is another lake where you were seen by the sages as they partook from their heart-pleasing faces the grains of rice placed upon the steps of its bank;
but this is a pond in a hamlet, where hunters, hiding themselves here amidst the clusters of lotuses, surely devise some means to capture a simpleton like you.
The lotus plants have withered and the waters have been dried up by the rays of the sun.
This flock of birds, their vision shattered by thirst, has met its destruction;
even these trees on the bank still possess the beauty of their foliage. O royal swan, what is this pursuit of pleasure on the shore of a dried-up lake? || 7 ||
"Friend swan, that depth is gone and the bank is surrounded by hundreds of fishermen; rise up and run away from this lake first!
Before this talkative crane, his body fouled by mud and water, can place his pair of feet upon my head while crying out loudly.
Thus spoke the one who delights in the sweet songs of intoxicated bees settled upon divine lotuses.

Having abandoned its place in the Manasa lake for a mere puddle of water, the swan now settles upon a small irrigation trench out of a desire for false comfort; what wonder is there if a lapwing now sets foot upon that swan, who has been reduced to a field of humiliation? 9
Although the dull-witted and those of ruined intellect— possessing deluded minds— deem milk to be the essence of all desires, the sustainer of life, and the vessel of affection;
nevertheless, there remain some who are extraordinary in both their speech and their conduct.
Whence could there be royal swans possessing intellects steady enough to distinguish milk from water?
In the crow, blackness is unnatural; in the swan, whiteness is innate. There is a vast difference in their depth; as for the distinction in their speech, what need is there to mention it?
Even among all these distinguishing features, my friend, where this is observed—"Who indeed are the crows, and who are the young swans?"—salutation to that region!

Elsewhere there may also be bodies of water possessing a flow of water as beautiful as a collection of lotus pollen awakened by the beaks of cranes trembling in fear of the mass of waves; yet [that place is unique].
But purity of intention is not easily found in this world; therefore, having gone far away, the royal swan follows Lake Mānasa out of a boundless longing born of affection.
(12) His form is the ancestral home of loveliness, and his gait is languid with grace.

O Swan, although you possess this great abundance of virtues— contact with lotus-pools, a charming and extraordinary warbling— I cannot endure your agitation in this quarrel with unworthy gadflies. 13.
For some of them,
her face was placed upon every lotus, reaching to its very edge; she sat again and again in the shade of each lotus leaf.
The waters of the lakes, already lukewarm, were made tepid by the hot tears of the swan as he gazed upon the direction darkened by clouds while preparing to depart. Thus ends the "Swan’s Path."
By becoming fans and sunshades made from the plumage of peacocks—
even those fallen from their natural positions— protection from heat was provided for others.
Why should there be slaughter of the peacock, when its crest feathers can serve as an ornament even as they fall away in due course?
O curious one, will there not be gain again? The forest will become a thicket of venomous serpents. O King of the Goyidoyika birds!
Ho, peacock! Why do you dance in vain, spreading your tail feathers, at the clapping of the hands of the Śabara woman? You fool!
These Kirāta gamblers, their forms concealed by the vast expanse of your brilliance, are secretly slaying you.
O brother, these clouds are the givers of life to the world and are dear to you;
your kinsman is the son of Hari (Kṛṣṇa), and Śaṅkara is your friend through the beauty of his neck.
Even Indra, with his friendly glances from those eyes of yours, has likely offered these friends of yours— though they are eaters of air— to be your prey, O peacock.
O brother, you are the lord of winged creatures, and you are the foremost even among the mountains in your crest.
In the drama, you are another blue-throated one, skilled in the vision of a thousand eyes;

O auspicious Śrīśa, the assembly of serpents serves as your chorus, and by your songs, O fair-eyed one, [the world's suffering] is severed. Nevertheless, due to the power of Time, these qualities of yours remain worthy of honor.
To whom do these belong on this Malaya mountain? What is the use of those various [birds] that are ineffective?
Even a single one from the flocks of crows, owls, pigeons, and cuckoos standing nearby—
If the peacock were to cry out, then the sandal tree— its bonds of entwined serpents shattered— would become worthy of service here, bringing joy to the minds of all people.
(Vasundhara)
O friend, who would abandon us—us of such variegated plumage who have long followed behind you? Or rather, let him abandon us!
Alas, O king of peacocks, this loss is yours alone; our station shall once again be upon the head of a monarch.
O blue-necked one, tell me, my friend, where are those sages today?
Those for whom your exquisite grace produces supreme delight—
alas, these cruel Śabaras, having suddenly heard this sound from afar, hasten to kill you with their feathered arrows! 8.
Thus ends the *Mayūrapaddhati*.
Oh, the delusion of that wretched crow, that he [should act] out of passion!
She dances and moves about in the vicinity of the peacock and the swan.
Even until death, these wretched crows, though they caw in rivalry with the peacocks,
do they know how to produce the *kekā* cry?
For those two who have heard the words of the royal swan, silence alone is appropriate for the crow;
fie upon the noisy vulture who, despite having heard the song of the sweet-voiced cuckoo, remains talkative!
O crow, having by chance reached this mango grove bent low with fruit, why do you deafen our ears with your harsh, clamorous cawing? Śrī Vallabhadeva.

If you maintain silence under the mistaken impression that you are a male cuckoo embarking upon the burden of love-making, why do the flashes of the innocent girl's sidelong glances not still move toward you?
How wonderful! How wonderful! Alas, alas! This is a great wonder, truly marvelous! This is the work of Haribhaṭṭa.
By chance, the Creator has produced a fitting arrangement:
that the nimb trees possess ripe fruits whose sweetness is worthy of being tasted, and that the world of crows is skilled in the art of devouring them. (5)
If,
seeing on some empty path a pot of curd that has fallen and is uncovered, one who is arrogant raises his neck with pride;
If the one-eyed crow does not perform its various natural actions, agitated by hundreds of transformations, when will it ever do so? (6) —
By Bhallaṭa.
Having searched through the streets, refuse heaps, crossroads, pits, and the ground outside,
and having by chance encountered a dead mouse wandering here and there due to its own dizziness,
a crow— cawing harshly from his hollow— boasts of his equality with Tārkṣya, who snatched away the nectar before the very eyes of the gods when they were defeated in battle.

Is he like Bhaṭṭa Rudranātha, his body adorned with a crest like a peacock; or like a parrot, a reciter of texts; or like a swan, a teacher of the gait of beautiful women; or like a śāri bird, sweet-voiced?
Or rather, alas! By what quality was this crow, who drips nectar into the ears like a cuckoo raised by a bird-keeper, placed in a golden cage?
It has neither beautiful feet, nor a lovely beak, nor speech that ought to be spoken.
Your gait lacks playful grace, nor is this your pure attachment to your own side;
O fool, crow, are you not ashamed here to utter such cruel, shrieking, and ill-omened words, thereby exposing your dissimilar nature while pretending to be a swan? 9.
Thus ends the "Track of the Crow.
Even while living, the crane is seen like a sage as he swallows fish;
yet the vulture does not eat even the dead. Fie upon the wretchedness of outward appearance! 1.
O crane, since you desire to abandon the conduct appropriate to your own kind and attain the state of a swan,
even so, if you must persist in the vow of a crane, then cast off this restraint.

Having reached the sky, what indeed does this heron not do? Seizing it with its beak, it scatters the excrement of Bhaṭṭa Govindarāja; it scratches the heads of the gods with the tips of its feet; and with its pride destroyed, it wanders fearlessly upon the heads of the virtuous. (3)

O crane! If you display such arrogance by stretching out your neck here, and carry this whiteness [of yours], yet you are one whose water is agitated by the excessive act of swallowing—why do you not, with this very beak, repeatedly [strike]? Who is equal to you?
Having quickly placed [him] nearby, you inspire confidence through the appearance of tranquility.
This crane, a master in the deceptive art of the heron, repeatedly desiring to seize each individual minnow,
practices his gravity by momentarily casting his eyes in all directions to feign indifference and by touching his own body with his beak. 5.

O you wretched crane! O you learned one! On the banks of the celestial river, you perform such a vow of asceticism with a mind intent on the enjoyment of the Unblinking One through meditation—[thus says] the illustrious Bhojadeva.

Thus, it is indeed improper for you to desire the path of the mind; for that [path] belongs to the swan whose intellect is purified by the discrimination between milk and water, and not to anyone else. (6) — By someone.
Let that cleverness of yours remain for now— cleverness sufficient to distinguish the true nature of milk from water,
those conversations of yours, and that graceful charm consisting of the pleasant placement of soft words;
provided, O crane, you understand even a small portion of this matter.
O friend, how is it that you, a swan, do not even remain silent for me?
For you possess no noble birth in the mind of Bhaṭṭabhallata, nor is your conduct marked by pure lotus stalks.
Neither by carrying a sacred thread nor by attaining stainless fame, nor by the arts of speech, does one become pure;
rather,
it is the deceitful heron who, white only on the outside, wanders about with pride and, with his neck falsely held high, vies with the swans.
"O crane, we call you 'baka' (the eater) because of the minnows in some small pond;
your livelihood there is appropriate, but it is not fitting for you to plunge into the ocean.
For there dwells the Lord of Waters, whose fish-eating crocodiles are single-mindedly intent on swallowing mountains, which are tossed about by the play of waves that lick the very clouds. (9)
These two [verses] belong to both [authors]. Thus ends the *Bakapaddhati*.
Let the poets weave a variegated garland of jasmine flowers.
There was a certain bee, an expert in discerning that fragrance.
(1) Although the bee approached out of greed for the scent of her lotus-face, the lotus-eyed woman nevertheless regarded him as one who had come for the purpose of stinging her. (2)
O bee, just as you here follow the species of the *madana* flower, so too do you here possess an intense passion for that which is of a different species;
therefore I know, O fool, that it is not merely your body that is black in this way, but even your conduct, O friend, is entirely black.
O young bee, do not fall into despair because you have not found the excellence of honey hidden within the *ketakī* flowers;
that very thing will be your gain if you pass through them with your body unhurt by the rows of thorns. 4.

"The night will pass; there will be a beautiful dawn; the sun will rise; the splendor of the lotuses will return"—while the bee, confined within the calyx, was thus reflecting, alas, alas! the elephant has uprooted the lotus plant. (5)
That very bee who once drank the honey from the lotus that was the abode of Śrī, from the lotus in the celestial river, and from the navel-lotus of Hari—
now, trembling with the pain caused by the contact with the heat of the rising sun’s rays, he wanders through the desert lands of the forest.
O bee, although you have become full of festive joy by smelling this fresh cluster of blossoms on this mango tree— which is worthy of being an ear-ornament for young women—
it is nevertheless improper for you to forget that venerable blue lotus.
Having reached the honey [of the flowers], you have cooed charmingly with your head shaking;
yet for some,
these [bees] are joyless in the *kunda* honey and distressed in the honey of the young *bakula*.
The bee does not linger for even a moment upon the *sāla* tree, nor does it find delight in the *lavaṅga*;
it forms no association with the *priyaṅgu*, nor does it frequent the *cūta*; rather, it drinks the honey from the play-lotus of the Goddess of Fortune. 8.
She for whose sake he did not care for the ponds filled with blooming blue lotuses out of his longing for union,
and embracing whom with a mind eager for her, he attained supreme bliss.
Seeing that sandalwood creeper broken by the bee, that it still lives with such fortitude—let it be so; yet it has not acted in accordance with its affection.
From afar it abandons the *campaka* flower, and it does not resort to the pollen of the lotus clusters.
He does not even smell the fragrance of the pāṭalā, nor does he find delight in the mango;
since he shows disregard for the mandāra and finds no satisfaction in the vicakila, I think, my dear, that this young bee must have tasted the mālatī somewhere.

These two [tusks] are unprecedented in their reversal of function as tongues; that restlessness of his ears and that gaze which has forgotten the distinction between self and other due to intoxication— what more need be said?
"O bee, you have forgotten everything! Why, brother, do you still serve this elephant whose trunk is empty within? What kind of obsession is this?
— Bhallaṭa.
Thus ends the *Bhṛṅgapaddhati*.
Whatever [in it] touches upon the moon rather than the sun has been composed by some wicked person who gave the name "firefly" (*khadyota*) to an insect. 1.
The moon, the lord of days, has gone somewhere, hidden by the clouds along with the stars;
O firefly, you may indeed shine in the empty sky. (2)
The moon shall depart, the splendor of the stars shall perish, and the jewel-lamps, having consumed the darkness, shall remain extinguished.
O firefly, that all this world shall become blind while you alone attain the dawn—that is far-fetched.
That night has passed during which even miserable worms like you shone in the profound darkness.
"Now that the day has arrived with the ten directions illuminated by the rays of the sun, even the moon does not shine here; O firefly, what then of you?
These [stars], though possessing only slight luster, shine resplendent in the sky made dark by clouds, their light unobstructed by others. Such is the verse of certain [poets].
Fireflies, whose brilliance has become exceedingly manifest, do not appear until the Lord of the Day (the Sun) has arisen; so too,
when the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) has come within the range of vision of this Lord of the Earth (the King).
When the moon has become a mere remnant of its glory and the host of planets has lost its luster,
the world has become so blinded by the onset of the rainy season that these fireflies are counted as skillful in the darkness.
O wretched one, you display such brilliance as Ānandavardhana’s; yet those other nights, though they too shine, are indeed different, for their spaces are shrouded by vast and dense darkness.
There stands a certain firefly, the foremost among the luminous, before whom even the talk of splendor among others in this world is silenced. (7) —
Śrī Bhojadeva.
Thus ends the *Khadyotapaddhati*: "O Cātaka bird, do not run toward this mass of smoke thinking it to be a rain-cloud;
for here, there will be nothing but water from your own pair of eyes."
That water, appropriate for his own elevation and timely for the occasion, was bestowed upon the *cātaka* bird by the cloud;
yet the wind drank it up in the interim—that certain wind which drew the rain toward its own desired destination.
Whatever was conceived in the heart of the *cātaka* during the rising of the cloud, even without the thought of a great desire, [the wind carried it away].

"Alas, what misery! From this very cloud, which was the cause for the method of bestowing desired fruits, there now falls the fire of a thunderbolt!"—these words belong to someone. "O swans of the pond, do not let your hearts be dejected by the sight of us, who are plunging into the sky, which betokens the contraction of your own dwelling."
These are your deer, who, among those who uphold vows honored by the world, are free from desire, for whom even the oceans are as mere blades of grass.
Delay your departure until the end of time; terrify them with the flashing of your lightning.
Frighten him greatly with your vast thundering roars and display the deep blackness of your face;
O cloud, for the sake of testing the mind of this cātaka bird who has no other resort,
you may inflict all these things upon him here, yet he will not beg for anything more than that from you.

O brother Cātaka, it is true that you, by begging, have made even such a one as he blacken his face, produce terror with his lightning flashes, and split the ears of those who pray for more with his own roars.
The cloud has indeed become equal to these two— [the king and the elephant]— in their state of being suppliants;
for [the cloud], having abandoned the lotus-pools of the illustrious Bhojadeva, leaving the rivers, and forsaking the oceans.
Having now abandoned the row of wells, alas, you have taken refuge in me alone;
therefore, O cloud, release two or three drops of water into the hollow of the beak of this deer who is fainting, lamenting, withering away, and parched with thirst. 7.
Though someone may possess wells of shimmering form and auspicious rivers on all sides,
nevertheless, for the cātaka bird, only the rising of a rain-cloud yields fruit.
O brother Cātaka, having abandoned on all sides the lotus-pools that contain masses of water to dispel heat,
and the ever-awake oceans whose forms resemble nectar—
seeing what in the sky do you, agitated by thirst, approach?
Why then does this cloud, like a great thunderbolt of fire, prepare itself against you?
O Śrī Vaidyabhānupaṇḍita, follow the bank of the lake; what enmity is there here with yourself?
O proud cātaka bird, drink but a little water;
the ancient cloud has been driven away by the winds of dissolution, and this new one is mercilessly discharging its mass of lightning bolts. 10.
Thus ends the section on the Cātaka bird.
Now begins the section on the lion, concerning those who move upon the earth. (22)
If even a lion endures being bound firmly and tightly,
how then can the jackals bear the royal insignia? (1) By whomsoever [composed].

Even this lion, whose mane is drenched with the blood of rutting elephants torn apart by the tips of his sharp claws, does not give rise to excessive or harsh anger, for he possesses abundant illusory power (or: abundant majesty). 2.
Of the Lord of the Blind (Andhaka).

O Lord of Beasts, if you have merely been occupied by mean mice dwelling in some hole they have somehow discovered within your cave, is that reason enough for you to harbor such despondency regarding your own prowess? —
By Śrī Vallabhadeva.
Although the lion fell into an extremely difficult well due to a deficiency in his ritual performance, even so,
he constantly desires in his mind the splitting of the frontal globes of elephants. (4) [Of someone]
His body is not towering, his tusks are not thick, nor is his trunk long;
truly, O elephant, this is no lion cub vying with you in mere outward display.
An invincible seed of splendor was indeed planted in his heart by the Creator in the past.
Because he is such a person, he considers even one like you to be a beast fit for his meal.
What is the use of the leaps of elephants, O Ānandavardhana? And what is the use of the fruitless displays of jackals?
O deer and buffaloes, abandon your pride; for are there no heroes in this empty place?
When the enemy elephant—possessing a mane fierce and bristling with the swelling of his rage—emits a low "hum" that resounds like the ocean, only then does his roar truly become a roar.
May the members of the assembly look on with smiles as that young elephant, intent on battle, stands equal to the lion who dispels the fever of pride from the elephant herds.
Even there, some loudly proclaim the equal strength of those two;
others suggest doubt, while still others are decidedly mistaken.
(Bhīmapaṇḍita)

He who formerly sported upon the mountains— their minerals washed away by the torrential downpours of fresh clouds shattered by the effortless play of his plowshare— that very same leader of the deer herd, now with his legs broken by the fall of a mountain peak, angrily devours his own paws once more at the shrill howling of female jackals. (8) [The sound of the kettledrum]
Let jackals, their excellence throbbing with an excess of rut, gather together at the outskirts of the villages and let out their howling cries on all sides;
yet there is another sound, as deep as the roar of a rain-cloud— the growl of the lion.
He who was heard of by the elephants— with their temples drying, their trunks motionless, and their ears still—
as they looked toward the sky, their wrath aroused by the roar of this mass of clouds belonging to Ralhaṇa; || 9 ||
O crow, do not become agitated while feeding on scraps of carrion at the top of this tree;
the lion—who has whitened his mouthful with pearls from the frontal globes of rutting elephants torn apart by his claws acting like diamond-tipped thunderbolts—has no desire for this.
(10) [Of the King of the Circle of Kings]
Thus ends the *Siṃhapaddhati*.
Now, the *Gajapaddhati* (23):
When the water in the well was shallow, the elephant extended his trunk because of the heat.
Even he was not smeared by the milk; rather, his own body was brought to a state of extreme lightness.
O elephant, if you are intoxicated, why [be concerned] with these fragments of worthless, straight-growing trees?
Follow Hari; he removes the itching of the temples caused by harsh claws.
If there is no drum for the rutting elephant who bears the auspicious birth of Vallabhadeva, then what [is the use]?
Enough with this clamor of the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by nectar!
The Vindhya mountain, our father, has been abandoned, as has the river Revā, our mother-like deity— both of whom were like Mālatī and Mādhava.
Elephants, whose minds were once tender with the bonds of affection, have been abandoned;
yet out of greed for you, they daily offer their bodies to be bound.
You remain far away, while the cruel goads roll upon the surface of their heads.
Where is this form resembling a mountain, and where is this gait so languid with grace even in its speed?
Where are those eyes half-closed in playfulness, or where is that trumpeting of yours?
Where is the joy of goring the ramparts, and where is that trunk? Alas, how it has come to this!
Having mounted you, who are under the control of another, the child makes you move at his command with his foot.
These two [earrings], beautiful like the buds of conch-shells, are upon the ears of someone; and a cluster of jewels is upon the neck.

*Sindūraprakara*: "If the decorative arrangement of tinkling bells were obtained by a royal mount—an elephant in captivity—on its head or near its flanks, then why would a wild elephant, whose body is grey with the dust of the mountains, not be worthy of honor? (6)
Though he has become like a mountain by devouring rows of fresh leaves from the *ralhaṇa* tree,
and though he has never been distressed by harsh sunbeams within its shadows;
O elephant blinded by rut, why do you tear apart the trees of the Vindhya forest— those very trees that served as armor for the Kirātas when they were struck down by fierce blows?
(7) In those [trees], cold water was drunk and lotus-sprouts were chewed.

O lordly elephant, shame does not even awaken in you as you muddify the waters, churn the lotus-beds, and dig up the banks— when, by plunging into the middle of that very lake and freeing yourself from fatigue, you were relieved of your heat! 8.

Far away the talk of the herd has vanished, and even that beloved mate, possessing every charm, has fled somewhere; by the power of fate, the forest ranges of the Vindhya mountains have become nothing but a memory of meditation.
Yet, O lordly elephant, you have endured the humiliation of captivity—truly, you are fortunate!
By virtue of relying on their resolve to subdue [the enemy], kings enjoy sovereignty;
yet for some,
this heat has not departed, they are not emaciated by thirst, and the dust from their bodies has not been washed away.
The elephant did not act according to his own will by taking a mouthful of grass; what talk can there be of sport?
Alas, the lotus was not touched by the elephant with its trunk extended far away; rather, this causeless clamor of buzzing has been commenced by the bees.
Thus ends the chapter on elephants by Umāpatidhara.
The Path of the Camel (24):
O servant, if this jujube tree of a slave-girl pleases you, why [do you not desire] the grape? Is it not the very fountain of nectar itself?
The body of Karpūrakavi is of an uneven form, and his voice causes fever in the ears;
yet that collection of defects has been concealed by the swift gait of Karabha.

The camel, its neck held high and stiff, feels shame before the very same physical form, speech, and enjoyments of the Bhallaṭa [elephant] that cause people to feel ashamed; oh, how base is this camel! 3.
The body of a lamp is coarse, its form does not captivate the eyes, and its crackling sound never brings pleasure to the ears;
thus, nothing about it is good. Yet, O camel, it is excellent that you find such delight in a thorny tree, even though it is equal to the lamp in these respects. 4.
O Bhoja, if this thorn-bush were not one whose leaves have withered, it would indeed be the very pinnacle of your face.
O young camel, where would your sprouts—resembling branches of the wish-fulfilling tree and possessing the luster of pure coral—be suitable for that creeper? 5
The love of couples does not arise from the possession of beauty; rather, someone seen by anyone generates happiness within.
Yet, the gaze of those whose hair is singed by fire falls instantly upon the arid lands, tawny with the withered stalks of the *bhuruṭa* creeper.
(6) These two [verses] are by some unknown author.

Leaving behind the forest region adorned with lakes variegated by white water-lilies and blooming lotuses—which might be mistaken for emerald-green gems—the young elephant remembers the rough desert paths; that delight in familiarity is irresistible, not a hostility toward virtue. (7) By Jinanāga.
O beloved of the young camel, why do you cry out in longing when that honey, so difficult to obtain even once, which you drank while in the forest, is no longer available?
Maintain your composure with the familiar leaves of the *pīlu* tree found in desert lands; for in this entire world, whose attainment of uninterrupted happiness is there?
O camel, alas, you wish to bray impetuously—this will surely cause a fever in the ears [of others].
Or perhaps your long and crooked neck shall be our refuge;
for when will the tongue, exhausted by its movements through the many openings of the throat, emerge from the mouth?
Who knows what will happen to whom after some time? (9)
These two verses are by Bhallaṭa:

A Dāśeraka, with neck outstretched and half his teeth bared, cries out as he cuts down this vine of grapes, which is as delicate as tender sprouts and whose circular basin has been filled with water resembling nectar— water that was once used by the wives of kings to deceive the interiors of their ornate water-jars.
Thus ends the *Karabhapaddhati*, the *Dhavalapaddhati* of Umāpatidhara. (25)
Because of the very wickedness of virtues,
the ox that is burdened with them sleeps soundly, its shoulders bearing no calluses—
so says the sage Vyāsa.
If the path were not mired in the mud of attachment,
O leader of the herd, then how could this quality of yours as a draft-animal be made manifest?
(Vasupāla)
He has no strength to bear a burden, nor does he possess the quality of speed anywhere;
yet the ox of the temple eats sumptuous food.
He has seven teeth, a pair of wobbly horns, and a brindled tail-tip.
His belly is marked by a moon-like spot, his body is in full bloom, and his movements are those of one who has transcended ordinary beings;
yet, in the mind of this rustic bull—who is ignorant of the multitude of qualities belonging to the foremost of bulls—there persists for a long time the delusion that he is a leader of the herd. 4.
This burden is not heavy for you; nowhere has your path been broken;
your strength is not shattered, nor is your body impaired by infirmity.
In this town, there is no one else equal to you in virtue; therefore, now—
O white bull, have you perhaps dropped your burden on the road while shaking off your load?
For the path is broken and thick with harsh, uneven stones,
and this driver is touching the limbs of those who have collapsed.
And just as these proud bulls, having practiced on the training grounds, now move about,
so indeed has that white bull Dhavala surely become distant at this time—
he who was the ornament of the cowherd settlement and who bore even the heavy burden on difficult terrain.
Even though all the draft animals have been made ready by their drivers, they cannot lift the shoulder-yoke simultaneously;
now, in this very town, the sale of that very white bull with its worn-out blanket is being proclaimed, for his body has been overcome by old age.

Purified by the excellent rites of the Śrauta tradition so that he might not fall into a state of indigence, he was accepted as a bridegroom by the gods Tripurāri and Hari with their celestial brides;
and by the dust of his footprints cast forth, the hosts of ancestors became enjoyers of the fortune of the gods.
"Fie on fate! That bull which formerly used to carry a garland around its neck has now become a beast of burden in the house of a Turuṣka.
[Colophon: These [verses] belong to certain [authors]. Thus ends the *Dhavalapaddhati*.
The Path of the Deer (26):

Granted that deer in the forests live on grass, which is easily obtained without effort; yet they do not display wretchedness before the wealthy. Alas! We, it is said, are animals, though we consider ourselves wise.
This is a deceptive man made of straw, with arrows of grass and a bow of grass;
yet even so, O young deer, you abandon the stalks of rice in the field.
These two [verses] are by some unknown authors.
A fresh cluster of rice blossoms, sweet as dripping drops of milk from a broken stalk, was by chance encountered by a deer wandering at will;
its inner anguish was revealed by the tender grass it had consumed, now appearing as if scorched by the fire of its sighs.
Meditating upon her every day like a sage in the forest, he withers away.
Alas, how many deer do not roam again and again on every peak and in every forest of Dharmakīrti?
Yet, even that—some indescribable fragrance of the forest—shines forth as a cause for the delight of the minds of certain people. 4.
Come slowly, chew your cud, fall into sleep, and then cast off your fatigue; wander about as you please!
That vulgar person is far away; these are indeed sages. O young deer, why do you fear them without cause? 5. [This verse is part of the preceding context.]
"This belongs to two [deer]," "this is that very clearing," "this is a thicket of fresh grass sprouts," "this is that very doe"— thus pride arose in the heart of the deer.
But he does not know that here, concealed by the creepers, comes a hunter equipped with a sharp arrow.

Alas, what cruel fate! Though the days for this deer— whose hooves were crushed by Indra’s thunderbolt, whose limbs were covered by splashes of blood clearly visible from the strikes of arrows, and who was distressed by the heat of a forest fire— had reached even the hermitage, they were all full of compassion for everyone else.
Even when saying "Do not fear," this sage remained silent;
for the sun blazed in the midst of the sky, the forest was consumed by forest fires,
the quarters were obscured on all sides by columns of smoke, and the paths were jagged with rocks.
Thus, while the deer ran toward the slaughter-pit smeared with blood as fast as its breath would allow, the hunter, out of compassion, did not even fix arrows upon his bow.
Alas! This deer has no support even in the sky, and it is without refuge.
Where shall he go? Where shall he come? Where shall he dwell? Where shall he enter?
The quarters of the sky are ablaze and the earth is empty of the company of the virtuous;
Time, the lord of the base, strikes again, feigning indifference. 9.
Thus ends the section on the *hariṇa* meter.
The Pathway of the Ocean (27):
You are always the refuge for the great life-force of living beings and you never abandon your boundaries; within your womb there exist multitudes of jewels.
Thus, O Ocean, why was such great majesty displayed by you in the midst of the waters—
that sinful Aurva fire, which brought about the destruction of your life and filled your own belly?
[This was done] for the sake of the Four-faced One and Mahādeva.
It is neither contempt nor a lack of discernment on the part of the ocean;
rather, it is its very greatness that great jewels lie submerged in the mud upon its shore.
(2) By someone.
Just as the ocean does not observe the boundary known as the shore,
so too [the world] does not observe this other rule: "One must not provide assistance to those who are thirsty," according to the *Bhāgavatāmṛtadatta*.
Although he was bound by mountains, and although his entire wealth was plundered during the churning of the mountain,
nevertheless the ocean remained consecrated to the protection of the mountains who were terrified of the thunderbolt.
What, then, has been gained by this wicked sea, having taken up water from the mouths of rivers on all sides?
It has been turned into alkaline ash, offered as an oblation into the mouth of the submarine fire, and cast into the hollow depths of the belly of Pātāla.
May there be well-being for Rīṣuka;
salutations to the forest of corals; may the string of pearl-oyster shells be auspicious.
I have obtained everything from this ocean that I desired, insofar as I have not been torn apart by its cruel sea-monsters. (6) Indrakavi says:
"Alas, we merchants feel great shame, for even we are entering this mass of waters!"

O Lord of Waters, there are others in this world who bear the conceit of greatness, whose thirst is inflamed as they draw water from wells near the banks of your own waves— waves that have been superimposed upon your very body— and who devour the three worlds; why then are you alone placed at the forefront of those doers of harm?
O Vāḍava fire, you who alone delight in the moon—the source of all defects—and who, desiring the destruction of the world, always carry that fire while disregarding the loss of your own body; alas!
[This is] of Śrī Bhojadeva.
That Paśupati became adorned with the crescent moon as his ornament; that Viṣṇu was graced by Śrī; that the Lord of the Gods became the occupant of Airāvata;
and that immortality was attained by the gods, whose pairs of eyes were blossomed with joy.

All this is indeed due to the wonderful power of the Ocean, whose abode is the service of others. O Lord of the World, who among those who bestow the Lakṣmī-jewel, the Kaustubha, the Pārijāta tree, wine, elephants, horses, swords, and nectar—has not been made successful by you here? Who has not been made a recipient of his desires? [This is followed by: O Indra-kavi, who in this world has not been rendered fulfilled by you, the Lord of the Earth, through your generosity? [The list of gifts follows: the Goddess of Fortune, the Kaustubha gem, the Pārijāta flower, wine, elephants, horses, swords, and nectar. Who has not been made a recipient of these? Who has not been made successful? (Note: The text provided contains a mix of the Ocean's praise and a specific address to "Indra-kavi," likely a poet or patron. The translation reflects the structure of the verse as it appears.)
But, O Ocean, because you were presented to the Lord Śiva— who was standing nearby— after he had been worshipped with a moon-flower, we suffer from that very poison.
Ah, O Mass of Waters, out of fear of the wrath of the wielder of the thunderbolt, the Son of the Mountain has approached you with affection on his wing.
If, moreover, this submarine fire dwelling within you scorches every limb with its flames, then who will be his refuge?
O Ocean, you who have surpassed the Bodhisattvas in sportiveness, what is the use of further words?
There is no one else like you who has taken a vow to bring about the welfare of others;
for out of compassion, you provide assistance to the desert, thereby bearing the weight of fame acquired through your readiness to perform acts of kindness for thirsty travelers.
What need is there for your [glory], which pervades all the quarters of space with the play of waves that spread, roar, roll, flash, surge, tremble, sink, rise, and flow?
Alas, O Ocean, you who reflect upon your own righteousness, your vast salt water is of no avail for quenching the thirst of a traveler exhausted by the summer heat; it is merely a great waste.
For with your waves you touch the sky, with your jewels you illuminate the depths of the netherworld, and with your waters you cover the earth.
Fie on all that, O Ocean, that you have been abandoned on your shore by travelers who, eager to take water, instead shed streams of tears!
Even as one ascends to heaven, one desires to shield oneself from the brilliance of the luminous.
The rain-cloud thunders loudly, filling the earth with its waters;

yet, O Ocean, having quickly provided certain drops of water for the livelihood of others, there is no change in your majesty, even though you possess vast accumulations of water in your presence. 15.

Travelers drink even brackish water from a marsh; nowhere else do they find water because of the saltiness of you, O Ocean. Thus, this name "Samudra" (the Ocean) alone is fitting for you, yet these other names of yours are not meaningless, as they do not denote a different reality.
Ambhodhi, jaladhi, payodhi, udadhi, vārāṃnidhi, and vāridhi— these are synonyms for the ocean;
yet for some,
even if it lacks such vastness, it still possesses that depth of the ocean.
Or perhaps such compassionate grace toward all sentient beings would not exist;
for by the powerful submarine fire, which blazes within, consumes the waters, and emits a wreath of flames, who would not have been reduced to nothing but ashes? (17)
Thinking, "This is the sole abode of pearls" and "This is a mine of jewels," we have resorted to this ocean with minds agitated by thirst.
Who could have known that a sage would, in a mere moment, drink it up along with its mass of gasping whales, having placed it within the hollow of his own cupped palms? 18.
Thus ends the *Samudrapaddhati* by Vararuci.
(28) *Ratnapaddhati*: How many pieces of glass, even when adorned with gold, do not steal the splendor of a jewel?
And how many of the unintelligent do not carry those very same pieces on their heads, mistaking them for jewels?

Those who wipe away the darkness from the eyes, and by whom the ocean is truly called a "mine of jewels"—alas, those gems are indeed distinct; yet even among them, there are further distinctions known to the connoisseurs.
Make bracelets with lac-dye, or fashion a crest-jewel out of glass!
You are skilled in the deception of an artisan; this merchant is a rustic and ignorant master.
Indeed, your audacity is excessive, O unshakable one, in that you take pride in yourself even before those who know the truth of being burnt, placed on the grindstone, and rubbed by the whetstone.
What kind of purity belongs to that dull crystal stone compared to Vimalasarasvatī,
which is split apart by an adjunct entering within it according to its own whim?
Is the moonstone of Bhallaṭa not as clear as the sunstone?
Yet, there is a distinction between the two in their emissions: one produces nectar, while the other produces fire. (4)
Indeed, that single jewel alone was born within the ocean, the mine of gems— that which,
resting upon the chest of Murāri, does not wander among the palaces of wicked kings.
It grew from the rays of the moon within the belly of the great ocean.
The gems of the necklace, though they touch the heart, speak of the removal of its fever; yet,
by virtue of their physical proportions, do these jewels become more illustrious than those [gems] of Vallabhadeva?
Nevertheless, those very [rays] sport upon the crests of kings, not upon the boulders of the mountains.
O fool, why do you strike at someone? O blind one, why do you scorch? Or why, O wretched one, do you torment the moon-gem?
O brother, the birth of this [work], which possesses an inexhaustible essence, can be accomplished solely through the favor of the nectar-like rays [of the moon].
O Indrakavi,
why do you vainly wish to protect those merits of yours, even while accepting this very flaw?
O pearl, because of your stainless nature, these [other gems] reveal themselves even more clearly than you do.
Yet, due to the delusion of someone, or perhaps through the misfortune of those who dwell upon the peaks of the mountain-kings, if the emerald has not been recognized by anyone; || 9 ||

Likewise, having fallen even upon the street, what does he not do? The quarters of the sky seem as if smeared with waves of blossoming blue luster. O Jayadeva, by what pitiless person have you been uprooted from your position of ease?
Or by whom in this land has it been desired to sell?
Let alone a buyer capable of bearing the burden of such an expenditure of wealth—O brother emerald, there is not even one capable of examining you. 11.

May it be well with you, O Sarvavarman; do not even in your dreams entertain such a thought as to how these [Vedas], having fallen from their established state, might somehow survive after me on Mount Rohana.

yet now, O Campaka, you put me to shame with your flowers so replete with fragrance. 30. Aśoka.

for otherwise, with its very self distressed by the ripening of fruit, it would be truly sorrowful. 31. By someone.

Though longing intensely, they do not taste the sweet and soft fruits with unrestrained relish;
[this is] the breadfruit tree of the illustrious King Bhoja.

Out of regard for others, it is as if its sheath of beauty has bristled with horripilation in the guise of thorns.

remembering the little water they drank in their youth, [long for it].

The fruit of the plantain and the palmyra tree, having borne fruit without providing any benefit,

Having known your heart, that very [knowledge] causes it to split asunder; for this reason, you are to be revered. (36) —From the birch-bark manuscript of Śrī Bhojadeva.
