Moreover, a single *mālatī* flower alone dispels the illusion that it is a bee.
O cruel *mālatī* blossom, why do you distress someone?
"Who indeed will not place you upon their head— this [flower] which was surely plucked by someone from the tip of a creeper, possessing such purity, sweetness, form, and dignity? (40)
O Nammaya,
where is your abode among these blossoming ketaki creepers?
You possess a most wonderful fortune,
since the bee, unaware that its own body is pained by thorns, begins to serve you alone. 41
O Great God, the grandfather of kings,
you have respectfully disregarded the fruit-bearing trees that bend low along every path.

For that palm tree, which has no shade to offer, what can be said of its fruit? Even with its withered leaf, it failed to provide any use to the simple-minded traveler who, out of distress from his long journey, had approached its foot from afar seeking refuge. 432.
What is the use of those other trees grown and tended by someone else when there is the true *aśvattha* tree?
The Nyagrodha tree of Mādhava-Māgadha protects one who has grown [in strength], guards from hell, and destroys misfortunes when touched. 43. Mādhava-Māgadha’s Nyagrodha.
May the earth, his mother, be abundantly shaded by the banyan tree, whose hundreds of lofty branches are spread wide with the weight of its fruit and where flocks of birds are nestled. (44) —
Vallabhadeva.

The Madhūka flower’s brilliance was endured by its leaves during the summer heat; its moisture during the onset of the rains; and its coldness during the winter—by those very leaves which formerly had nothing but it for their refuge.
"Even though the time for fruit has now arrived, what is this [fruit] without them?"—
remembering these words, the madhūka tree weeps as if in grief with its falling flowers. (45) By someone.
The śālmali tree has a body defiled by thorns and possesses no dense shade; whence could there be sprouts? Its flowers have lost their fragrance, and its hollow of leaves is not captivating.

What can we say of its ripening fruit, that we feel shame even at the mention of it? O silk-cotton tree (śālmali), by what merit have you become a boundary-marking tree? Your flower is scentless; your fruit is useless for hunger; and your leaf is incapable of any purpose.

This sapless body of yours is surrounded by external thorns and potsherds; its growth only serves to attract vultures. O brother Śālmalī tree, what more can be said? There is nothing worthy of your great stature. 47.
For both of these,
the babūla tree— though itself bearing no fruit— suffers cutting, splitting, and being dragged upon the ground.
This babūla tree, having endured its fall into a ravine, now stands as a thorn hedge;
alas, like a wicked man, though possessed of abundant fruit and joined with the sky, it does not allow the virtuous to enjoy even a portion of them due to its sharp thorns. 48.
O Nimba tree, what is the use of saying more? Your fruits are fruitless, for these crows devour without exception those that have reached maturity. 49
Whether one strikes a neem tree with an axe, or treats it with honey and ghee, or honors it with perfumes and garlands— it remains bitter to everyone. (50) [These are also among them.]
O Khadira tree, we tolerate venomous serpents for the sake of the sandalwood; how can a beautiful object remain unprotected?
Tell me, for what purpose have you gathered these thorns to guard your own inherent excellence? 51
In this world, there is no place belonging to Bhallata that is not covered by thorny khadira trees;
nor are those khadira trees absent which are themselves shrouded in crooked thorns.
Those crooked thorns are nothing that do not pierce the vital organs;
therefore, abandon this futile exertion and, alas, endure the fatigue of the journey. (52) Śāli.
There exist on this earth even more trees whose branches have ceased to grow, yet they possess abundant fruits that dispel the suffering of living beings;
nevertheless, we praise the loftiness of the *śāla* tree, whose body is adorned with only two or three leaves.
By which virtuous man, having given his own head, has no one been gratified?
By whom we were brought forth and daily nourished with affection—that Nammaya—[who has not been honored by that deed]? 53.
He who formerly was not even able to endure our being pressed like blades of grass,
having now recognized the time for his fruit, desires to cut off our heads;
yet the rice plants seem to cry out with the clusters of droplets falling from their frosty tears.
Cotton is praiseworthy, for by its virtues it has won over pure pearls,
which now shine beautifully within the jar-like breasts of young women. 55
Even the crushing [of the body] is more unbearable for him; alas, the ordeal on the scales,
the tearing of the nails by village women,
the pain of being struck with lutes, the drinking of drops of water from the temple floor smeared with elephant ichor, and the blow of the ritual brush!
With the mind intent on accomplishing the welfare of others, what indeed has he not accepted for the sake of cotton?
For some, even these are flax.
The birch tree endures the cutting away of its own bark for the sake of helping others;
whereas the hemp plant serves only to bind others—behold here what kind of difference there is between them! (57) The thorn-apple.
Maheśa bears you upon his head; through union with you, the victorious purification of mercury turns this triple world into gold. O golden tree, surely no one other than you extends such service!
Who indeed could exist beyond that, had you not attained the state of being easily accessible?
O Madman, [you did so] by perceiving the thorny fruit of the *prahlādana* tree as its opposite.
You harbor enmity toward the jackfruit tree for no reason at all.
The virtuous laugh [at you] but do not associate with you; even if they were to associate with you, they would become deluded and would never associate with you again. 59
Even for a blade of grass born along the bank of a river, its birth is beautiful,
since it becomes a support for the hands of distressed people sinking in the water. 60
O Vallabhadeva, what is the use of these lofty trees that touch the sky yet bear no fruit?
Blessed indeed is that Ulūṣa tree standing on the riverbank,
for he has resolved thus: "By the power of these rising waves tossing with the water,
I shall either rescue the people who are drowning, or else I shall drown along with them."
"Of Rāṇaka":
thus ends the description of various trees.
Thus concludes the section on trees in the *Sūktimuktāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva.
The Path of the Forest Fire (34):
O forest fire, those virtuous trees dwelling on the mountain peaks have been needlessly burnt by you, incited by the winds—O deluded one! 1.
The greatness of this fire, the consumer of dry wood, has been witnessed as it burns the forest— an unimpeded sacrifice for the multitudes of twice-born men of diverse castes.
It is he whose immeasurable bow-staffs, possessing great majesty, are themselves endowed with excellent qualities.
As you burn that bamboo thicket, what discernment does this forest fire possess?

O forest fire, even when a cloud has risen—one that captivates with its singular, profound affection for the world—the trees do not abandon their graceful dance of exultation; therefore, that fault is yours alone.
The beasts and birds are scattered, the deities of the groves have been brought to distress, the quarters of the sky are obscured by naturally dark smoke, and the earth is scorched,
having reduced these great trees— along with their flowers, sprouts, and fruits— to ashes.
By a surging forest fire, the woods have been reduced to nothing but anthills;
by some others,
the entire circle of the quarters has been blackened with the grass and ashes of trees, down to their very roots.
Everything has been consumed, and not even a single fawn remains among the herd of does.
Alas, what a tragedy! Even the sages dwelling in the forest have been scorched; having thus performed the work of Death, what is the use of this forest fire, whether it be extinguished or blazing?
He climbs a tree, enters a chasm, vies with mountains, bares his fangs, struggles on the surface of the earth, and hides within the interior of a thicket— such is the state of Umāpatidhara.
It wanders within the hollow of the tree-trunk, it clings to the creeping vines— what is there that the fire, having fallen under the power of the wind in the forest, does not do?
O you who cause forest conflagrations and bring about the end of the woods, your flames do not please me; for people do not desire the growth of one who is intent on burning his own refuge—
this mountain whose roots were fashioned by the ill-disposed Creator to encircle him.
Or who would not have mistrusted you, O forest fire, who bring such distress to the world?
Thus ends the section on Forest Fires in the *Sūktimuktāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
The Path of the Gods (35):
Here is a terrifying flock of crows; here is the cry of owls;
here is a formation of vultures; and here is a family of herons.
In this cremation ground, which is devoid of all virtues and like a blasted desert,
there are indeed not even two or three birds with sweet voices. Everything has wandered away with extreme speed, and the earth has resounded with a great clamor.
Alas! For so long, what has this traveler not done—standing there in dejection with sighs for tears? And yet, the cruel desert, naturally harsh, has not, alas, become even slightly moistened.
Why are you dejected, and why do you appear to be momentarily deranged?
Furthermore, none of your actions are undertaken with prior reflection;
for even knowing it to be waterless, you have entered the desert.
O desert well, since you provide cool and sweet water which the traveler desires,
the day has ended and we have rested; you have done us a supreme favor, O well, and we are too ashamed to describe what remains.
"By your own meritorious deeds, may you become one whose waters never dry up for travelers;
and may this śamī tree on your bank also provide dense shade for them. (4) — By Kasyapa.
That which experiences pain for the sake of another, which is sweet even when broken,
and whose transformation is indeed desired by all here— if it does not reach full growth, it is simply because it has fallen upon unsuitable ground.
Is this the fault of the sugarcane field, and not rather of the desert land which lacks all virtue?
O traveler, why have you fallen down so unexpectedly, O King of the Moon? What other recourse is there for you?
To you who are thus parched with thirst, this man of wicked mind conceals the water; O traveler, be angry at this misplaced and untimely craving,
for the desert path, whose majesty and power are renowned throughout the three worlds, remains as it was.

Are Abhinavagupta’s mango trees lovely, their heads bowed down by the weight of fruit? Are the plantain trees delightful, providing cool shade that dispels the heat? And are the campaka trees fragrant, now in full bloom?
These are those very [mirages] before you, licked by unrestrained and fierce camels and then abandoned;
O fool, why do you wander aimlessly in this windless desert, falsely seeking to die?
(7) — By Prakāśavarṣa.
Thus ends the section on Maru (36), the section on descriptions of miscellaneous subjects, within the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa:
"If you roam about with a bull, what indeed is the lightness of the elephants of the quarters?"
You fashion bracelets and earrings from serpents; there is no loss to the gold.

If you carry on your head the dull-rayed moon, what indeed is the disgrace to the friend of the lotus, the lamp of the three worlds? You are the lord of the worlds—what more can we say? (Umāpatidhara)
O Viṣṇu, by you, having abandoned the Lord of the twice-born who possesses stainless wings, a great burden has been placed upon the serpent;
for those whose intellects are generally deluded by fortune do not know—without doubt—what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. 2.
[Of the four-faced Mahādeva]
O friend jackal, you have raised your tail high, placed it upon your head covered in withered matted hair,
swallowed morsels of flesh from elephants that perished by chance,
and dwelt for a very long time within the hollow of an empty cave.
What can we do about this, since you have not attained the status of a lion?
By fate, Bhaṭṭendurāja’s forest is burning all around on an exceedingly powerful forest fire.
When the lion, arrogant with pride, rushed into the jackal’s deep cave and slew him,
it was not out of compassion; rather, because of that, he now runs about with tail held high, crying, "I am the one who grants safety to the lions in this forest!"

O boar, that playful sport of Abhinavagupta in the forest of his five-faced [Śiva]—which churned the mire of the fat and marrow from the elephants he tore apart and served as a lake for the sport of drinking [the blood]—has been defiled by you because of your remaining lifespan.
While another sow gives birth to offspring capable of making the lotus pond stalkless, the marshland withered in parts, and the water turbid with mud,
this [earth] remains submerged within the tusk by the mass of waves from the four oceans.
Only she whose child remains upon the earth is truly possessed of sons and elephants;
Indra alone knows the amorous dalliance with Rambhā—
does a rogue who employs a pot as a servant know the celestial nymphs?
For whom does this Garuḍa—who effortlessly bears Dāmodara, who has placed the worlds within his belly—act as a remover of fatigue?
Upon which tree might he perch to dispel his weariness? May he remove [our] exhaustion. 8.

For what reason does Hari constantly endure hundreds of misdeeds— such as the felling of the sandalwood tree that delights and increases the essence of passion for Mālatī and Mādhava— despite being a celestial elephant? 9.
Let other people be somewhat terrified by the word "non-serpent" (ahirahi), for it is a term of alarm;
yet the food of the Lord of Birds is as beautiful as the petals of a fresh lotus-stalk.
Even though Vāsuki indeed dwells upon the head of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva).

Nevertheless, Śeṣa alone is indeed more praiseworthy among all beings, for he is capable of bearing the world's burden. O Rohaṇācala, who could possibly measure you against the mountains? Thus says Vallabhadeva.
For whom even fragments of stone are the ornament of the mountains;
is the ocean not the abode of jewels? Is the earth not firm?
Is the sky not a vast expanse? And what indeed is not high for those of meritorious deeds?

O Rohaṇa! Indeed, by your acceptance of the patient endurance of the unhesitating wounds inflicted by the multitude of supplicants, you, the ornament of your lineage, have become worthy of worship by the three worlds.
For those whose minds are awakened to the happiness of contentment, you are no different from common clay.
For those men whose minds are agitated by greed for wealth, [Mount Meru] remains far away.
For whose sake, then, was such a place of riches created by Fate?
To me, Mount Meru—whose golden majesty is complete within itself—does not appeal. 14
The Pathways of Love by Vidyāpati:
The Pathway of the Departure of the Beloved (37)
May that Kāma of wondrous deeds, by whom the three worlds were conquered through his union with the formless maiden, grant you the fulfillment of all desires. —
Kṣemendra.
I praise those beautiful-eyed women who, with their very glance, restore to life the God of Love who was burnt by the eye of the Odd-eyed One (Śiva); they are the victors over Virūpākṣa.
(2) — By Rājaśekhara.
At the rising of the sun, the traveler’s mistress— her heart trembling at the sound of the birds of dawn—
dispelled her sleep with tears warm from the corners of her eyes falling upon his shoulder.
I am unable to endure even a moment in the presence of this woman, whose body is scorched by the fever of separation as if it were made of red-hot iron.
Thus, the mind of the fawn-eyed woman, unable to remain still, departed along with her beloved who was traveling abroad.
From a thousand well-spoken verses, these two alone have clung to the hem of her silken garment; her creeper-like arms were not placed upon the threshold of the door.
Neither did she fall at his pair of feet, nor were the words "stay" spoken by her;

yet, when the time came for that rogue to set out on his way—his path darkened by clouds like rows of bees—the beloved was blocked by the slender woman through a river-flood created by the torrent of her tears. 5.
He was gazed upon for a long time by her with timid eyes; he was entreated with folded palms; afterwards, he was held back by the hem of her garment and embraced without artifice.
When that cruel and deceitful man, having thus rejected everything, proceeded to depart—

"First my life was abandoned by my beloved, then you, my lover; whether at the end of the first watch, in the middle of the day, later than that, or even when the entire day has passed— O dear one, will you come here?"— these two verses belong to Amaruka.
Thus, with words choked by tears, the young woman prevents the departure of her beloved who wishes to go to a land reachable in a hundred days.
When the departure of her lover— whose name is pronounced with a *jhalla-jhalla* sound— has somehow been announced, she bows her head for a moment, her limbs tormented by the pangs of separation.

Then, beholding him and asking, "When did you arrive?", the innocent girl embraced him and attained great joy. (8) "Placing you—who would have utterly destroyed all my sorrows—into sorrow myself, why should I consider departing?
This descent of yours into the waters, never before witnessed by my eyes, will surely today lead to the fall of my very life. (9)
The superior man, performing virtuous deeds, protecting all that is to be protected, subduing his enemies, and spreading his fame, enjoys the objects of the senses with ease.
Any other person here is inevitably like a moving log; all this [distinction] arises from energy.

"O lady whose face is as beautiful as the moon, it is possible that for a few days this separation from you may be endured by me; yet, even on some occasion, you should remember us from among your thousands of elegant sayings."
This might indeed be so, O Lord, if Fate were to grant me the memory of my past births;
but how could there be such recollection even in a single life, O Beloved?
My very life-breaths have departed along with you—where, then, can there be a single birth in common until this day? (11)
Others, wretched women, seek to turn back their departing lord of life with trembling tears, oaths, and prostrations at his feet.
"May it be an auspicious day; may it be a blessing; may it be a fortunate morning for you as you depart.
My dear, once you have gone forth, you will hear from me whatever I have done out of love that was appropriate for your journey. — Amaruka.
Listen to all these words in brief, O friends: this friend of yours is surely the complete fruit of our lives;
for in this separation, she trembles violently like a lamp in a gale.
While she exists, we who are free from darkness must protect her in every way.
Oh, what a fortunate man he is, who has provided for us protection from the evil of separation by means of these thousands of well-spoken verses!
You wander at your own will; why do you not consider that this brings us terror? Alas!
During these days made noisy by the songs of cuckoos proceeding in the fifth note, and during the moonlit nights, what indeed can we helpless ones do? 14.
"O noble one, what good fortune do we speak of for you as you travel on the road? Or rather, our minds are bewildered by doubt as to whether her very life-breaths will depart here as she goes.
Yet, through our auspicious merits, may there be a journey resulting in well-being, and may she return here to us."
"May we see you again when we have returned; tell us, do life-breaths ever turn back?
Where is that coral gem which possesses the luster of her bimba-red lips, even in a dream? (15)
O traveler, what can even austerities resembling the beauty of her smile achieve? Can pearls ever equal the luster of gold, even after hundreds of plunges into fire?
Why do you abandon your beloved wife, who is like a jewel, for the sake of some wealth? 16.

"You are my life from a thousand well-spoken verses; you are my second heart; you are the moonlight for my eyes; you are nectar upon my limbs"—having thus entreated that slender maiden with hundreds of such endearments, she has become peaceful; or rather, what is the use of anything further?
As long as Bhavabhūti’s heart does not attain confidence through long acquaintance,
and as long as his face does not release the warmth of his hand entirely, [so long shall this work remain incomplete].
"O dear friend, these tresses of mine do not at all attain evenness; nevertheless, today he departs on a journey toward me, utterly merciless.
(18) By someone.
The departure was made by the bracelets; it went incessantly with the dear friends, the tears; not even for a moment did she remain with her fortitude; and her heart resolved once more to go.
When the beloved had set her mind on departing, everyone set out together.
When one must depart, why is this caravan of life, dear friends, and loved ones abandoned?
Thus ends the section on "Departing for Beloved Ones" in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
[Someone] has cast their helpless body upon a bed...
Having quickly entered there by her own effort, she rises and ascends the palace; looking through the openings of the windows at her husband’s path, she falls into a state of delusion. || 1 ||
Having heard some sound somewhere outside and thinking it was the return of her beloved, the charming woman rose from her bed and, having restrained herself upon hearing sounds from the side...
Then she, whose eyes were filled with no small curiosity, listened.
These two [are derived] from a thousand well-spoken verses.
Having approached the gateway, she looked toward the quarters,
sighed deeply, and rested her hand upon her cheek;
then, realizing he was right there before her, she became filled with agitation.
Having realized it was false, was she not like one who had merely painted [the image]? || 3 ||
Of Pṛthvīdhara.
The sandalwood paste applied between her breasts, dried by the heat,
shone like the ashes of a mind consumed by the fire of the god of love.
Of someone.
"May these [rivers] never be interrupted"— out of compassion,
as if wishing to lead the rivers to the ocean with incessant floods of tears,
[so spoke] Śrī Vaidyabhānu Paṇḍita. 5.
The lotus stalks, capable of dispelling the heat, were not available for the lady with the arched brows; for how can one's desire be fulfilled by those who procrastinate?
(6) — Bhaṭṭavṛddhi.
Even though her heart was being consumed by the fire of love,
that the affection remained exactly as it was— this was like a marvel. (7) [By Śakavṛddhi]
The young girl draws lines but does not count them; her palm-surface is washed by a flood of intense tears, as she fears that the final day of the appointed time might arrive. (MORIKĀ)
As she utters words of sorrow, her tears repeatedly choke her throat,
as if out of fear that her meager remaining life is about to be extinguished. (9)
— Bhaṭṭabāṇa.
Whatever lotus petal was placed upon her body by her friends to allay her feverish distress,
that very thing would wither away on every side, as if out of shame at its failure to provide relief. (Verse 10) —
By Kasyapa.

How can a slender woman pass her days— days that are enveloped in the fragrance of clever bees and whose quarters are made terrible by the mingled cries from the throats of cuckoos warbling with intoxication? (11)
— By Taruṇabāṇa.
"O necklace of lotus stalks, having fallen from the midst of the weight of her breasts, why do you wither?
There is not even space for one of your fine fibers there; how much less could there be for you?
— Śrī Harṣa.
The lotus garland placed upon her body to soothe the intense heat [of love] shines like a polished sword-blade wielded by the five-arrowed god [Kāma], who has released his shafts. (13) By Devagupta.
Her limbs are withered like crushed lotus stalks, yet through the entreaties of her attendants she somehow manages to perform her daily duties; moreover,
she bears the beauty of the stainless moon.
The cheek is as fair as a freshly cut tusk of an elephant—
thus [it was said] by Bhavabhūti.
The interior of the breasts of the beloved wife of the lover is drying up from the fire of passion.
With all its legs firmly stuck in the thick paste of fresh sandalwood,
this bee is seen submerged with its wings spread above, appearing like the remaining shaft of an arrow of the God of Love plunged into a flower.
Having discharged every weapon at the very first attempt, he again made an effort to slay the helpless woman.
Alas! That very body of the Flower-armed God became at that time both his single target and his quiver;
this broad lotus leaf remained upon his chest.
She does not describe her internal state, arising from the god of love,
as clearly as she reveals it through the two circular depressions on her breasts, which have been withered by excessive torment.
Faded on both sides from contact with her full breasts and hips, yet remaining green in the center of her waist because it had not reached that area;
this garment is now disarrayed by the tossing and turning of her limp, vine-like arms.
The bed of lotus leaves speaks of the fever of the slender-limbed one.
These two verses belong to Śrī Harṣa:
"When this tear falls from her eye, even upon reaching the young woman’s cheek, it finds its way onto her jar-like breast."
Furthermore, the orb of the hips, possessing its appropriate grace,
makes even calamity a source of pleasure for those who are naturally pure;
so it was said by someone.
The tears that were restrained by the slender-limbed maiden in the presence of her elders have flowed inward; with them, the fire of love born of separation has been drenched.
I believe that this [tear] which has emerged from her face is the very flame of that fire now casting forth its rays.
A column of smoke, appearing under the guise of the line of bees drawn by her sighs and exertion; (20) Amaruka’s.
Her fever of separation is not to be tested by the touch of the palm of the hand.
Even as her circle of affectionate friends, out of fear, prepared a cooling bath with water,
all the gems of her pearl necklace burst forth with a crackling sound like parched grain, for they rendered powerless the application of sandalwood paste and medicinal herbs.
The musk-paste design on Rājaśekhara’s face, which she wears as if weary,
seems like a heavy burden upon her broad chest where the thick sandalwood paste has fallen.
How great, alas, is the cruelty of the Creator, that upon her— who already bears her very limbs with extreme longing through sheer exhaustion— he has placed yet another heavy burden of grief! (22)
— By Śrī Bhānuṣeṇa.
The innocent girl, having welcomed the touch of her beloved's hand when he appeared in a dream by means of her creeper-like body bristling with horripilation,
suddenly cried out repeatedly to the empty air in anger, "Do not touch me, my dear!"
She was laughed at by her friend and repeatedly made to grieve with anxiety; on the contrary,
she did not participate in this festival of Rudra, which is like a festival of the god of love.
"Daughter, you must remain here now without food; let something be placed in your mouth.
When the old woman had spoken thus, the traveler’s wife somehow managed to swallow a morsel as the day drew to a close, while her tears washed it away like a stream of water.
O friends, my day has come to rest, made resonant by the manifold songs of the cuckoos; now I am free from fear, so cast away all doubt regarding my life.
At the end of the day, alas, as she spoke as if her fear had vanished, the evening—
terrible to the moonlight-lotuses— struck her down into a swoon.
(From the *Sūktisahasra*)
"Quickly take up residence in the underground chamber; why do you play with your life?
O cursed woman, do you not see the moonlight that has entered through the lattice window?
Thus did the fair-browed women in their homes, afflicted by the intense fever of love, speak.
The distressed voices of my friends emerge like the cries of deer out of fear of the moon;
O brother Bilhaṇa, O traveler, have you encountered any other wayfarer on the road?
"O child, describe what my beloved is like—he who, when seen, causes the eyes of women like you to expand with joy.
Having thus informed the traveler, "He is to be known as my beloved," she fell into a swoon. (27)
Having been entreated by someone, the Goddess herself, the Blessed One, approached their residence with humble salutation; she appeared there separately from them,
and even the life-restoring words that indicated the imminent reunion with their beloved were recited.
From a thousand fine sayings.
Thus ends the section on the description of the states of a woman separated from her lover, in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
That you make your moon-like face half-bowed as if eager for conversation;
that you place the bolts of your vine-like arms upon the slope of your breasts as if out of fear of being discovered;
and that you are everywhere agitated by suspicion, wondering what these people might be whispering.
That is known: some youth, mature and hidden, dwells within your heart.
For Bilhaṇa’s face has become pale as a ripened palm leaf, and there is a gloom in his eyes.
Since this boil has transferred its five fingers through your service to Pāṇini,
let Gaurī be angry if no young man dwells within your heart;
fie, fie on you, that even in the world of childhood friends who played in the dust, you practiced such concealment!
Abstention from food, complete withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects, the fixing of the eyes upon the tip of the nose, that which is the one-pointedness of the mind,
this silence, and this entire universe you describe as empty— [all these are but the preliminary stages].
"O friend, tell me, are you a yoginī, or are you a woman separated from her lover?"—
thus [he asks] Rājaśekhara,
with glances that are languidly turned, moist with the tenderness of love, and repeatedly half-closed like buds.

O charming girl, tell me, who is this fortunate man that you gaze upon today with eyes that for a moment are turned toward him, trembling with modesty, then averted by winking, as if vomiting forth the very intention of their heart?
Amaruka’s [verse]:

With her face blooming, the slopes of her breasts glistening, her creeper-like brows quivering and wandering, her slender body drenched with drops of perspiration, and her modesty slipping away, she was possessed of horripilation.
"O charming one, some fortunate youth must exist whose face is now being graced by your glances, which resemble the mass of foam from the great ocean of milk."—

Even though you have practiced walking upon the surface of your hips, this gait of yours is languid with perspiration;

by means of that, I shall be able to behold the ten directions marked with the seal of her face.
— Rājaśekhara.

That torment is cruel; that creeper-like body, so beautiful with its blossoms, has become a source of immense fear from the rival [lover], accompanied by shame. Alas, how could she not lose her life? Or rather, let it be—peace!—for she is my beloved.
Fate will surely behold here the marvel of Śiva’s craftsmanship;
though the heart of the joy of his lineage bursts with intense agitation, it does not split in two.
The impaired body carries on, yet it does not release its consciousness;
the internal burning inflames the frame, yet it does not reduce it to ashes; fate strikes, cutting through the vital organs, yet it does not sever life itself.
He is indeed beyond all determination and outside the range of words— he who has not entered the path of experience in this birth,
yet whose dense thicket of great delusion has increased through the destruction of discernment.
Some inexplicable transformation within both causes them to feel dull and yet produces heat.
These two were born by the divine Sun from Yamunā, who was made hot by Gaṅgā— thus says Bhavabhūti.

May the waves of the river of the lord of the Malaya mountains— whose waters were once boiled by the flames of the fire from the eye upon the crest of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva)— come together and remain before me for my service, flowing through hundreds of mouths of sandalwood trees. 41.
Let the Snowy Mountain be hurled quickly upon your breast for the sake of coolness;
or rather, let it remain, for it would surely melt away until nothing but stone remains.
Abandoning the salt water of the ocean, [let us instead seek] those filled with the waters of the Ganges.
May the waters of the clouds quickly become a cloak for my body!
If these rays of the moon are indeed Bilhaṇa’s hands dripping with nectar, why then does my mind [not turn toward them]? Why my sight? [42]

Corrupted by dwelling amidst the masses of Kālakūṭa poison, do they not consume my life-breaths? Or rather, am I protected by the syllables of the mantra that is the thought of my beloved? Alas, alas! I fall into a swoon; I do not know what this state of affairs is. 43
If the moon of the illustrious Abhinavagupta were itself a pool of nectar, and if its spot were a forest of blooming blue lotuses;
Then, perhaps with my limbs rendered numb by the sport of bathing, I might at last escape the torment of the fire of love.
(Rājaśekhara)
Thus ends the section on the Lamentations of the Separated, within the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Ārohaka Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
When her friends began to relate your story, O fortunate one, in order to secretly discern the cause of her feverish passion for love—
Ah, she speaks with her back arched, the tips of her full breasts thrust upward, and her arms encircled by bracelets, as she stretches her limbs with graceful, languid movements.
By whom? By some [man].
Do not go, O lover of women, for you have been entreated by me with hundreds of sweet words; yet this young girl will fall into a most wretched state when you have reached the courtyard.
Moreover, what will she do with her limbs, which are afflicted by the god of love and intent on pressing against the jars of her breasts?
Our house, its lattices of curtains daily falling away and becoming threadbare,
repeatedly prevents the deer-eyed Morikā from going out from the courtyard due to her shyness.
With a meaningful faltering of her voice and a play of graceful gestures, she cannot say how much;
a flood of tears does not permit her to look at you as you pass on your way.
O fortunate one, her involuntary physical reactions (*sāttvika-bhāvas*) become her attendants whenever they behold you.
She is broken by the forceful breaths of Hari-Hara; she is exhausted by the warm tears from his eyes; and she withers, pressed down by his palm which sheds drops of perspiration.
Having perceived this, O friend, she— with her face turned aside, her eyes cast obliquely, and her hand thrust far away— sprinkles your play-vine.
(4) By Ratnacandra.
With her hair standing on end from the gentle breeze coming from your country,
with her gaze captivated by a beautiful picture-board inscribed with your form,
and with the hollows of her ears sprinkled by the nectar of your name at the window facing your path—
Day and night he remains with his voice low, filled with the singing of the fifth note;
on the body of Trivikrama is the fire of the fever of love, and in his eye is the mudrā of meditation.
Her life-breath resides in her throat, her cheek rests long upon the sprout-like hand,
her braid lies upon her shoulder, sandalwood paste is on the region of her breasts, and silence dwells in her speech;
thus everything remains as it was, yet her heart is nowhere except with you.
While this moon,
anointed with the splendor of a vast pool of sandalwood paste,
was anointing the circle of the quarters, the merit of that deer-eyed woman [shone forth].

Tears in your eyes, your face in your hand, your life-breaths in the hollow of your throat, you yourself in your heart, shame on your back, and only your virtues in your speech—such is your state, O King Śekhara. 7. Rājaśekhara.
In her breath there is heaviness; in her mouth, palms, and cheeks there is paleness;
on her speech there is a seal of silence; in her eyes a flood of tears; and in her body the onset of a burning fever.
This much has been told of that slender-limbed woman which exists in her heart; what more remains?
Do you not know, O fortunate one, that her noble conduct there is praiseworthy?
She, with her lip bitten, wipes away the moon— the delight of her lineage— painted there with sandalwood paste.
O fortunate one, since she plucks the clusters of flowers— saying, as it were, that Kāma has flower-arrows—
and since she reviles the adorable God of Love by repeatedly snapping the fingers of her hand, it is clear, O handsome one, that this fair-limbed woman has learned the nature of a madman through you.
While this moon, the delighter of the world, with its serene luster and the brilliance of a blossoming kunda flower,
has ascended the eastern sky, you have gone far away from your own beloved.
Her breath acts like a night-lily bud, her face acts like a lotus,
her passion acts like the ocean of milk, and even her glance instantly acts like the moonlight. (10)
— Bhīmaṭa.
O fortunate one, if that young woman dwells within your heart— which is as firm as a diamond—
then it is indeed well for her as she is being struck by the arrows of Love.
O fortunate one, as she remembers those amorous gestures of yours again and again, [she suffers].
Her gaze became for a moment one of startled alarm, for a moment blossoming with joy, and for a moment mingled with tears.
[These two verses belong to Śrī Vaidya Bhānupāṇḍita:
"Unfold them! Tear them with your nails! They are blowing; cover them with the hem of your silken garment!"

"O handsome one, in your absence, her friends resort to the pleasure-grove, frightening [the birds] with the tinkling of their bracelets; thus do they converse among themselves in secret signs with the *vañjula* trees, the southern breeze, and the cuckoos.
(13) By someone.
The young cuckoo awaits the splendor of those with long, dangling locks; the swarm of bees obstructs the beauty of the mango buds and proclaims their good fortune.
But what more shall I say? O merciless one, her condition has reached such a state.
Just as a cruel spring breeze desires to blow away even one’s sighs,
she casts upon the flower-gathering women a glance that bears a trace of the graceful movements she has studied from Paraśurāma.
Caitra asks the astrologers with great care for an auspicious moment;
he delights in the cry of the cuckoo and, out of anger, abandons his pet parrots.
O Niḥśoka, since you are so difficult to obtain, what else can that wretched woman do? 15.
Free from passion, she does not even look at her own face in a mirror before the moon;
terrified even by the warbling of the cuckoo, she does not release her own voice;
yet it is a marvel that she maintains hatred even for the flower-armed god, who inflicts unbearable burning.
O fortunate one, that innocent girl cherishes ever-increasing love for you at every step.
Listen, O fortunate one, to this marvel concerning that fawn-eyed maiden who has grown thin from the wound inflicted by the sharp point of the arrows of Love.
Out of fear of the unprecedented, the pet deer flees from her;
even the birds of the domestic garden offer no consolation throughout the entire world.
Having accepted the betel-roll with great difficulty at the words of her attendants, she—
O fortunate one, she remembers you within her heart even though the night has passed;
her hand remains just as it was, grasping the sprout of the betel-creeper, and her mouth remains just as it was, accustomed to the row of areca nuts.
An intense and indescribable fever born of separation from you is manifesting in that fair-limbed one;
what more can we say, O fortunate one? Out of curiosity, let your retinue be allowed to see her!
For she has placed the remainder [of her message] upon her neck with a voice faltering from agitation, while her friends look on.
All the qualities of the fair-limbed one— the friend of the heat of passion— have been abandoned;
for while one fainting fit fades away, another arises, so that there was some indescribable state between these two throughout the entire night, O fortunate one.
As she was writing a love letter to you there with flowers as arrows,
even the first portion of the word "Svasti" (well-being) did not reach completion. (20) —
These are by Bilhaṇa.
When you were meditated upon by the Creator, he strung his bow;
when your pair of fingers approached to take up the bowstring, the arrows were fixed to it;
and as your act of painting began, they were greatly distressed by the discharge of weapons from the bow.
Clinging swiftly to the wall, she remains there for a long time like a painting, O pitiless one;
for she considers you, the Lord of Siṃhala, to be standing before her, transformed by her steady internal contemplation.
Just as the charming girl eagerly began to embrace him up to her armlets,
she suddenly clung to her own body; seeing her thus afflicted by pain, I believe even the clouds wept under the guise of rainwater.
O fortunate one, having imagined you through her thoughts, she, with her hair standing on end,
embraces herself with a pair of arms that move as if in an empty embrace;
moreover, after a long time, she attains a swoon that soothes the pain of separation.
She revives by the syllables of the mantra of your name falling upon the root of her ear—
she who repeatedly casts her gaze, bright with favor when it falls on "you," yet languid with grief when it encounters a person appearing at the gateway, saying "It is not you."
Arising from joy and distress, occurring at every moment like a fever of sweat and heat,
these drops of tears nourish and wither upon the slope of her breasts.
(24) By whomsoever [these were composed].
O cruel one, I shall tell you how to remove her torment:
place a fresh lotus petal upon the chest of that lotus-eyed woman whose heart is aflame;
first it withers, then it shrivels, and finally it turns to dust.
Afterwards, becoming like a flickering ember, it burns her friend who is shaken by her sighs.
Moving from the house to the courtyard, and from the courtyard outside to the exterior, and back again to the house—
if that fair-faced one herself understands her distress, what more need we say?
Even your couch, made auspicious by contact with her limbs, was turned into a circle of rain-showers by the streams of perspiration from her as she rolled about upon it again and again.
You have always remained in the heart of that beloved, which is perpetually scorched by the mass of flames from the fire of separation.
O merciful one, that young woman truly does not dwell even for a moment in your heart, which is like a spray of frost.
Alas, with bowed head, I beg you for this alms from my friend;
if there is no love, then at least show a tiny drop of compassion.
That state of hers is composed of her own good deeds; what else could it be?
Is it a resting place in delusion, or perhaps death itself that serves as its remedy? (28) — by some [poets].
She has shed unrestrained tears for her kinsmen, placed her distress upon her friends,
cast her wretchedness entirely upon her attendants, and entrusted her anxieties to her elders;
yet she will surely find relief today or tomorrow— alas, she is now tormented only by her sighs.
Be confident; the sorrow born of separation has been shared by her.
When the day of the appointed deadline arrived, Amaruka watched for a moment at the window of the path leading to you.
Having approached again and again, that merciless one deliberated for some time;
and only this very moment, having tearfully informed her friends of the playful cries of the young Madhavi, she performed the piteous ceremony of taking the hand of the mango tree as her husband.
O playful one, while you were seated in the midst of your residence, someone else,
having brought his house to a state of blazing heat, followed a few steps toward it.
Thinking "the wind blows swiftly within Marutta," did that lamp of yours not go out by that thought, even though there were a hundred doors?
(31) [O you who possess a lamp as your wealth.]
That slender woman, lying for your sake beneath the dense foliage in the house of assignation, does not perceive even the coiled serpent within her bed as a pillow;
for she is lured by the fragrance of her own breath mingling with the scent of flowers falling from her braided hair.
Even he, experiencing the playful touch of sandalwood paste for a long time, remained motionless.
O Lord, what can we say of her audacity in coming to meet you at night— she who fears even a snake carved in a painting?
As she went along in the darkness, the innocent girl, out of fear of revealing herself, very stealthily placed her hand upon the serpent’s hood on the path to block its gaze.
These two [verses] are by Hari and Hara.
Thus ends the "Messenger's Speech" in the section on Separation within the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.

A cool breeze, carrying the first spray of water from the clouds, blew before her; sent by her beloved, it brought consolation to her emaciated body, as if to the earth exhausted by the scorching heat of the intense summer sun.
Her message was delivered while she was overwhelmed by prostrations from her friends as well;
it was conveyed with hair disheveled and used as ear-ornaments— hair remaining only from the binding of her braid—
and placed upon her jar-like breasts which were heated by the flow of warm tears.
Embraced by the reddened eyes from incessant weeping, was that letter praised? What could she not have done that was unworthy of her love, which had transcended all bounds?
Unrolling the letter herself, her fingers were as if covered with the sweat of joy.
Seeing the sequence of letters in that [letter] rendered indistinct and blurred by the sprinkling of water, she weeps, crying:
"What is this? Now I am truly ruined; alas, such was my condition! This is the tear; alas, this is the trembling of the hand! || 3 ||
"Does no tear arise for him? Does his hand not tremble at the sight of the letter? Do you know how his heart is now so utterly devoted to you?
Having spoken thus to her, the friend took the letter from her palm.
A certain woman of bold speech, out of curiosity, gradually recites:
"Having heard from the mouth of the letter-carrier that my path is free from danger, that the outcome of my undertaking will be auspicious, and that my return is now very near..."
"Remain at ease; remember again that state of exhaustion previously described by me, O proud one. Let there not be a festival for our enemies.
From these verses, [the play] *Śṛṅgāra-kiṃnara* is a nāṭaka.

Having departed from my side and gone far away, you wept for a long time with an unrestrained throat; then, wiping your eyes, you prostrated yourself with your slender body trembling. O beloved, as for what you said to me when the darkness was thickened by the swelling mass of clouds at the end of an aeon: [The remainder of the verse follows: "In that time, I remained here, having abandoned all fear, intent on protecting your life. (Note: This is a translation of the first half-verse and the introductory context of the second half-verse from the *Meghadūta*, specifically the "Pūrvamegha" section.)
Even a Kāpālika wanders away from home at this time; this pains my heart.
Where can my eyes find rest, being intoxicated by drinking the nectar of your form?
And from where could there be anything worth hearing for my ears, which are intent on the task of listening to your words?
"How can we endure with these limbs, which possess the intense joy of your embrace?
Alas! Through separation from you, we have now fallen into a miserable state.
(7) These two [verses] belong to some [unknown author].
That blue lotus which was submerged in the water, possessing a luster equal to your eyes, has vanished;
O beloved, the moon that imitated the radiance of your face is hidden by clouds;
and those royal swans whose gait mimicked yours have also departed.
"Even a mere diversion consisting of your likeness is not tolerated by fate for me. (8) [From] Śrī Yaśovarman:
"With my limbs constantly and densely bristling with horripilation from the chanting of your virtues..."
O beloved, with our minds fixed solely on beholding the moon of your face, we dwell in happiness;
yet, as my body is enveloped by the fierce flames of fire arising from separation from you, please, out of compassion, dispatch the cloud of news regarding your own lotus-feet to bring me relief. 9.
"How can these nights of three watches, so long in their divisions, be shortened as if into a single moment?
And how might even the day have its heat become faint and slow in every circumstance?
Thus, O lady with tremulous eyes, my heart harbors a prayer that is difficult to attain.
It has been rendered defenseless by the intense fevers of the agony of separation from you.
Knowing me to be well from this gift of a token of recognition, O dark-eyed one, do not become distrustful of me because of public rumor.
They say that all forms of affection perish when there is separation, for they vanish through lack of union;
yet, when directed toward a beloved object, those whose essence has increased become a mass of love.
(11) These two verses are by Kālidāsa.
Thus ends the section on "Messages from Separated Lovers" in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa:
The messenger, having been questioned, related in due order and without artifice the entire account of her beloved from the day of his departure, as it unfolded for that deer-eyed woman.
By describing her condition— and that of her circle of friends— as one overwhelmed by compassion, distress, and delusion, and as befitting the height of their love; and [describing] how,
among the pairs of trees and creepers closely entwined with one another, [she felt] a state of anxious longing.
For the most part casting his gaze, filled with tears, upon the play of pairs of birds; and beholding the deer near the vicinity of their beloved mates as if they were in a state of misery,
he proceeded along those paths that were fraught with the fear of piteous distress.

We ask: has your husband transcended all else—that he remains free from pain even amidst those various nights spent in the midst of moonlight, jasmine, and the gentle breeze fragrant with night-lotuses;

that he brings you before his mind’s eye through the path of thought; and that his delusion strikes at the heart-rending agony of your long wakefulness, which is so endless and most difficult to bear?
Among these, one thing is certain: he has lost his delight in the sport of striking elephants with their trunks against the riverbanks.
Seeing the elephant—who, despite his longing for a meal of young *lakī* shoots that do not even exist in thought—shedding profuse tears from his eyes, your beloved said:
"Oh, the ancient sin of ours must have been equal, O king of elephants! (4)
Listen further: during the final watch of the night, having somehow attained a little sleep through our merits, he asked, "O fair-limbed one, what is this?
Where is the end of these eyes of yours?"
Why does he, with arms outstretched, speak and attain awakening?
Because his heart is fixed upon the words and syllables of these thousands of well-spoken verses, and he is skilled in the contemplation of poetic figures and ornaments.
"O young woman, for your sake that youth has been utterly deprived of sleep, like a poet.

Thus ends the description of the state of the lover in separation, from the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa. "O messenger, have you gone? "I have gone, O fortunate one, to the presence of that amorous man."

"Did he do anything for a very long time after being seen? Did he engage in the pastime of playing the lute? Was he arrogant due to the rise of his good fortune? Did he say nothing, or did he fail to give an answer?
Was it out of pride, or was it because his voice was choked with tears? For that is indeed the deception of a rogue. (1)
"Tell me, O clever one, where was he seen, how, for how long, what was written by him, what did he say, and when will he come here?"—
thus were the elaborate inquiries fashioned by the outburst of manifold affection.

"Stories about one's dearest beloved do not go to ruin even when the subject is trivial. These two [verses] belong to certain [poets]. "Enough, enough with the name of that pitiless man! That very same story has returned; that time has passed again."
"Speak, speak! Even so, O messenger, your reply must be respected even by an enemy.
Thus ends the section on the heroine’s questions to the messenger in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.

O messenger, by this lover who is free from passion like a lower Buddha, the emptiness of all things has been declared to you without artifice. Your breast-slope is stripped of all sandalwood paste; your lip is rubbed bare of its redness.
Your eyes are far from kohl, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation.
O messenger who speaks falsely, you who do not understand the arrival of suffering for your own kin: you have gone from here to bathe in the pond, and not to the presence of that base man.
O messenger, by these two of yours— the lower lip possessing height and the arm oppressed by its curve—
my mind is agitated like the ocean by Mount Mandara with its red hue.
O messenger, what is the use of much speaking here regarding Viśalya? For the sake of accomplishing my purpose, even his own flesh was given; what then need be said of other things? 4.
Why does Vararuci’s breath come so quickly? Why is she thrilled with horripilation? Why has this favor been shown?
Her braid has become disheveled from falling at his feet, and her sash has slipped away from its place.
With a face moist with sweat from the distress of the heat, you are emaciated—what need is there for excessive words?
O messenger, what will you say of his lip, which bears the luster of a withered lotus?
(5) —By Śilābhaṭṭārikā.
O messenger, if your beloved did not come even after making such an oath,
why then did you, being so angry, bite your lower lip with your teeth? Abandon this trembling that causes drops of perspiration to fall, and resort to composure.

Who, being a friend to this world so crooked by nature, will know its inner intent? On another night, due to the reversals of sexual union with a group of rowdy youths, [I committed] what was improper.

How is it that this garment of mine, which was somehow stolen by that friend, has been recovered by you through the gift of your own clothing? O messenger, how can one so skilled in providing remedies for a slip be like you? 7.
Thus ends the mockery of the female messenger in the section on separation (*vipralambha*) within the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
In this regard, even the mere mention of the name "heroine" is heart-gladdening and agitates the mind;
how much more so the sight of her, whose eyebrows quiver with playful charm?
Let there be only the sight of Kāmandakī’s beloved; what is the use of other sights?
By that alone, even with a mind still possessed of passion, one attains liberation.
I think that when this woman of restless eyes has come within the range of vision,
the very arrows of the five-arrowed god (Kāma) become his own enemies.
These two [verses] belong to some [unknown] poets.
I believe that this moon-disk is the mass of honey which Viriñca squeezed out; from it flowed this stream of nectar.
It was by that [squeezing] that he fashioned its heat, hardness, mobility, and lack of fading.
The means for its manifestation was through lamps, jewels, lightning, and flowers.
By which gods, by which mountain, and from where did this new Lakṣmī arise from the churning of the ocean— she who consists of nectar and the digit of the moon?
Haste does not lead to the highest good for men; what is done today?
Hari seized this Śrī by force while she was unaware that she was about to depart. Alas! Out of delusion, he did not wait for even a short time for her to leave.
Smara stepped forward at the wedding, supported by Gaurī’s mother alone.
These [verses] are in the Pañcendulekhā meter,
composed by her whose eyes are as tremulous as the waves of the milk-ocean.
For even this essence-less saṃsāra appears as if it possessed an essence.
[She], who shakes lotuses playfully with her cheeks like the sky, speaks to us of her great partiality.
"Whose mind does she enter? She is like a royal swan depicted in a painting."—Śrī Harṣa.
"O, who is this at the window of the play-pavilion?"
The tinkling of her anklets awakens the flower-bowed god of love;
oh, how this pair of eyes shines, transcending the path of the ears!
How is it that Madana does not conquer the three worlds with his smiling face? 11
Standing before me with your face slightly turned, look, my friend; if you do not behold these, your eyes will surely remain full of sorrow.
Look toward these palace turrets, resonant with the tinkling of shimmering girdles.
"Who is this who, on the outer wall, adorns herself with the splendor of the moon?
O Bilhaṇa,
direct your eyes toward the top of the rampart and consider for a moment."
In the sky, what is this cool-rayed moon whose deer has vanished,
scattering its pure moonlight— which resembles the ripening of fresh *lavalī* fruit— pursued by the *cakra* birds of the garden who have filled their beaks with nectar? 13.
Even without a cloud, from the sky-surface smeared with intense radiance,
a streak of lightning— beautiful with its spread of golden luster— shines forth.
Even without the celestial Ganges, a forest of blooming blue lotuses quivers in the sky along with the frantic tumblings of leaping fish.
Nectar is indeed nectar, the moon is indeed the moon, and likewise, the lotus is indeed the lotus— [of Jayadeva].
Delight is indeed delight, love is indeed love, and honey is indeed honey;
thus, an object generally does not partake in the discourse of another.
Therefore, how can this woman possess a fortune that embodies all things? 15
A lotus in a place where there is no water;
a blue water-lily upon that lotus; these [lilies] upon a golden creeper; and she herself is so delicate and beautiful—what is this succession of portents? 16
What indeed is this other ocean of beauty belonging to Śrī Śaṅkara’s retinue? For here the blue lotuses float together with the moon;
here the temples of elephants emerge, and here there are other stalks of lotus stems and lotus fibers.
Above the two pillars of plantain, which are inverted upon two lotuses,
there is a surface of jeweled stone; beyond that, it is something truly inscrutable.
Then there are two jars, followed by lotus stalks and tender sprouts, and upon those, a water-lily with bees; what indeed is this? It belongs to someone. 18.
Of someone.
First there was a mass of darkness, followed by the full moon;
then a pair of cakravāka birds, and after that, nothing remained.
Then there was a whirlpool in waterless space, followed by a pair of plantain trunks.
Then, two lotuses facing downward— what a most wondrous arrangement!
I think this was long ago prefigured by Devabodha, as if by a crescent from the middle of the full moon.

With limbs of wondrous grace, this woman, whose form is distinct from all other creations of the Creator perfected through his vast learning, shines forth; even now, her lunar body appears as if the sky were being gazed upon through the openings of her apertures.
In this lake of Bilhaṇa’s, the water of loveliness is tossed by the waves of the folds of her belly, intent upon crossing the sandy bank of her hips.
I believe that the elephant of Love, with his manifest jar-like breasts submerged, has plunged into this lake whose moving eyes are the darting fish;
having crossed the pair of thighs with difficulty and wandered for a long time upon the region of her hips.
In the middle of her waist, which is uneven with the waves of the three folds, my gaze has become motionless; now, as if thirsty, having slowly ascended her lofty breasts,
it gazes repeatedly with longing at her eyes that drip with drops of water.
The eyes of Śrī Harṣa— eyelashes slightly smiling with the mingling of waves of bliss,
inclined toward the outpouring of love, softly opened, and possessing a glistening pupil.
This very eye of the fawn-eyed woman, with its creeper-like brow slightly arched from the habit of bearing the weight of inner thought, captivates the heart—so says someone. 23.
Kasyāpi.
In this world, there are indeed those victorious things— such as the crescent of the new moon and others— which are naturally sweet and delight the mind;
yet for me, it is she who has become the moonlight for my eyes in this world.
In this life, that alone is a great festival which falls within the range of one's eyes. (24) — Bhavabhūti. Thus ends the "Beholding of the Heroine."
Then,
having somehow overcome the restraint of her elders with great difficulty, a certain woman set out toward the place where the hero was;
alas, even the weight of her full breasts became a heavy obstacle to her swift movement.
One woman, prevented from going outside by her mother, approached the lattice of the palace to see her beloved;
in an instant, her eye was seen to resemble a minnow caught in a net set by a fisherman.
Another deer-eyed woman, having indeed finished her play with the ball, emerged from the courtyard with her body adorned with the dust raised by her brow.
Having sported for a long time in a forest of full-blown lotuses, she appears like the Goddess Lakṣmī, grey with the pollen of the filaments.
(27) These [verses] belong to the lover of metaphors (Utprekṣāvallabha). Thus ends the section on the glances of the heroine and the hero in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Śrī Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
