Through slender bodies, by the wise, and by those whose opportunities were well-timed, incomparable glories [were achieved].
These two verses belong to Vallabhadeva;
whatever man on earth acts with daring, even if his fortunes do not come to him by the power of fate—
Even though vast [misfortunes] may arise, alas, why indeed should his stainless fame ever be destroyed?
Heaven is his inner apartment; the city of the serpents (Pātāla) is his ground-floor room; the clouds are his ceiling;
the world is his dwelling; and the mountains are the pillars supporting his head.
The oceans leap over the continents like pleasure-pools—alas!—for one who possesses world-surpassing audacity and a treasury of incomparable prowess.
This earth has the ocean as its moat; it is so vast and without support.

This sky is indeed only so vast; yet the journey to the netherworld is difficult for those who love fame, until—having placed their feet upon the head of Fate that thwarts their exertions—their very lives are cast into the balance of uncertainty by heroes. 5.
To whomsoever these [verses belong].
Thus ends the Section on Boldness (*sāhasapaddhati*) in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
(115) The Section on the Description of Glory (*śrīvarṇanapaddhati*).
A person remains cool and gentle in touch toward both others and their own kin only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity,
just as frost remains cold until it is driven away by a wind.
One who possesses prosperity, yet is blameless among men, and who is brave without being boastful— [such a one is rare].
One with equal vision and a lord—these three persons are difficult to find.
From the Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa:
even the dull-witted become connoisseurs of the conduct of the wise through association with the illustrious.

It is the very intoxication of youth that teaches amorous gestures to passionate women. That Fortune should, by a mere chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, bestow her affection for even a moment upon one who lacks self-control— this is simply the fickleness inherent in her womanhood.
"Kṛṣṇa played with cows"—among those who have such a notion of him as being equal to cattle, Ravigupta’s Fortune is indeed partial;
oh, how devoted is that goddess! 5.
Fortune hates the vision that beholds the path of the righteous as if it were a rival wife;
without it, even powerful lords fall here and there like the blind.
This is the established order of the world: "This one is the master, this one is the servant."
In that regard, the fruit [of success] depends upon the grace or lack of grace of Śrī.
Among all the goddesses, Śrī is the supreme deity;
without her, the rites of worship and other such acts for them simply do not exist.
Among all women indeed, Śrī is truly the most fortunate,
for even the great desire her, despite her being one who acts according to her own will. It is surely a falsehood to say that there is nothing in this world dearer than one's own life.
For the sake of Lakṣmī, men count their very lives as mere straw.
(10) Cruelty, egoism, greed, harsh speech, and a fondness for base objects—these five are the companions of Fortune. (11)
The wise have rightly said that for one devoid of auspicious marks (lakṣaṇa), there is no Lakṣmī;
for what other mark could there be beyond the attainment of Lakṣmī herself?
O Moon, Horse, Nectar, Kālakūṭa, Wine, and Airāvata, listen!

I am not so much scorched by the submarine fire as I am by this daughter of Fortune— who daily and forcibly pursues the wicked and abandons the virtuous. Laziness attains stability, while fickleness assumes industriousness.
Folly spreads the quality of measured speech, and simplicity becomes straightforwardness; the mere lack of discrimination between the worthy and the unworthy leads to nobility of soul.
O Mother Lakṣmī, by the power of your grace, even faults become virtues. 14
That Fortune, who is worthy of being the refuge for all glories— possessing the quality of the rays of the lotus-like command—
is resplendent through her generosity like the form of a noble, auspicious elephant;
and that generosity increases incessantly with honor, like the new moon.

Pride is like a blade of grass that withers away slowly, its vigor fading through familiarity. Fortune creeps toward the lowly as if drawn by the waters of the ocean; yet, like a lotus plant whose feet are entangled with thorns, she places her foot nowhere else.
Furthermore, it swiftly drives away the consciousness of men, as if from the proximity of poison.
By enjoining the gift of the Dharma, this fruit of hers is to be accepted by those possessed of virtue.
Anger is established as "splendor," misconduct as "sport," deceit as "skill in worldly affairs," and ignorance as "purity. (16)

Salutations to that Fortune (Śrī) by whose power even a fault is designated as a virtue by the wise in the presence of the wealthy—on account of which they call "rudeness" the very act of speaking plainly.
One trembles before the harsh; one does not remain steady before the mild, out of fear of being treated with contempt.
She hates the fool and does not show affection even toward the most learned;
she fears those who are more heroic than heroes and mocks those who are utterly timid—alas, Fortune, like a courtesan who has gained her freedom, is exceedingly difficult to serve! 18.
Of Viśākhadeva. Thus ends the section on the Description of Glory and the section on Generosity in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Śrī Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa. (116)
Even piercing the earth, this jewel-sword ascends; even from the sky, clouds bowing down pour forth rain.
The giver of wealth consisting of the jewels of time and its primary qualities bears fruit according to one’s desire at the very moment it is wished for.
(Candragomin)
On the summit of Mount Meru, shattering with his chariot the jeweled stones fallen upon his path,

he destroys the dharma, fame, and happiness of women whose husbands are away as they set toward the sunset; yet when they have returned, O wonder, these noble wives of good family turn back [to their virtue]!
The excellence of the jar-like breasts of the Blessed Vyāsa, adorned with the ornament of fullness, possesses glances that are sweet with internal transformation.
The limbs of noble women, which betray their inner passion, cause distress even to the minds of those who are firm-souled—
those very limbs by which the lotus-face of a virtuous wife was kissed with downward, slow glances constrained by modesty.
How can they have any attachment for the mouths of courtesan-wives, whose lips have been wounded by the teeth of many men?
(3) There is no lineage higher than this, no character superior to this, and no field of action for the senses greater than this of the deer-eyed woman:
that she wiped away with her foot—placed upon her husband’s lap even though he was at fault—the single tear-drop from his eye. (4)
On the fourth day,
that which was brought forth by accumulations of merit, fully perfected and protected with effort,
becomes a refuge in prosperity and in adversity, as well as a treasure and a friend. (1)

For someone here, this [ascetic life] with its skull-bowl, water-pot, bark garments, white and red robes, and mass of matted hair— is the fulfillment of a vow undertaken for a purpose by those of radiant minds. II.2.
Sorrow should be recounted before that Vallabhadeva by a man beset with grief—
whether he be one who alleviates the sorrow or one who suffers along with him. (3)
Having disclosed one's sorrow to a master who recognizes merit, to a virtuous servant, to a well-behaved wife, or to a friend who does not seek personal gain, one becomes happy.
A foolish friend always deserves to be avoided; for while showing respect with his replies he causes shame, and while exalting one, he belittles them. || 5 ||
Preventing one from what is harmful, encouraging engagement in what is beneficial,
and not abandoning one in times of misfortune— this is the threefold characteristic of a friend.
To some of them these wives were shown; they ate in their homes without hesitation; secrets were told to them—what greater sign of friendship could there be? (7)

By whom was this jewel created— the two syllables "mitra" (friend)— which provides protection from the sorrow, distress, fear, and terror of the Blessed Vyāsa, and which is a vessel for joy and confidence? (8)
Because of its sweetness, extreme coolness, purity, and its ability to soothe the heat of thirst, milk is rightly called the supreme friend of water;
yet even there, a description of the ocean flashes before my mind, for it is by union with that [ocean] that milk increases.
For by that very [fault], the milk of his friend will first of all be consumed within the decoction itself. || 9 ||

Ah! To whomsoever these two may belong, some person enters the mind of someone else somewhere from somewhere, by some means, gradually, in the manner of the tiny insects within the fruit of the udumbara tree.
Even when this [body] is torn, split apart, burst open, mangled, crushed, completely dissolved, or shattered, will that [consciousness] emerge or not? || 10 ||
By Māhila. Thus ends the section on Friends in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
Let effort be directed toward virtues; what is the use of ostentation?
Those devoid of milk are not sold even with bells. || 1 ||
Behold the greatness of virtue: even a lotus born from the mud ascends to the crest of the peacock’s head; the mud is cleansed even by its foot. 2.
For in this world, someone attains renown through even a very small quality;
an elephant carries the world with a single trunk, but the sun does not do so even with a thousand.
(Prakāśavarṣa)
"O brother, show respect for virtue, never for wealth;
for those who possess virtue, wealth is easily obtained, whereas virtues are difficult for the wealthy to find.
Since virtues are to be achieved through effort, and that effort resides within oneself,"
Who could endure even while living the thought that another is the foremost among the virtuous?
(5) How could a hole ever arise in those who are flawless? That [hole] is produced by virtues alone, as in the case of a pearl. (6)
O brother, do not show disregard for virtues, even if you possess great fortune;
for by the loss of virtue, a jar—even if full—falls down into the well.
Just as a water-jar in a well sinks to the bottom when empty, so too one who is devoid of virtue sinks low, even if endowed with many qualities.
Behold, even though it is devoid of qualities, the water-carrier is borne upon the heads of people.
Those fortunate ones whose minds are not stained by the dust of worldly attributes sleep in happiness;
they have understood the true nature of exertion, even as children who do not yet know the letters of the script.

But for us, who behold the three worlds as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of our hand, this body of Śambhu is being carved away by these qualities—which are like wood-worms—just as a tree trunk is hollowed out by them.
Who knows the virtues placed in others? And even if someone knew them, who would speak of them?
Or rather, who indeed would not feel resentment when these things are clearly stated?
Or perhaps no one at all would feel resentment; yet if there were someone who rejoiced because of them, how could such a person, alas, be counted among mortals? (10)

How could there be any search for that serpent, who has submerged himself within the waters of the Kālindī, possessing a luster as dark as a split fragment of sapphire and resembling a mass of collyrium?
For his circle of hoods would not be visible were it not for the jewels upon them, shining with the brilliance of stars.
By the very same means through which the virtuous attain eminence, they likewise fall into calamity:
the lotus from the mud, the moon from the ocean, the blue lily from cow dung, fire from wood, the jewel from the hood of a serpent, and the yellow pigment (rocanā) from the bile of a cow.
Silk comes from a worm, gold from a stone, and even dūrvā grass from the hair of a cow;
those possessed of virtues attain prominence through the manifestation of their own qualities, not by virtue of their birth.
Those virtues which, like a single kākiṇī coin, find refuge only in the hollow of a beggar’s bowl wandering among the great coins, do not receive their due recognition.
Having gained the friendship of the lotus-hands of those skilled weavers and craftsmen, they entice even kings.
To whom does this belong? Thus ends the section on Qualities (*guṇapaddhati*) in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Bhagadatta Jalhaṇadeva.
Even if it is lowly, one should live by manifesting that fraction [of virtue] by which one lives;
one who conducts himself according to the standard of the virtuous is not mocked by buffoons.
A single fraction of dharma is superior.
Even in a temple made of stone, it is said that a single stone is a deity;
by the very greatness of its merit, even among inert things, the bearer of the inert is worthy of worship.
— Ādityabhaṭṭa.
When even a single day has passed devoid of dharma,
one’s heart burns for a long time, like that of a man robbed by bandits.
Even with a mind occupied by other affairs, dharma must be practiced continuously.
For even a bull, though bound by a yoke, will graze upon a patch of grass while wandering;
likewise, hospitality is a duty even toward an enemy who has come to one's home.
A tree does not withdraw its shade even from one who has come to cut it down.
The merit of the Blessed Vyāsa is not diminished by the waters of the four oceans, which surge forth unrestrainedly at the time of universal dissolution.
They fall upon the edges of swords and enter the ocean;
what hardship do men seeking wealth not endure in this world?
This alone is the power here.
"O Goddess Tṛṣṇā, salutations to you! You take delight in four places:
among those afflicted by disease, those without offspring, among ascetics, and among the aged.
— Bhaṭṭadeva Viḍaṅga.
This pit of craving is bottomless and difficult to fill; by whom can it be filled?
Even when great things are thrown into it, it is merely dug deeper by those very fillings.
There is no acquisition of what has not been done, and no destruction of what has been done.
All at once, O Thirst, this world has been enslaved by you.
The constant rising of the mind, when restrained by hopelessness,
is impossible to fill even with tens of millions of cosmic eggs through the touch of desires.
Even though his throat was scarred by the blows from the staffs of the gatekeepers of the blessed Vyāsa,
he nevertheless continues to serve him; oh, how great is the power of craving!
Like a *piśācī* demoness, it enters within; like a shadow, it does not move away.
Like a courtesan, it causes one's hopes to wander; like a maiden, it rains down sorrow.
Even a barren woman maintains hope for a son, and even a greedy man, intent on wealth, maintains hope.
Afflicted by separation, one perceives hope in all things, yet hope knows nothing of propriety.
For whom does the creeper of craving—nourished by the support of hope—not produce the fruit of worldly objects? (Kṣemendra)
Day after day, the sun, having acquired a taste for it, consumes Pisces, Aries, and Taurus;
while those blessed ones dwelling in the interior of mountain caves meditate upon the supreme light of the ocean of jewels.
Birds sit fearlessly upon our laps and drink the tears of joy from our eyes;
yet for us, our supreme lifespan is spent merely in the play of pleasure gardens, ponds, and palaces constructed by the whims of our own desires. (Bhartṛhari)
If eloquent men, out of wretchedness, speak falsely even with untruthful qualities while praising the king without weariness,
that indeed must be the entire power of craving; otherwise, it would not be so.
Even for those who are effortless, the Lord is an object of contempt like a blade of grass;
yet even thirst seeks its fruit at the feet of Viśākhadeva, though they are unassailable.
The restless monkey of craving does not remain in one place for long;
even when its mind is not restrained, it surely runs toward everything. Yet craving obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman seeking a lover.
In this world, craving— like a night of black darkness— terrifies even the steadfast, blinds even the keen-eyed, and exhausts even the peaceful mind.
In one moment it descends to the underworld, and in another it ascends to the vault of heaven.

Craving, like a female bee, for a moment wanders through the bowers of the quarters, hovering over the lotus of the heart. Like the rays of the sun upon a lotus, craving— a woman afflicted by disease— quickly makes even a deep mind shallow.
O Brahmin, neither the edge of a sword, nor the flame of a thunderbolt, nor the sparks of glowing iron are so sharp as this craving that resides within the heart. (Vāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa)
Oh, how difficult it is that those whose intellects are purified by the discernment of self-knowledge renounce even wealth that provides enjoyment, being entirely free from desire;
for such wealth was not acquired in the past, is not possessed now, nor is there any firm certainty of its acquisition in the future.
We are not even able to renounce those things which consist of mere desire;
yet a man might desire that by which no one else exists.
Then, when asked by one seeking further wealth, what answer would you give?

"This is obtainable, this is obtainable, and more than that is obtainable; from that, its root is obtainable, and yet another is obtainable"—alas, you contemplate wealth as something to be obtained incessantly!
"You do not know of rebirth; however, before long, the demoness of hope will forcibly devour all this world, which is shrouded in the darkness of great greed.
— Kṛṣṇamiśra.
They wander through difficult forests, traverse formidable foreign lands, plunge into the depths of the ocean, practice agriculture with great hardship,
and serve others.
Five things arise and perish simultaneously for a poor man who lives off others:
debt, misfortune, laziness, hunger, and a large family.
Of Hemacandrasūri:
"What indeed could be more grievous than even the miseries in the hells—that which a base person is unable to do for the sake of pleasing one who is dear? (2)

Due to the misfortune of the people in this world, when they beg from the blessed Vyāsa, even the great oceans become mere pools in the summer heat, the mountains lose their status as trees with climbing vines, and even wish-fulfilling gems turn into common clods of earth.

O King, at this moment our two dwellings are equal: the home of the scholar Śrīharṣa, with its vessels of abundant gold and all its attendants adorned, and yours, dense with sporting female elephants. (4)
Wandering through Janasthāna with a mind blinded by the golden mirage, I have uttered to every person the tearful lamentation, "O Vaidehī!"
I have performed the composition of verses for the faces of the Lord of Laṅkā;
I have attained the state of being Rāma, yet I have not obtained the status of having Kuśa and Lava as sons. || 5 ||
"This is the deserted village of Bhaṭṭa Vācaspati; here before me lies this ruined temple; the pond is dried up, and yonder tree has its branches withered."
And we, these travelers whose fortunes have reached a state of utter emaciation— this common bond, though bitter, delights my heart.
There is but one fault in those who possess forgiveness; a second does not exist:
that people consider such a person, because of his forgiveness, to be weak.
This world belongs to the forgiving, and the next world likewise belongs to the forgiving.
In this world they deserve honor, and in the next, a favorable rebirth.
These two [verses] belong to the venerable Vyāsa;
for those ascetics whose wealth is their austerity, the power of their spiritual practice is supreme among all forms of strength.
The torrential stream of malice and violence brings misfortune both in this life and the next, whereas patience is the pacification of such calamity.
If people find satisfaction through my censure, then surely this is a favor to me, bestowed without any effort on my part.

For men seeking their own welfare abandon even wealth acquired through hardship for the sake of securing the favor of others. (4) If I were not to exist, these people, being without refuge, would fall into wicked thoughts;
therefore, it is surely a source of shame for me alone that I should personally incur the sin of associating faults with others. (5)
Just as I strive for the attainment of what is dear to myself, so too [should I strive] for others, and especially so;
for if they were to obtain what is undesirable to me, how could they not act toward their own self-interest?
These two [verses] belong to the *Jñānāṅkuśa*.
He who, being powerless, constantly practices patience even toward a person who is his enemy, is certainly like a serpent deprived of its fangs;
for it is the powerful man who, when capable, practices forbearance here in this world, and thus he is one of virtuous conduct.
That radiant one, desiring to conquer both worlds, is victorious.
[Colophon: Thus ends the section on Forgiveness (*kṣamāpaddhati*) in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa, [a work] of the teacher Kṣemasiṃha.

May compassion alone be extended toward all living beings; for what is the use of those various undertakings of austerity? [Compassion] is the playground of merit, a whirlwind that sweeps away the dust of misdeeds, a boat for the ocean of existence, a mass of clouds for the fire of calamities, a messenger for the meeting with glories, a ladder to the dwellers of heaven, a dear friend of liberation, and a bolt against miserable rebirths.
If a pressing-stone were to float upon the water, if a ship were to be launched toward the west, if the seven-flamed fire should somehow attain coldness,
or if the surface of the earth were to rise above the entire world; [only then might this be possible].
Even that which brings forth living beings is nowhere considered a slaughter; rather, it is a virtuous act.
Such are the speech, soft as butter, and the heart, tender with compassion, of the venerable Soma-prabha-sūri.
This is the definition of direct perception for those whose [minds] proceed from a single seed.
Kṣemendra should first cultivate equanimity toward self and others with such reverence as this:
All beings, being equal in their experience of suffering and happiness, are to be protected by me as I am myself.
(4) The suffering of another must be dispelled because it is suffering, just like my own suffering;
likewise, others too are to be favored by me because they are sentient beings, just like my own self. (5)
From the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*:
For a noble person of pure soul in this world, compassion and truth are indeed ornaments.
Those who have compassion for living beings are humans; those who are merciless, they know them here to be serpents. (6)
Truthful speech is not truth, nor is untruthful speech falsehood;
that which is ultimately for the welfare of living beings is truth, and the other is falsehood.
Giving to all sentient beings and compassion toward all beings—[these are the highest forms of virtue].
For even a single gift that excels all others is superior to the giving away of all sentient beings.
Generosity leads the poor to heaven; forbearance, the powerful; austerity, the young; silence, those possessed of knowledge;
the cessation of desire, those accustomed to pleasure; and compassion toward living beings leads them to heaven.
To whom do these [verses] belong?
Thus ends the section on Compassion (*dayāpaddhati*) in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.
For whom is dispassion (*vairāgya*) not dear, if detachment (*virāga*) arises?
For a hunchback, lying on one's back in comfort is indeed not fitting.
If you have been deprived by the unaccumulated riches of Kṣemendra, which are appropriate for the upliftment of the destitute;
That enemy who holds you back has departed for the forest to practice asceticism.
Vallabhadeva says:
"I am alone; no one belongs to me, nor do I belong to anyone else."
I do not see anyone for whom I do not exist, nor anyone who does not belong to me.
Through thousands of previous births there has been separation and union,
yet even so, my heart remains pitiless and still longs for the company of the beloved.
Who could feel affection for things that are impermanent,
when one may not see a beloved again for thousands of lifetimes?
Whatever object is experienced becomes a subject of memory.
Everything has passed away like an experience in a dream; one does not strive for it again.
Many have been gainers, and many have been famous;
yet, along with their gains and fame, they are no longer known—where have they gone? (6–7)
Even for this single body, the fragments of bone born with it will go their separate ways; how much more so for another, beloved person?
In childhood there is no capacity for earning, by which one might be happy in youth.
Youth passes away through its own acquisition; what can an old man do with sensual desires?
(9) What has happened to the body if the sandalwood is fragrant?
Why should one be attached elsewhere because of a fragrance belonging to another? (10)
Whether lying here on my bed or standing in the midst of kinsmen,
I must alone endure the agony of the severing of my vital organs.
When Impermanence first embraces the newborn, it takes him into its lap.
Then, like a nurse or a mother, what exhaustion could there be from grief? (12) If ignorance were not the cause, and separation were the cause, [of Śrī Harṣa’s state].
As the days pass by, does sorrow ever cease for those who remain?
From here comes death, from here disease, from here calamity, and from here old age— [all] belonging to Kṛṣṇamiśra.
The impermanence that destroys the world possesses four factors of equal strength.
This is the time for the Blessed One Vyasa, [just as it is] for the falling mosquitoes, gnats, and flies.
Having become a great tree arising from the udumbara-fruit of the universe,
some crow of Time has surely built its nest upon your head.
That which shines under the guise of grey hair is the whiteness of his excrement;
it is my conviction that this old man is surely pervaded by the moon,
for its web of rays gleams upon his body in the form of grey hair.
Having observed the head-gourd of the venerable scholar Vaidyabhānu, now withered and grey with the salt of old age, Time indeed— the Lord— consumes it. 17
Let incapacity, distress, and misfortune remain within the inner apartments of this body, which is white as a plaster of lime; let the women dwell there in comfort.
Adversities come for but a moment, and prosperity likewise lasts for but a moment.

O Sage, birth and death occur in a mere moment; how then can anything else not be a moment? It would be as reasonable to attempt to bind the wind or to shatter space as it is to have any reliance on the body, for it is impossible to string together the waves.
When the entire host of enemies has been put to flight and prosperity has gathered from all sides,
one may enjoy these pleasures for as long as they last, yet death arrives from somewhere or other.
It is like the rush of the Ganges water splashing against the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks.
O Sage, that very same breast of a woman which was once seen in the cremation ground and at the edge of the horizon, radiant with the splendor of a pearl necklace,
is now being devoured by dogs like a small morsel of food at the appointed time.

For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, wandering in the mud of the mind, woman is the line of evil tendencies and the baited hook. He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one who is without a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment?
Having abandoned a woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy. Poison is the imbalance of the sense-objects; poison is not called true poison.
Sense-objects destroy future lives, whereas poison destroys only a single body.

From the Vāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa: [He beheld] a woman with disheveled hair, intoxicated by the drinking of wine, laughing with her throaty voice like a cuckoo, and biting with her teeth and scratching with her nails [her lover].
"How is it that these men do not tremble at night upon seeing this girl with her neck covered in gaping wounds, drinking fat, marrow, and honey-liquor, like a female demon?
— Bhāskaravarman.
By those whose path this earth has been adorned through sacrifices,
and by whom, having conquered this circle of worlds, gifts were bestowed upon the twice-born;
[all else in] this worldly existence is but the play of a cluster of bubbles shimmering upon a lake.
Having seen them again and again, even they have suddenly fallen once more into dissolution.
Here, the vulture of anger displays its own wing;
here, this jackal of craving runs ahead with its mouth wide open.
From here, cruel desire wanders like a piśāca for a long time;
alas, this saṃsāra is a cremation ground—what person who has fallen into it can remain here in happiness?
Having realized that life is as fragile as the breaking of water-waves, one should dwell in ease.
Those by whom wealth is constantly regarded as perishable like a dream yet remains attached to enjoyments;

those by whom women—who resemble pillars of clouds—are embraced with love under the thought that youth is fleeting; it is by those very same people that one is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence, while by them alone is the common man bound. 45.
Hope for stability has been fixed upon the moon reflected in water, restless with waves;
a dream that perishes in an instant has been imagined to be long-lasting and indestructible— this while [the world] is as flickering as the tip of a banner struck by the wind.
Attachment to the body brings about the destruction of the supreme human goal.
By whom have the splendors of kingship not been enjoyed—those whose feet are worshipped by the crowns of gods?
And who has not been reduced to worms by the millions, putrefying within the belly of hell?
Thus, although the highest degree of both pleasure and pain has been reached, nevertheless, the hearts of those whose minds are shrouded by ignorance do not turn away from everything.
Let that intellect go to destruction; let even a thunderbolt be hurled at it.
Let your virtues enter the fire, terrible with its flames, leaping forward— those virtues which,
though as pure as the autumnal moon or the kunda flower,
bring about once again the agony of dwelling within the womb of a woman, that very hell. 48.
In some empty dwelling of the Wielder of the Trident, having attained a state of tranquility, you— some blessed person— sat upon the uneven ground; then,
from your own cave, [a serpent] emerged over your body as your mind remained motionless in meditation.
Wandering about, the serpents form a dense couch-like posture.
These ten belong to Indrakavi;
this is Guha’s own [abode], this is the foot of a tree, and these are the stone slabs on the riverbank.

Even for one dwelling in the forest, this attachment arising from the notion of relationship is a cause for bondage to worldly existence. (50) Is not a beautiful palace roof suitable for dwelling? Are songs and the like not pleasant to hear?
And is not the joy of union with one as dear as life not supreme in bringing delight?
But having perceived that everything is as flickering as the shadow of a flame trembling in the wind from a moth falling in its confusion, the wise have departed for the forest.

(51) "The arrival of flowers has come with blossoming blooms; this autumn, adorned by the moon, has arrived"—at this, people indeed rejoice greatly. Yet, my mind does not fall into despair at the thought, "My life is now exhausted. (52)

The feet of Candragomin have been worshipped here by me, the son of Dharmarāja, along with Bhīma; and here too were recounted the stories of Arjuna and the twins who followed him. Indeed, those places are truly sacred; they are not mere mortals. 53
Where there were many, in some house, there now remains but one;
and where there was but one, thereafter there are many, yet at the end, not even one remains.
Thus, these two—night and day—are like two eyes, swinging back and forth.
Time indeed plays for a long time with Kālī, using living beings as its dice.
Something belonging to the moon is being produced, yet something else perishes as soon as it has been produced.

Just as a dry vessel perishes immediately upon being placed on the fire before it is fully cooked, so too do these living beings perish in this world after reaching various stages such as birth; indeed, there is no certainty whatsoever regarding the timing of death. 55
"Today this, tomorrow that, and next year this, and the year after that that"—
O man, how can your mind be thus constantly and undisturbedly occupied with such thoughts? For at that very moment, the forest fire of the wilderness of your desires is blazing forth.
O friend, there is still some moment when you will remember the Wielder of the Staff (Yama).
O Death, release me; O Old Age, do not seize me harshly by the hair with your hand!
For Passion and the rest stand as my guarantors against fleeing from this cycle of existence.
Do you not know that this world is being bound by the bonds of craving?
Will I not come at your respectful invitation, "Come here"?
Even that which is clustered with musk and other perfumes becomes foul-smelling from afar. 57.

The end of those who here daily inflict harm upon Dharma has been seen—either as a swarm of worms or as a heap of ashes. O friend, why this delusion of yours? For what is this body that you thus protect through the deception of others? 58

Even that Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the three worlds, who became a lion in order to slay with his claw-like thunderbolts the arrogant lord of the Dānavas— who was intent on his own self-interest— out of partiality for the gods whose heads were bowed in supplication for their own welfare; he too is present here.
Whose state would not be that of a beast whose mind is obstructed by passion and hatred?
(59) What authority is there for the body to remain beyond the present moment?
Nevertheless, alas, one’s anxiety for life extends even unto the end of an aeon! (60)
Life-breaths have exhalation as their limit, and that exhalation is but wind.
There is nothing more unstable than wind; that which continues to breathe is truly a marvel.
(61) [This is] of some [authors].
One considers that the state of the wind within the many cavities of the body is manifold;
yet even so, those with deluded hearts do not, by any means, reflect upon its departure. (62) — Vallabhadeva’s commentary.
Whether by night or by day, whether old or a child,
he travels alone and unobserved upon that path whose true nature has departed;
yet he carries as his provisions for the journey the great merit of virtuous deeds, which remains untouched by the fatigue of worldly existence.
Alas, as it passes away, the world falls into manifold grief!
O Vaidyabhānu Paṇḍita, what welfare can be asked of those embodied beings who have fallen into this cycle of existence?
Once one has fallen into the mass of fire, what question can there be as to whether one is burned or not?
(64) Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, finds delight, that very thing, having become a thousandfold suffering, stands before it. (65)
These two verses belong to the Blessed Vyāsa;
they are like a goldsmith’s scales for that wise man whose intellect has attained a state of equanimity between stone and gold.
Even when one's wealth is exhausted, it can be brought back again by means of the body;
but once the body is exhausted, wealth is unable to bring it back.
When will the wind of discernment, arriving as an aid, cause our lamp to blaze forth?
The fire of dispassion consumes the fuel of play with the objects of the senses in their manifold varieties;
upon the surface of the mirror of knowledge, which has attained incomparable purity through its cleansing by that fire, the lords of yogis perpetually behold their own singular Self. (68)
These heaps of gold, glowing like lamps, were bestowed by Mdaṇa upon supplicants;
and in debate, the words of the elephants among disputants— proud of their mastery of the scriptures— were refuted.
One must play with kings like dice—uprooting and replanting them—if it is the will of fate that this be done; even in that regard, we are ready.
(Vikramāditya)
The speech of those with deer-like eyes is refined when mingled in the assemblies of the virtuous;
their conduct consists of humility and lack of pride, and they have no fear even of the crooked Fate.
(70) — Vallabhadeva’s.
O brother, if you desire to wander upon the path to the eternal city, then provide yourself with every means of protection by donning the armor of self-restraint;
otherwise, the thieves of the senses will forcibly pierce your mind with hundreds of sharp-pointed, flashing spears of intense anxiety, and the jewel of discernment will be snatched away from you.
When someone’s mouth is parched with thirst, he drinks sweet and fragrant water;
when afflicted by hunger, he devours grains of rice mixed with morsels of meat.
While the fire of passion blazes, people embrace their beloveds more firmly; they mistake the remedy for a disease and perceive it as pleasure.
(72) — Bhaṭṭa Jayanta.
Not knowing it was a trap for moths, the moth falls into that fire; alas, not knowing it, even the fish swallows the baited hook.
For we here, though fully aware, are entangled in the snare of calamities.
We do not renounce our desires—alas, how profound is the power of delusion! (73) By Gobhaṭṭa [Bhartṛhari].
Thus ends the section on Dispassion in the *Sūktimuktāvalī* composed by Śrī Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa.

The Goddess of Speech, intoxicated by aesthetic flavor, praises Śiva despite her greatness being unknown; for where can women find restraint regarding propriety when they are overcome by an excess of passion? (1)
O all-pervading Mahādeva, though my mind may wander here and there due to its fickle nature, where will it go if it leaves you? II.2.

If I am incapable of being a subject for Your praise, what of it? For even the Lotus-born Brahmā was likewise submerged in the ocean; what difference is there between a particle of clay and the King of Mountains?
O Lord, even the Kālakūṭa poison resting in the hollow of Your throat is for me a great nectar;
yet the nectar itself, if it were to exist as something distinct from Your body, would not please me. 4.
O Utpaladeva, even your mere mention does not remove my dust; do you not possess even brilliance, nor darkness?
You do not even behold the sun and moon; are you not even the wind that touches them?
How is it that even the earth does not support you, and why does even the sky not grant you space?
O sacrificer, why do you alone remain slow to bestow gifts out of compassion for the supreme among the gods?
5. For the best of the Maruts.
O Śiva, O Kinsman of the World, this path of Your sovereign power is unprecedented: for those who bow down with devotion to Your pair of feet,
it is not merely their evil that goes to destruction.
Everything, even that which was long-accumulated or well-performed in this very moment, dissolves away.
For some, sense objects do not appear for long even in dreams; they utterly collapse within.
Having somehow reached the vehicle, those who are incapable [of proceeding further] remain silent and suffer only great distress;
yet even they, swallowed up by the waves of your compassion, become perfected masters of knowledge (*vidyādhipa*).
Or rather, for whomsoever you are pleased, even a mere pillar becomes a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*). (7)
In some delightful region on the banks of a most holy river, those who worshipped you, O Destroyer of Smara, as you stood in the form of a *liṅga* along with their sons and others,
enjoyed the sport of swinging upon the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees on the shores of the celestial Gaṅgā.
These sky-dwellers sport, their creeper-like arms acting as bolts for the swinging ladders;
they play with their nails shattered by the intense friction against bodies bruised by date-palm branches—
those very beings by whom you, O Mahādeva, were once beheld even during the commission of a hundred sins through some chance encounter.
Those sky-dwellers sport in the heavens, their nails curved with the playful grace of scratching the dense, full breasts of celestial women who are languid from the juices of the mountain caves.
O beloved of Gaurī, destroyer of Kṛtānta, Lord of the World, embodiment of the three Vedas— human beings such as Brahmā and others are experts at meditating upon you for even a single moment.

How limited is our intellect, and even that is not free from impurity; therein lie waves of suffering. Who is capable of contemplating You? Indeed, we are not worthy of Your mere compassion. [For] the lord of a few cities is difficult to win over even at the cost of one's own body.
"Alas! Previously, I was led astray by delusion;
now, having regained through my intellect the Lord of the Three Worlds—who is worthy of worship and the bestower of his own station—I am tormented by the passing of that former day. (11)
O Destroyer of Tripura, from the manifestation of this very form of the resonance of the drum, it is inferred that in a previous birth you likely never bowed down to anyone at all.
O Great Lord, I am now free from pride and shall henceforth be without pride; therefore, may these two offenses of mine—offenses that are beautiful—be forgiven. 12.
Of the one whose offenses are beautiful.
Your own, your work, and all things such as juice, flowers, and fragrance— I offer them to you every day with devotion as my very own; yet,
though you are praised for that devotion and your deeds are well known, you do not acknowledge it.
"O Śiva, is that which is my ignorance actually your own straightforwardness?
O Mādhava, friend Sāraṅgadeva, O wise one, shall I tell you a certain secret?"
Having uttered a "hum" and become upright, the beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter, whose splendor is now dispersed,
may be deceived in this secluded place with two or three flowers of the arka or darbha grass;
thus we shall seize the royal fortune of the three worlds, whose feet are caressed by the crowns of the gods.

May there be auspiciousness for you from Mādhava’s smearing with ashes; may there be welfare from the rosary of Rudrākṣa beads; and oh, what joy from the succession of steps adorning the abode of the Beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter!
Today, by the Lord, who has been gratified by our worship, we are cast into the great delusion called liberation, which cuts off the vision of the happiness found in serving you.
[We shall receive] from someone else the dharma of one who wears the skull of Brahmā, and fill our bellies with alms-food.

Desiring the destruction of desire from the god of love, and the total eradication of worldly existence from existence itself, and the severing of hope from you who are intent on its destruction—I am driven mad by the rising of my longing for liberation.
O Hara, may you be gracious; you do not abandon even one who is insane.
O Lord whose head is graced by the dancing Gaṅgā, was there no offering for you from Umāpati Dhara, since his five morsels of food consisted of the five great elements fashioned from his own body?
What use are mantras to the Creator of Mantras, or what use are heaps of flowers to you, the Lord of the Sky?
Since there can be no worship of you in this manner, O Bhava, let the mere contemplation of you lead to the cessation of worldly existence.
(17) — Śrī Harṣa.
You yourself are Sthāṇu, Aparṇā is your beloved,
and your son is the famous Viśākha, O Three-eyed One;
yet even so, you remain without a shadow, along with your entire family.
It destroys the affliction of the threefold suffering for all worlds—
whether it belongs to me, O Lord, who am liberated like Jayadeva, or to one who is bound by a multitude of qualities.
Let your worship be like the employment of a heap of flowers;
let my sattva-guṇa, which I desire, fall before you, for it is dear to me as the dust from the trampling of your feet.
Since the other [rajas] is unseen and the tamas is already fashioned, O Lord, how could I pray for the destruction of the three guṇas? 19–20.
These two belong to both.
